items.author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
items.content:
On 29 October 2019, as many as 27 Members of the European Parliament, mostly from far-right parties, went on a pilgrimage to Indian-occupied Kashmir. The visit was an optical surgical strike against the unexpected perception of isolation enveloping New Delhi after the 5 August decision to revoke the territory's statehood and bifurcate it.
Unexpected, because every duck was supposed to be in a row. Pakistan was expected to shrug, reasoning that ending statehood did not alter the disputed status. A compliant international media, now influenced by Indian interests, was programmed to ignore it, while the foot traffic of world leaders would normalise the manoeuvre. Instead, Islamabad took a firm stand, pockets of Western media resistance fought back, diplomatic traffic halted, and the matter reached the UN Security Council. Desperate to manage optics, the Modi government flew in these MEPs, staging a global endorsement for domestic consumption.
But were these politicians duped patsies, or was their presence symptomatic of deeper ideological alignment? In 2019 and 2020, the EU DisinfoLab exposed the 'Indian Chronicles', revealing how the Delhi-based Srivastava Group used fake NGOs and resurrected dead experts to manipulate European politicians. Yet Modi's accession had rendered such outfits redundant. Why run a convoluted side hustle when mainstream global media and Indian civil society were already offering what Professor Timothy Snyder calls 'anticipatory obedience'? These far-right MEPs shared the BJP's pathological hostility towards Muslims, both capitalising on the war on terror's Islamophobia. Did a desperate Modi government seek help from ideological twins, then throw a redundant Srivastava Group under the bus to hide the true extent of this collusion?
Almost a year later, the FinCEN Files exposed a vast financial shadow economy, flagging 44 Indian banks for facilitating over 2,000 suspicious transactions. Between 2011 and 2017, they processed over $1 billion in flagged dark capital, much of it vanishing into shell networks. Crucially, that is the period that saw the revival and mainstreaming of the modern far-right, from the American Tea Party to ultra-nationalist European populists. The leaks hinted at a dark symbiosis. The dominant order manages such outbursts by misdirecting attention, so the world forgot the flagged Indian operations.
The symbiosis, one suspects, relies on a multi-phase playbook. The first phase was a massive intelligence and policy blind spot, engineered at the zenith of the Global War on Terror. Intellectuals like Samuel Huntington, platformed by editors like Fareed Zakaria, laid the theoretical timber by framing Islam and China as the world's inherent enemies. India positioned itself as the indispensable natural ally, securing sweeping concessions and elevating its elite into the West's highest echelons. By harvesting Israel's weapons-grade Islamophobia and the West's Sinophobia, India manufactured the blind spot for its domestic, regional and eventually global ambitions.
With international cover secured, the second phase normalised domestic extremism. The elevation of a leadership defined by the Gujarat riots, managed by a political enforcer who had faced tadipar (extirpation or exile) orders, signalled that secular moderation was over. The militant consolidation of the Hindu Right was mainstreamed, immune to Western censure because the West had locked itself into the GWOT blind spot.
The final phase of the Vishwa Guru project is reshaping the global order in India's image. By pitting the West against China and Islam, India makes itself diplomatically inevitable. It also dismantles the West's Enlightenment principles, Christian egalitarianism and human rights sensibilities by financing the rise of the Western far-right. As that far-right rejects egalitarianism, it retreats toward the "golden age" of pre-Christian paganism. India intercepts this retreat, appropriating global paganism under the banner of a shared "Indo-European legacy".
This osmosis is no accident; it realises a century-old blueprint. The project is fundamentally anti-Western and anti-Abrahamic, rejecting democratic equality for a rigid, birth-based order. VD Savarkar, architect of militant Hindutva, subordinated democratic principles to ancient hierarchical codes, declaring the Manusmriti "the scripture which is most worshippable after Vedas... even today it is the fundamental law of Hindus."
This reverence for caste over universal rights was globalised by Savitri Devi, born Maximiani Julia Portas. Disgusted by the egalitarian foundations of Judeo-Christianity, this European fascist relocated to India in 1932, convinced the caste system was the last living remnant of pure Aryan paganism. She left an indelible Nazi mark on the Hindu Right's formative years. In 1939 she met Savarkar, who backed her efforts to weaponise Hindu nationalism. She praised Hinduism because it "never admitted the absurd dogma of equality."
For today's Hindutva establishment, these are active operational directives. Devi's ideological virus remains potent, her texts hosted on platforms run by William Pierce, architect of The Turner Diaries. Backed by a rising economic state's processing power, this hatred of monotheism and equality escalates toward a global Brahmanic order designed to supersede Western democracy.
But what does this mean for Pakistan? The recent Shanghai Cooperation Organisation planning meetings in Islamabad gave a stark answer. In an exclusive PTV News interview during a rare visit, India's National Coordinator for the SCO, Alok Dimri, claimed that the SCO presidency had arrived in "our and the Persian civilisational neighbourhood". This was no gesture of inclusivity. By subsuming Islamabad into an Indian civilisational sphere on state television, New Delhi unveiled its own corollary to the Monroe Doctrine or the One China policy. After last year's May war, when India reacted with bitter tantrums to Pakistan's diplomatic attention, the establishment realised it needed a formalised doctrine of absolute subcontinental dominance.
For over a decade, the Modi government has strung the Pakistani establishment along with promises of a peaceful settlement, while investing in every conceivable Pakistani fault line to weaken the state from within. New Delhi has no genuine intention of making peace.
As the old adage warns: if the horse befriends the grass, what will it eat? To expect peaceful coexistence from a project built on hierarchical conquest is a fatal miscalculation. The diplomatic charm deployed in Islamabad is the anaesthetic for Akhand Bharat, a warning that the Vishwa Guru is no longer just consolidating its borders but executing its endgame.

items.title: 'NAZA' and a world in disorder
items.summary:
In his pithy but poignant commentary on the documentary film NAZA, British journalist Jonathan Cook identifies a malaise that helped lift Western civilisation to its current strength.
Today's Western privileges were built on a long history of naked, racist colonialism - greed, pillage, slavery and genocide - that we have never truly renounced or forsaken.

items.content:
In his pithy but poignant commentary on the documentary film NAZA, British journalist Jonathan Cook identifies a malaise that helped lift Western civilisation to its current strength.
Today's Western privileges were built on a long history of naked, racist colonialism - greed, pillage, slavery and genocide - that we have never truly renounced or forsaken.
NAZA is not just about Israel and Gaza. It is about the evil lurking in us all, says Cook, in a bitter reminder of the conflicts, land grabs and democratic repression taking place across the world.
What Cook points to is a world in disorder, propped up by a new form of colonialism: bigger powers relying on smaller, amenable states to pursue their objectives while practically ignoring the rule of law and human rights.
One wonders if the turmoil following the imposition of Governor's Rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa is also a manifestation of this global disorder and quest for absolute power.
The 48-member Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC), comprising tribal elders from 12 districts for looking after the ex-FATA regions, recalls a proposal discussed in the 1990s to replace the existing FATA administrative arrangement with a tribal advisory council. The crucial difference is that the 2018 merger brought these areas under the provincial system, with courts, police and other civilian institutions. Whether the new council will work within that framework or gradually undermine it by restoring the influence of federally appointed or politically favoured tribal intermediaries.
The composition of the council has already raised doubts about its acceptability. Five nominated members – Shahabuddin Khan of Bajaur, Baz Muhammad Khan of Bannu, Maulana Misbahullah Dawar of North Waziristan, Maulana Saleh Shah of Upper South Waziristan and Malik Jamil of Lower South Waziristan – had refused to join or distanced themselves from the arrangement. Can the council members exercise authority over communities whose members have not elected its representatives?
The concern is that the council could become a buffer between the authorities and the population. Critics also fear that a council dominated by status-quo figures could facilitate a return to the old FATA system in practice, even if the formal structures of provincial government remain in place.
Will the council be able to oppose decisions that conflict with local interests, or will they serve as intermediaries for policies they cannot meaningfully influence? For some tribal elders, participation may carry the risk of alienation from their own communities.
There is also a wider regional dimension. The former FATA lies along the porous and sensitive Pakistan-Afghanistan frontier. Afghan objections to the Durand Line and the presence of militant groups on both sides of the border complicate security and governance. Calls for a return to the previous administrative arrangement have therefore been viewed by some observers in the context of regional political and security calculations. Suspicions have also surfaced whether the system responds to specific demand by the Haqqani network or the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)?
As for tackling terrorism, the military has for years played a leading role in border security, intelligence-based operations and counterterrorism, alongside the police and the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD). The relevant question is, what will change under the new arrangement? Will it improve coordination among civilian authorities, security agencies and local communities or will the council create another administrative layer without resolving the underlying problems?
Another reality facing Pakistan is that the TTP and the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP) operate through different organisational structures, although both pose serious security threats, presumably with the same objectives.
Neither the creation of an advisory council nor the appointment of tribal elders can, by itself, dismantle these networks which the authorities claim are foreign proxies.
Residents of Waziristan, Bajaur, Kurram and Khyber have reason to ask why militant violence continues despite the substantial presence of security forces. They also question how some militants appear able to move across the border or travel within the region despite repeated assurances about security arrangements.
Locals in these regions also point to another factor – the American quest for critical minerals. Since these areas possess a number of minerals and rare earth, they fear that the political changes are only meant to extract natural resources with the help of status-quo tribal elders. The former tribal districts contain mineral resources that could generate revenue and employment, but the distribution of benefits has long been contentious. Some residents suspect that the new council could facilitate resource extraction while keeping local communities at a distance from decisions about licences, royalties, ownership and environmental safeguards.
The central issue is therefore not simply whether Governor's Rule is lawful or whether an advisory council can be established. It is whether the new arrangement strengthens representative government or replaces it with indirect control over natural resources of the region. A council that lacks public confidence may become another source of friction rather than a means of stabilisation – unlikely to deliver lasting peace and meet public aspirations.
The people of the former tribal districts have already experienced major changes in their administrative status, repeated security operations and prolonged instability. They need functioning courts, accountable policing, representative local government, security from militant violence and a fair share of the region's resources.
Ultimately, three questions remain unanswered. Will the council strengthen the political and constitutional integration achieved in 2018, or weaken it in practice? Will it help reduce militancy through public cooperation and accountable civilian institutions, or merely add another layer of administration? And will the region's mineral wealth benefit its people, or deepen their distrust of the state? Until the authorities provide clear answers, doubts about the purpose and legitimacy of the new arrangement are likely to persist.

items.author: Yumna Zahid Ali
items.content:
Karachi is a beautiful city with one small problem: everything here tests your patience as if patience were a compulsory subject in the CSS examination. You leave home to reach somewhere in thirty minutes and return with a new personality, three emotional problems, and enough anger to write a letter to the United Nations. Actually, scratch that…the UN should write a letter to Karachi asking what on earth is happening here.
And if you think the city is testing your patience, wait until you see what it has done to the roads.
For starters, why does every road look as if it has survived a war nobody told us about? One moment you are sitting peacefully in your car, and the next moment your head hits the roof because your tyre has discovered a pothole the size of a swimming pool. Honestly, driving in Karachi has reached a stage where I do not need Google Maps to find my destination. I need a satellite to warn me about the next hole trying to swallow my car.
The potholes, however, are not the only obstacle. The speed breakers then enter the picture. I don't understand why there are so many speed breakers? Is the city trying to stop speeding, or is it trying to stop people from reaching their destinations altogether? Some roads have so many bumps that your car starts feeling like a washing machine on the spin cycle. You leave home with your bones in the correct places and arrive at work wondering whether your spine is still under warranty.
At this point, Karachi does not need a traffic police department. It needs a physiotherapy department at every signal. Yes! Speed breakers here are not speed breakers. They are spine breakers. I have started measuring distance not in kilometres but in the number of times my head hits the roof. Oh, you live ten bumps away from me? Nice, we're practically neighbours.
In fact, I don't even bother asking for directions anymore. I just ask, "How many head injuries away is it?"
The person who invented speed breakers in Karachi deserves an award for "Most Creative Way to Torture the General Public Without Going to Jail". It's brilliant, really. Diabolical, but brilliant.
Then there is this road that gets repaired, dug up, repaired again, and dug up once more. What exactly are we searching for underneath? Gold? Oil? The remains of an ancient civilisation?
Of course, once you finally escape the roads, traffic welcomes you with open arms. Karachi traffic has its own rules and, apparently, nobody has read them. A car wants to go straight, a motorcycle wants to go diagonally, a bus wants to become a train, and a rickshaw believes it has a sab chalta hai licence. Everyone is in a hurry, but somehow nobody is moving. And then come the horns. Why does the person behind you keep honking when you are stuck behind another hundred vehicles? What exactly am I supposed to do? Grow wings? Fly over the car in front of me?
Well, the noise is only half the problem. Some drivers seem determined to attack your eyesight as well. Karachi apparently believes that if your ears have suffered enough, your eyes should not be left out. Yes, these are the people who drive with their high beams on at night. Why? Are you driving a car or landing an aeroplane? I am trying to get home, not apply for a pilot's licence. One look into the rear-view mirror and I can see my ancestors waving goodbye.
So in Karachi, Google Maps should stop saying, "You have arrived." It should say, "Congratulations. You survived."

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Companies change course in good times and bad. For Zetwerk, the key turn came after it raised $150 Mn from D1 Capital Part­ners in August 2021 when Indian startups raised a record $42 Bn in the calendar year.
And what began as a platform to connect manufacturers to vendors and suppliers, turned into a full stack manufacturing play on the back of a bevy of acquisitions in 2021 and 2022.
The company, founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan and Vishal Chaudhary, made its stock market debut today (Friday, October 23) with that full-stack promise at the centre of its pitch. No longer is this a marketplace, but a full-fledged platform that manages everything from procurement, supply, manufacturing, specifications and delivery.
While the listing itself was not at a massive premium like some other new-age tech stocks, that’s besides the point when looking at the business model and the sector.
The thesis around manufacturing remains strong for years to come as companies in key segments such as electric vehicles are looking to bring more of their component sourcing to India including in vital areas like precision machined parts. This was the opportunity that Zetwerk wanted to capture with its shift from marketplace to manufacturing.
In FY26, its revenue from operations rose 40.4% YoY to ₹15,913 Cr, from ₹11,331 Cr in the previous fiscal. Yet, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606 Cr from ₹371 Cr in FY25. This loss includes an exceptional charge of ₹836 Cr from continuing operations and a ₹453 Cr impairment related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business.
Those are the realities of working in the manufacturing space. Opportunities come and go and companies have to react in terms of pivoting their operations. The impairment itself is not a major number, but what could worry investors is that adjusted EBITDA stood at a mere ₹421 Cr, translating into a margin of just 2.65% against the revenue.
Plus, cash flows present another challenge. Zetwerk’s cash outflow from operations widened to ₹682 Cr in FY26 from ₹386 Cr a year earlier, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.4% to ₹12,370 Cr.
A larger order book offers revenue visibility, but fulfilling those orders requires the company to fund procurement, production and logistics, while managing payments to suppliers and collections from customers. Let’s dive deeper into this as this is what investors will look at.
The Two Revenue Pillars
Zetwerk operates through two main business segments: manufacturing and ecosystem. The latter operates under the Terra91 brand and supplies industrial raw materials such as steel, aluminium, copper, zinc, lead and bitumen.
The manufacturing business, which focuses on custom-made industrial products and related projects, is the largest of the two.
Together, the two businesses generated ₹15,913 Cr in revenue from continuing operations in FY26, up 40.4% YoY. Manufacturing accounted for ₹9,375 Cr, or 58.9% of revenue, while ecosystem contributed ₹6,539 Cr, or 41.1%.
Simply put, the manufacturing business earns revenue by working with third-party manufacturers and Zetwerk’s own facilities to fulfil orders across energy products, precision machined products and capital goods.
Its earnings depend on the price charged to customers relative to supplier payments, materials and fulfilment costs. More complex work, such as precision manufacturing requiring tight tolerances, can command a higher take rate than relatively less complex products.
Notably, Zetwerk doesn’t disclose these margins and fees as it is likely to depend on the product and client needs, since this is how the industry functions.
In an earlier Inc42 interview, cofounder and CEO Acharya said the company does not consider commission when accounting for revenue. He described the model instead as a take rate for services. He said rates vary across product categories depending on the complexity of the work.
The manufacturing segment reported a standalone EBITDA of ₹565 Cr in FY26, translating into a margin of 6.03%.
The other side is the ecosystem, which has grown considerably since 2022 as we indicated in the beginning.
Unlike manufacturing, where Zetwerk coordinates production, the ecosystem segment aggregates demand for industrial raw materials, procures them in bulk and resells them to customers.
Its economics are driven by the spread between procurement and selling prices, after accounting for logistics and other fulfillment costs. The segment’s Adjusted EBITDA stood at around ₹81 Cr, giving it a margin of approximately 1.24%.
The thin margin means that changes in commodity prices, sourcing costs or delivery expenses can have a significant impact on profitability, which we will see soon. Plus, the margin is considerably thinner than in manufacturing.
These segment-level margins offer a view of Zetwerk’s economics, but the company has not disclosed commission rates or order-level profitability.
Zetwerk’s revenue from operations includes the sale of products, income from construction and project contracts, sale of services and other operating revenue.
Product sales cover manufactured goods, products sourced from third-party suppliers and industrial raw materials sold through the ecosystem business. Construction and project contract income relates to projects involving broader execution responsibilities, while service revenue includes activities such as job work and related services.
Here’s the key difference from any other marketplace: Zetwerk acts as the principal in these transactions rather than simply connecting buyers and suppliers for a fee. It takes responsibility for sourcing, quality and delivery, meaning the revenue it reports reflects the value of goods and services sold, while procurement and fulfillment costs are recorded separately.
This is precisely the turn that Zetwerk’s 2021 fundraise and subsequent expansion allowed.
Zetwerk’s Big Opportunity
Having said that, as we mentioned in the beginning, the problem for the company is that it operates with razor thin margins. Even as the adjusted EBITDA margin has improved year-on-year, it’s still not quite robust enough.
Fulfilling industrial orders starts with a substantial procurement bill and procurement costs almost always escalate when there is a disparity in the order book. The key thing for Zetwerk will be to double down in one or two categories which will allow it to maximise the arbitrage revenue.
Economies of scale will drive arbitrage revenue in the manufacturing business, especially when Zetwerk owns and controls the procurement side of the business. So manufacturing cannot drive profits on its own and Zetwerk will have to flesh out both sides of the business at the same time.
Owning procurement removes third-party broker fees, distributor markups, and structural inefficiencies. The company captures the full margin that middle-men usually take.
Add to that, sourcing inputs from low-cost regions which allows you to absorb fixed costs of logistics, customs, and compliance.
And as the procurement side of the business scales up, Zetwerk will also have leverage for exclusive, long-term low-price contracts.
But it’s not a flick of the switch, buying in extreme bulk can exponentially increase warehousing, insurance, and inventory carrying costs. Moreover, commodity price volatility is another factor since companies can get locked in to massive forward contracts even as market price shifts. So any arbitrage advantage gets flipped here.
In FY26, the company spent ₹9,880 Cr on purchases of stock-in-trade and another ₹3,964 Cr on materials consumed, making these its two largest expense heads. Together, they accounted for nearly 86% of its total expenses of ₹16,142 Cr.
Purchases of stock-in-trade largely represent goods bought from suppliers and resold to customers. This expense head rose 45.3% YoY to ₹9,880 Cr in FY26 from ₹6,800 Cr in the previous fiscal.
The cost of materials consumed includes materials used in manufacturing and project contracts — which increased 31% YoY to ₹3,964 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹3,036 Cr. The two expense heads reflect the procurement-heavy nature of Zetwerk’s business, where revenue growth requires the company to source goods, materials and manufacturing capacity to meet customer orders.
Why Revenue Growth Is Not Translating Into Cash
Zetwerk’s cash flow numbers point to the pressure of achieving the balance between procurement and manufacturing. In FY26, its net cash outflow from operating activities widened to ₹682 Cr from ₹386 Cr in FY25, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.3% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹12,370 Cr.
A growing order book provides visibility into future business, but it does not immediately translate into cash in the bank. Zetwerk still needs to source materials, pay suppliers and coordinate production to fulfil orders, while customer payments may come in only after goods are delivered or project milestones are met.
This gap between spending on fulfillment and collecting revenue can tie up cash as the business expands.
The company’s procurement-heavy model means it’s particularly important that Zetwerk gets this balance right. As order volumes rise, the company may need to deploy more working capital to support the procurement, manufacturing and fulfillment needs, even if each order itself is profitable.
The challenge is therefore not simply to grow revenue or expand the order book, but to wring out inefficiencies in terms of arbitrage price, production bottlenecks and generally save costs through tech and AI.
This will help the company mitigate the risks of delayed cash inflows and receivables. In FY26, Zetwerk’s trade receivables increased by ₹336 Cr, while its other financial and current assets rose by ₹715 Cr.
Zetwerk’s ability to improve cash conversion will depend on how efficiently it manages inventory, supplier terms, production timelines, fulfillment and customer collections as it scales. Converting the order book pipeline into cash remains a big test of its business model.
Which is why Zetwerk is looking to capture more value by taking on design and engineering responsibilities, rather than simply manufacturing products to customer specifications.
Its original design manufacturing (ODM) contracts accounted for 13.93% of manufacturing gross merchandise value (GMV) in FY26. Such work can offer better margins because it involves design and co-development, while also making customer relationships harder to replace.
Zetwerk is also trying to balance its supplier network with greater control over complex manufacturing. It operated 26 manufacturing facilities across four countries as of June 2026, while continuing to rely on third-party manufacturers for most of its manufacturing business.
Products sourced from third-party suppliers accounted for 80.46% of manufacturing segment revenue in FY26, down from 96.51% in FY24. This suggests that Zetwerk is gradually reducing its dependence on external capacity, but has not moved away from the model that helped it scale without investing in every stage of production.
But is scale alone enough to improve profitability? And now as a public company, Zetwerk will have to answer this tricky question.
[Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam]

items.title: NCCIA rescues 13-year-old Karachi girl in probe into suspected dark web network
items.summary:
What began as an online interaction allegedly drew a 13-year-old girl into the orbit of a suspected dark web network, where children were reportedly assigned tasks and paid to produce pornographic animated content. A timely intervention by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has now brought the case to light, raising concerns about the online exploitation of minors.
The agency rescued the girl during a crackdown in Karachi's Rabia City, uncovering what investigators suspect is a wider network involving child exploitation and the production of pornographic cartoons. The probe has also revealed suspected links to individuals in Germany and the United Kingdom, according to NCCIA officials.
Investigators are examining whether children were deliberately targeted, manipulated and paid to carry out tasks as part of the alleged operation. Officials have also launched a probe into the possible use of so-called “red rooms” on the dark web to assign tasks to minors.
items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
What began as an online interaction allegedly drew a 13-year-old girl into the orbit of a suspected dark web network, where children were reportedly assigned tasks and paid to produce pornographic animated content. A timely intervention by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has now brought the case to light, raising concerns about the online exploitation of minors.
The agency rescued the girl during a crackdown in Karachi's Rabia City, uncovering what investigators suspect is a wider network involving child exploitation and the production of pornographic cartoons. The probe has also revealed suspected links to individuals in Germany and the United Kingdom, according to NCCIA officials.
Investigators are examining whether children were deliberately targeted, manipulated and paid to carry out tasks as part of the alleged operation. Officials have also launched a probe into the possible use of so-called “red rooms” on the dark web to assign tasks to minors.
Read: NCCIA arrests 4 suspects over child sexual abuse material trafficking in Islamabad
Speaking at a press conference, NCCIA Deputy Director Shehzad Akbar said the agency had acted on credible information about the suspected network. The girl’s father was informed, and the two devices used by the child were seized with his cooperation.
Akbar rejected suggestions that the initial task assigned to the girl involved killing a cat. He said, however, that the child was allegedly being subjected to psychological manipulation similar to tactics attributed to dark web groups operating internationally. Had the network not been exposed, the situation could have become more serious, he added.
The investigation is continuing to establish the role of suspected local handlers and identify other children who may have been targeted.
According to information shared by the officials, the wider case involves 42 suspects, including 12 juveniles. Investigators are examining evidence that children were allegedly paid to produce pornographic animated content, with some reportedly receiving around $100, described in the information provided as approximately Rs6,000.
The agency has seized 19 mobile phones from Pixel Craft, a company reportedly operating for around two years, five phones from Art Office and 17 from Art Design, which reportedly employed 17 people. Officials are investigating the companies’ possible links to the suspected network.
Akbar said a man identified as Fudan was allegedly operating the network. Preliminary findings also indicate that the companies provided logos, banners and other digital design services to foreign clients. Investigators are examining whether these businesses were connected to the alleged exploitation activities.
Also Read: NCCIA arrests accused in $126m US postal fraud
The deputy director said the agency had previously detained a boy in Karachi who was allegedly searching online for ways to take revenge on another person. In a separate case, the NCCIA arrested a suspect identified as Hamza on Thursday over alleged anti-state propaganda. Officials said the allegations were being investigated further.
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) Karachi Zone has arrested an absconding accused nominated in a case involving alleged unlawful social media activity. The arrest was made in Gulistan-e-Johar, Karachi, on the directions of DG NCCIA Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi.
The… pic.twitter.com/jG3zXygBRt
— NCCIA (@NCCIAOFFICIAL) October 23, 2026
Cybercrime crackdown
Akbar said the agency had recovered 39 accounts on WhatsApp, Instagram and other social media platforms over the past 15 days. It had also blocked 95 accounts allegedly linked to financial fraud and taken action against 38 accounts suspected of harassing women through fake identities.
The agency is pursuing cases involving the hacking of social media accounts, online financial fraud and harassment through fabricated identities. It has also received numerous complaints about the hacking of WhatsApp Business accounts.
Investigators are separately examining allegations that individuals have been operating social media accounts under women’s names and using fabricated identities to harass others.
The NCCIA said investigations into the suspected child exploitation network and other cybercrime cases were underway.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Streaming giant Netflix recorded its highest-ever quarterly paid net subscriber additions in India in the September quarter of 2026, crediting a strong local content slate and its first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart.
Revenue in India grew about 18% YoY on a foreign exchange-neutral basis, which excludes the impact of currency movements, Netflix said in its quarterly shareholder letter. Viewing hours rose 24% YoY, while viewing hours per member increased by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage.
Netflix did not disclose the number of paid net additions in India or how many came through the Flipkart partnership.
During its Q3 earnings call, co-CEO Greg Peters pointed to India as an example of how locally produced titles were translating into higher engagement, membership growth, and revenue.
Local Content Drives Engagement
Lock Upp, Netflix’s first daily reality series, recorded more viewing hours in India than any other title on the platform, measured over its first 91 days.
The scripted series Musafir Cafe recorded 9 Mn views, while Operation Safed Sagar clocked 11 Mn views.
The India performance formed part of broader growth across Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Peters said local titles in these regions were driving engagement and business growth.
He also said Netflix’s subscriber retention remained healthy across regions. Globally and in the US, churn – the rate at which subscribers leave the service – improved YoY in Q3 and was lower than the company had forecast.
Globally, Netflix reported revenue of $12.87 Bn in Q3 2026, up 12% YoY. Operating income rose 37% to $4.46 Bn, while its operating margin expanded to 34.6% from 28.2% a year earlier.
For 2026, Netflix expects revenue of $51.1 Bn, representing 13% YoY growth.
Neumann said membership growth, pricing, and advertising were expected to support strong revenue growth in 2027, although the company had yet to issue formal guidance for the year.
Netflix also plans to introduce its advertising-supported subscription tier in 15 additional countries in 2027, with the first launches scheduled for March.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The federal government has confirmed significant tax relief for imported mobile phones priced between $101 and $200, with the advance income tax reduced by nearly 89% and the mobile handset levy cut by more than 66%, according to a written reply submitted by the Finance Minister to the Senate.
The disclosed figures show that advance income tax for this handset price category has fallen from Rs. 930 to Rs. 100, a reduction of Rs. 830 per phone. Meanwhile, the mobile handset levy has been reduced from Rs. 600 to Rs. 200, providing additional relief of Rs. 400.
Combined, these two charges have fallen from Rs. 1,530 to Rs. 300, a reduction of Rs. 1,230 per imported handset in the specified price band.
The figures were reiterated in the Senate; the reply should not be read as announcing an entirely new round of tax cuts.
How Much Tax Has Been Reduced on Imported Mobile Phones?
The reductions concern two specific levies on imported mobile phones valued between $101 and $200 and do not apply across all handset price categories.

The written reply did not provide an estimate of the revenue impact or indicate whether the lower charges have translated into equivalent reductions in retail smartphone prices.
Sales Tax on Mobile Phones Remains Unchanged
Despite the reduction in these two levies, the government has not reported corresponding changes to the existing sales tax structure.
Imported mobile phones valued at up to $500 remain subject to 18% sales tax, while phones valued above $500 are subject to a 25% rate, according to the tax details supplied in the Senate reply. Locally supplied mobile phones remain subject to a general sales tax rate of 18%.
The reply also refers to a Rs. 250 sales tax on mobile SIM activation under the Ninth Schedule of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. However, the cited SIM-related provision ceased to apply from July 1, 2020, so it should not be described as a currently applicable charge without further legal clarification.
For consumers, the key distinction is that cuts to advance income tax and the mobile handset levy do not eliminate other applicable taxes, duties or charges. The final price of an imported phone will also depend on import costs, exchange rates and retailer pricing.
The Senate disclosure highlights targeted relief for lower-priced imported phones, but its practical benefit to buyers will depend on whether reduced charges are reflected in market prices.

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
US-based HR tech startup Firstwork has raised $15 Mn (over ₹142 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Earlybird Venture Capital, as it looks to expand its AI-led workforce automation platform across the US and Europe.
The round also saw participation from Legion VC and Deel Ventures, along with existing investors Gradient and Y Combinator. The latest fundraise takes Firstwork’s total funding to $20 Mn since its launch in 2024.
The San Francisco-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand its teams across applied AI, AI research, engineering and go-to-market functions. Important to highlight that about 80% of the startup’s workforce operates from Bengaluru.
It also plans to deepen its presence in the US and Europe and extend its AI agents to more workforce operations.
Founded by ex-Deel executives Vardhan Kapoor and Shubham Choudhary, Firstwork uses AI agents to automate HR operations pertaining to frontline workers. These include document verification, background and right-to-work checks, onboarding, training coordination, compliance management and worker follow-ups.
The startup’s platform integrates within existing HR systems, allowing employers to automate workflows without replacing their existing software.
According to Firstwork, more than 1.50 Lakh frontline workers start work through its platform every month. It claims that its platform has helped these customers cut the time spent by workers and HR teams on each new hire by up to 90%. Its clientele features the likes of Deel, Job&Talent, Relay, Wonolo and BGSF.
AI is seeing a broad band adoption in the human resource function and is rechanging the face of enterprise tech globally. While Firstwork is primarily targeting the global market, the Indian is projected to double in value to $2.3 Bn by 2033 from $1.12 Bn in 2024.
Leveraging AI, several Indian startups are building solutions to capture this booming market. For instance, Bengaluru-based Hunar.AI, which raised ₹40 Cr earlier this week, is using conversational AI agents to automate gig-worker hiring, onboarding, training and employee retention. Its clients include Swiggy, Zepto, Croma, Starbucks and Dr Lal PathLabs.
Hyderabad-based TurboHire also raised $6 Mn in a Series A round led by IvyCap Ventures in August 2025 to scale its agentic AI-based recruitment platform. Founded in 2019, the startup automates enterprise hiring workflows and claims to have onboarded more than 120 enterprises, including Cipla, Tata Motors, PwC, Lenskart and Britannia.
Other players operating in adjacent segments include TraqCheck, which offers AI-powered background verification and recruitment agents, and HireBound, which automates candidate sourcing, screening and evaluation, competes with Firstwork

items.title: The CFO Code: Perfios’ Prashant Mahagaonkar On Balancing Founder Ambition With Financial Discipline
items.summary:

items.author: Anirudh Trivedi
items.content:
Getting an acquisition across the finish line can take months of negotiations, due diligence, paperwork and financial scrutiny. But closing the deal is only half the battle. The real challenge comes when you integrate the business, unlock synergies, and deliver the value that justified the deal in the first place.
Much of this heavy lifting falls on CFOs, who are expected to go beyond balancing the books to evaluate acquisition targets, assess financial risks, structure deals and ensure the business derives long-term value from the transaction.
This is part of a broader shift in the CFO’s role, from financial oversight to strategic decision-making. Whether determining how to extract value from an acquisition or assessing if an investment in AI will deliver adequate returns, finance leaders are making critical capital-allocation decisions while ensuring the business stays on track to meet its growth ambitions.
At Perfios, a B2B SaaS fintech serving more than 1,000 financial institutions across multiple geographies, Group CFO Prashant Mahagaonkar sits at the heart of these decisions.
With more than 25 years of experience across traditional finance, multinational companies, M&A and venture-backed businesses, Mahagaonkar’s career has given him a front-row seat to the changing nature of the finance function.
For the concluding edition of The CFO Code series, Inc42 caught up with Mahagaonkar to discuss his experiences and learnings from decades of building finance systems, integrating acquisitions and working alongside founders and CEOs.
Speaking with Inc42, Mahagaonkar broke down how his role has evolved, what he has learnt from acquisitions, why CFOs need to question technology spending, and what he believes will define the next generation of finance leaders.
Walking The Tightrope Between Risk and Reward
Mahagaonkar’s career began in 1999 at Tata Motors, but he soon realised traditional audit and compliance work wasn’t where he wanted to build his career.
In 2022, Mahagaonkar joined Givaudan India, a Swiss flavour and fragrance major where he got his first real exposure to what a well-built financial system looked like. For Mahagaonkar, the experience became an education in how large organisations build systems and roll them out across markets.
Mahagaonkar then shifted to Essilor India, a spectacle lens manufacturing company, where he was exposed to acquisitions and moved from traditional finance to a more M&A- and business-oriented role.
He later joined venture-backed Amba Research, where he raised capital, worked with investors across geographies and eventually managed an exit. Moody’s acquired the company. Mahagaonkar moved to CitiusTech, where he became the company’s first CFO and worked closely with the founder-CEO to scale revenue from roughly $60 Mn to $500 Mn.
“Working with the founders to scale the team was a great learning experience for me. I realised how different a founder’s mindset is from that of a professional CEO. Their risk-taking appetite is very different, and they bring perspectives that a traditional professional may find difficult to act on,” said Mahagaonkar.
As Mahagaonkar puts it, the experience taught him how to keep the company business-friendly while also protecting it financially. According to him, while founders may be willing to offer more flexibility to win a customer, the finance leader’s job is to ensure the company is adequately protected.
“But the solution was not always to take the most conservative position. Instead, the finance team had to establish a playbook that clearly defined what it would agree to and where it would draw the line,” said Mahagaonkar.
He added that finding “the art of the possible” within an accepted compliance framework is one of the most important skills he has developed over time.
Making Acquisitions Work Beyond The Deal
Mahagaonkar’s M&A experience proved valuable when he joined Perfios in July 2025. By then, the company had completed three acquisitions, and his mandate was to integrate the acquired businesses into a cohesive organisation.
Perfios acquired an eFRM (Enterprise Fraud Risk Management) business, a segment it had not historically operated in. In another acquisition, it added a collections company, adjacent to its existing loan origination, approval, and credit underwriting businesses. Each acquisition required a different integration strategy.
Mahagaonkar shared that his task was to determine what should be fully integrated into Perfios, what should retain its independence and how each business could contribute to the broader ecosystem. All this had to be done while ensuring that every entity remained compliant with the applicable regulatory and reporting requirements.
Smaller companies often lack the same level of compliance infrastructure as a private equity-backed or larger organisation. “Therefore, the integration process involved bringing acquired businesses up to Perfios’ standards across areas such as information security, contracts, insurance, risk and statutory compliance,” the CFO said.
However, amid all the finance and integration of compliance functions, what generally gets understated and undermined is the integration of people and cultures.
Mahagaonkar argues that people integration is also a finance responsibility because acquisitions can easily leave redundant roles and overlapping functions in place.
“You need to put it together and be part of those discussions to help and make sure that we build that one organisation which is required,” he said.
AI Spend Under CFO’s Scanner
The expanding role of the CFO is particularly evident in capital allocation, where Mahagaonkar believes AI has fundamentally changed how technology investments are evaluated and prioritised.
“Today, product life cycles have shortened so much that companies may have just six months, rather than two years, to get ahead of competitors before they develop similar products,” he said.
For the CFO, this means asking harder questions about whether the company is deploying its capital into the right assets and whether its innovation engine is moving quickly enough to match the pace of competitors.
But in this chase, increasing AI spend may seem like the obvious choice for almost every problem, and Mahagaonkar believes companies need to look before they leap.
“Not every problem needs AI, particularly when a simple automation can do the job,” Mahagaonkar said.
At Perfios, the company has built an ROI matrix around its usage that monitors productivity gains, potential changes in hiring requirements and whether a particular use case should use AI at all, instead of automation or machine learning.
Becoming The CEO’s Co-Pilot
With the changing relationship between finance and technology, Mahagaonkar believes the CFO has moved from being a backroom player to becoming a co-pilot to the CEO or founder. He also mentioned that being a co-pilot to the CEO does not mean becoming the de facto CEO.
Mahagaonkar estimates that around 40% of a CFO’s decisions today require forward-looking judgement rather than relying solely on historical financial data.
When asked about the skill sets that will matter most for the next generation of CFOs, he said, “We must accept that today’s young people often know more than we do. They have greater access to information, and they can process and apply it much faster. The real test for the next generation of leaders, not just CFOs, will be managing such high-calibre talent, helping them find meaning in their work and creating an environment where they can succeed.”
According to Mahagaonkar, finance leaders of the past could succeed by knowing the numbers better than everyone else, but CFOs of the future will have to understand the numbers, the business, the technology and, increasingly, the people behind the decisions.
[Edited By Shishir Parasher]

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Update | October 23, 16:55 IST
Shares of Ola Electric ended the day 6.39% lower at ₹29.90 apiece on the BSE today, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,946.06 Cr ($1.58 Bn). The company’s shares are now trading 61% below its listing price of ₹76.
Original | October 23, 14:31 IST
Shares of electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric crashed as much as 7.6% to hit an intraday low about ₹29 on the BSE today (October 23) after a bearish outlook from Goldman Sachs.
A day after the company opened its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, Goldman Sachs downgraded its outlook on Ola Electric to “Sell”. The brokerage slashed the stock’s price target to ₹23.
It foresees a challenging path for Ola Electric to become cash flow positive given the relatively high interest cost and capex needs of the cell and E2W business.
It also cut the EV maker’s top line growth projections by up to 10% for the period FY27-29.
The bearish momentum comes a day after Ola Electric opened its rights issue for bidding. Within hours of opening the issue, Motilal Oswal and Calliope Capital Advisors applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by two promoter group entities — ANI Technologies and Indus Trust.
Founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the company’s proposed rights issue of up to ₹1,000 Cr.
Ola Electric plans to use the proceeds from its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue primarily to reduce debt and fund business expansion as it looks to strengthen its financial position and move towards cash-flow breakeven.
Of the total proceeds, ₹350 Cr has been earmarked for the repayment or prepayment of borrowings, including accrued interest and applicable penalties, while ₹400 Cr will be invested in organic growth across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses.
Ola Electric is yet to report its second quarter earnings results. As of Q1 FY27, the company trimmed its net loss by 22% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue declined 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26.
As of 13:52 IST, the stock was down 6.57% at ₹29.87 per share on the BSE, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,931.06 Cr ($1.57 Bn).
If losses hold, this would be the sixth straight session of the stock ending in red. In the past one month, the stock has lost over 20% in value.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Chennai-based dronetech startup Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹25.9 Cr in FY26, growing 41.1% from ₹18.4 Cr from the previous fiscal year.
In terms of operational profitability, the drone maker’s EBITA for the fiscal year jumped 31.8% to ₹35.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹26.6 Cr in the FY25.
Operating revenue surged 66.8% YoY to ₹206 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹123.5 Cr in the previous year. Sales of drones and drone parts brought in ₹99.4 Cr to the top line while the remaining ₹106.5 Cr via sale of services. Another ₹15 Lakh was earned from delivery charges.
Including other income of ₹26.5 Lakh, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹206.2 Cr.
“During the year, we continued to strengthen our manufacturing capabilities, expand our Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) operations, deepen our investment in indigenous research and development, and build strategic partnerships in India and international markets. We also advanced our capabilities in artificial intelligence, autonomous flight, data analytics, defence systems and specialised mission platforms,” cofounder and whole-time director Agnishwar Jayaprakash noted in a message to shareholders.
The improvement in the financial performance comes as Garuda’s proposed public listing plans take shape. The startup took the pre-filing route to confidentially submit its draft IPO papers with the SEBI earlier in April. The IPO was greenlit by the markets regulator in August.
While the startup is yet to file its updated DRHP for public access, its board approved plans to raise up to ₹750 Cr via the fresh issue component of the proposed IPO back in March. As per reports, the OFS component could result in investors offloading shares worth as much as ₹250 Cr.
In its annual report for FY26, the startup disclosed that its board of directors had approved a private placement of equity shares worth ₹57.2 Cr back in August. Investors who backed the startup were Umasankar Nistala, Rakesh Pillai, Jitendra Rana, Vimaan Innovators LLP and Aditum Management.
The proceeds of the issue would fuel business growth, working capital requirements, and be used for loan repayments.
The startup claims to have become India’s largest drone maker, having manufactured and sold over 3000 drones. It also claimed to be the first drone company to partner with three defence PSUs.
It has raised a total funding of over $37 Mn to date from investors like Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle, cricketer Mahendra Singh Dhoni, among others. It was last valued at $250 Mn after raising a $11 Mn Series B funding round led by Venture Catalysts.
Where Did Garuda Aerospace Spend In FY26?
Garuda Aerospace’s total expenses in FY26 rose 73.2% YoY to ₹172.2 Cr from ₹99.4 Cr in FY25. It reported no exceptional items during the fiscal but bore ₹8.2 Cr tax expenses.
Here are the main operational expenses of the startup:
Cost of Materials Consumed: Representing the largest operational expense, raw material costs surged 61.5% YoY to ₹116.8 Cr from ₹72.3 Cr in FY25.
Impairment Losses on Financial Assets: Impairment losses amounted to ₹11.1 Cr in FY26, compared to ₹6.5 Lakh in the year-ago period.
Employee Benefit Expenses: Garuda Aerospace’s personnel-related costs decreased 16.7% YoY to ₹8 Cr in FY26 from ₹9.6 Cr in the previous year.
Depreciation And Amortisation Expenses: The cost recorded under this line item increased 13.3% YoY to ₹4.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹3.6 Cr in FY25.
Other Expenses: Spending on items like professional expenses, travel, maintenance, rent, and other corporate overheads stayed nearly flat at ₹29.2 Cr.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Messaging platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram are reportedly set to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ (DoT) SIM-binding mandate from January 1, 2027, requiring their services to remain linked to the active SIM associated with a user’s registered mobile number.
According to a Times of India report, platforms must complete implementation by December 31, 2026, ahead of the reported operational start date the following day. The requirement could affect users who access messaging apps on phones without the associated SIM.
The mandate stems from directions issued by the DoT in November last year under the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024. The original directions named WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat, Arattai, ShareChat, Josh, and JioChat.
The department said some app-based communication services continued to function without the SIM associated with the registered mobile number being present in the device. According to the DoT, this allowed fraudsters operating from outside India to misuse Indian mobile numbers.
SIM binding requires covered services to remain continuously linked to the associated active SIM, rather than relying solely on verification when an account is first set up. The government said the measure was intended to improve traceability and curb phishing, digital arrest, impersonation, and investment scams.
The original directions gave platforms 90 days to implement the measures and 120 days to submit compliance reports. However, the government subsequently specified December 31, 2026, as the compliance deadline for SIM binding.
Platforms Prepare For Compliance
According to a CNBC report, Apple has updated its iOS software to support the SIM-binding requirements ahead of the implementation deadline.
WhatsApp and Arattai have confirmed that they are working to comply with the rules. Telegram is yet to clarify on its compliance status, while Signal has not responded to government notices, CNBC reported.
Snapchat has reportedly maintained that the mandate does not apply to its service because it does not use phone numbers to identify users.
Questions also remain about how individual platforms will support eSIM users. CNBC reported that WhatsApp and Telegram would require a physical SIM card to function, although the precise requirements for eSIM users have not been clarified.
The mandate could affect users who access messaging apps over Wi-Fi on phones without their registered SIM, as well as those who frequently switch SIMs. Its impact on access across multiple devices will depend on individual platforms’ implementation.
However, the DoT has clarified that international roaming will not be affected as long as the associated SIM remains in the handset.
The implementation push comes amid concerns over cyber fraud in India. According to data sourced from the home ministry, Indians lost ₹22,495 Cr to cyber fraud in 2025 compared with ₹22,845 Cr in 2024.
In June, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) said Indians had lost around ₹52,976 Cr to cyber-enabled fraud over the past six years, with nearly 8% of the losses linked to digital arrest scams.
Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi called on global technology companies, financial institutions, and telecom operators to work together to build a comprehensive framework to tackle cyber fraud and deepfakes.
“At a time when telecom and digital technology have become so important, it is equally important to make the security framework associated with it ironclad. It is our priority to secure mobile phones and networks,” Modi said, adding that trust was crucial for people using phones to communicate and make payments.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The government has allocated Rs352.5 million for the Prime Minister’s SPARK and ELEVATE technology programmes for FY2026-27, with grants of up to Rs200 million per project aimed at turning research into marketable products and accelerating technology commercialisation in Pakistan.
According to documents, the programmes will fund up to 60 research and innovation projects annually, including 30 projects under each initiative, through competitive selection.
The allocation was approved by the Board of Ignite – National Technology Fund and will be financed through the Research and Development (R&D) Fund, without any allocation from the federal budget or the Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP).
Government Allocates Rs352.5 Million for Technology Research Programmes
Under the programme, SPARK (Strategic Program for Advanced Research and Knowledge) will finance research projects aimed at developing functional prototypes, while ELEVATE (Empowering Latest age Engineering, Validation, and Accelerated Technology) will support the validation and commercialisation of technologies that already have functional prototypes.
The Prime Minister announced the initiatives on July 22, 2026, at the Indus RAS Expo 2026. They are being implemented under the amended Research and Development Rules, 2006, through Ignite.
The first call for proposals is open until October 26, 2026, for project concepts, while full proposals are due by the end of November 2026.
Under the funding framework, SPARK offers grants of up to Rs100 million per project, while ELEVATE provides up to Rs200 million per project. Both programmes will support projects for a period of up to 18 months, with funds released in milestone-linked tranches.
See Also: Pakistan Clears Rs 40.8 Billion PakSat-2 and Geo-AI Projects Under Uraan Pakistan
Ignite has envisaged two cohorts of grants every six months, with up to 30 projects under each programme annually.
The government has identified nine priority areas, including digital industry and advanced manufacturing, agriculture and water systems, energy efficiency, digital healthcare, smart cities, connectivity and digital infrastructure, cybersecurity and trust systems, education, and smart mobility.
However, the programmes are sector-agnostic, allowing proposals from different technology fields to compete for funding based on their merits.
The first two years will primarily cover project selection, grant awards and milestone delivery, with final outputs expected upon completion of projects.
Each SPARK-funded project will be required to deliver a functional prototype supported by verifiable real-world results, such as pilot deployment, validation in an operational environment or evidence of industry uptake.
Similarly, ELEVATE projects will be required to convert existing prototypes into market-ready products, supported by a confirmed pilot site or first customer. The programmes envisage up to 30 prototypes and 30 market-ready products per cycle, subject to the number of grants awarded.
The framework also encourages intellectual property protection, allowing funded projects to file patent applications in Pakistan or internationally through the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), with patent filing costs admissible under the grants.
The minister clarified that startup incubation is not part of SPARK and ELEVATE, as this function is performed through Ignite’s National Incubation Centers, which have hosted more than 2,250 startups. Startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), however, can lead projects under the two programmes.
See Also: CDWP Clears Seven Projects Worth Rs116 Billion Under Uraan Pakistan Initiative
Separately, the government expects the proposed $20 million Pakistan Venture Fund (PVF) to help address financing constraints faced by high-potential technology startups by mobilising private investment through professionally managed venture funds.
The fund will focus on technology-driven businesses, including artificial intelligence, robotics, augmented and virtual reality, deep technology, defence technologies, cybersecurity, financial technology, healthcare technology and agricultural technology.
The government expects the initiative to help startups expand product development, commercialise innovations, enter international markets and attract domestic and foreign capital.
No university or research centre has been designated as a primary implementation partner for SPARK and ELEVATE. The minister said eligible public and private universities, research organisations, startups and SMEs could compete through an open, nationwide selection process.
Successful applicants will be selected through Ignite’s Project Evaluation Ranking Matrix and approved by its board. ELEVATE projects will be industry-led, with universities and research centres participating as consortium partners.

PTA Recovers only 12.9pc of Rs4.27bn Penalties from Cellular Operators
PTML (Ufone) faced the highest penalties of Rs1.873 billion through 31 show-cause notices, followed by Jazz World Pakistan with Rs1.401 billion through 27 notices, CMPak (Zong) with Rs590.95 million through 17 notices, and Telenor Pakistan with Rs404.95 million through 21 notices.
The PTA has also taken measures to address disruptions in cellular services caused by power outages, requiring operators to restore affected network sites and services within prescribed timelines and maintain adequate backup power arrangements to ensure continuity of telecom services.
The regulator monitors compliance with applicable quality-of-service requirements and takes up service interruptions with the concerned operators for corrective measures.
The PTA has coordinated with the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA), the Power Division and distribution companies through a joint task force constituted under the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication to mitigate the impact of power interruptions on telecom services.
The proposed measures include dedicated feeders, smart-grid solutions and appropriate tariff arrangements to improve the reliability of electricity supplies to telecom infrastructure.
Corrective measures also include redundant backhaul and connectivity arrangements, enhanced network resilience, improved restoration mechanisms and adequate backup power facilities to minimise service interruptions.
The PTA monitors implementation of these measures and, where necessary, conducts re-verification testing to assess whether identified deficiencies have been rectified.

Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) has blocked 229,157 government employees or their spouses from receiving financial assistance after identifying them through audits, while recovering Rs712.4 million from ineligible recipients, the government has informed Parliament.
Minister for Poverty Alleviation and Social Safety Syed Imran Ahmad Shah, in a written reply to a parliamentary question, said the recovery comprised Rs545.784 million through the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), Rs21.550 million from BISP employees and Rs145.066 million from other government departments.
The minister said recovery proceedings had also been initiated against 236 BISP employees, with disciplinary action taken against delinquent officials.
BISP Blocked 229,157 Government Employees, Spouses as Beneficiaries
He added that updated data of government employees and pensioners had been obtained from the Controller General of Accounts (CGA), ministries, autonomous bodies and state-owned enterprises (SOEs), while more than six million records had been forwarded for profiling and further action.
According to the reply, 32,971 of the 229,157 blocked cases involving government employees or their spouses had been exempted from recovery because their monthly pension was Rs29,000 or below, in accordance with a decision of the BISP Board.
The minister said the process of data updating, profiling, blocking and recovery was continuing, adding that the number of irregular or ineligible beneficiaries and the recoverable amount could change as the exercise progressed.
Responding to concerns over illegal deductions, unauthorised charges, fraudulent biometric verification and other malpractices in BISP payments, the minister said complaints were examined individually and action was taken under the applicable rules.
Cases involving banks and payment service providers were referred to the relevant institutions for investigation and resolution. Depending on the findings, corrective measures could include penalties, recovery of irregular amounts and other action against those responsible.
The minister said legal or disciplinary proceedings were also initiated where fraud or serious malpractice warranted such action to safeguard beneficiaries’ payments.
BISP currently disburses financial assistance through the retail networks of six partner financial institutions (PFIs). The minister said these networks were monitored through field visits, beneficiary complaints, system-based controls, inspections and audits.
Where irregularities were detected, action could include suspension or blacklisting of agents, recovery of amounts and penalties under contractual provisions.
However, the reply did not provide the consolidated number of bank branches, campsites, agents, point-of-sale (POS) agents and ATMs involved in disbursement, or the total number of agents suspended, blacklisted or proceeded against. The bank-wise and province-wise details were referred to an annexure.
See Also: SBP Clarifies BISP Digital Wallet Charges, Says Online Transfers Will Remain Free
The government said BISP was gradually shifting towards digital and direct payment mechanisms through Social Protection Wallets (SPWs) to reduce human intervention and beneficiaries’ dependence on intermediaries.
The initiative aims to provide beneficiaries with greater choice, transparency, convenience and security while ensuring they receive the full amount sanctioned under the programme.
The minister said BISP had also developed and implemented an Integrated Grievance Management System (IGMS), integrated with partner financial institutions to streamline complaint handling and improve transparency and payment security within the State Bank of Pakistan’s regulatory framework.
Further development of the grievance management system would be undertaken gradually according to need, he added.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has rescued a 13-year-old girl in Karachi who was allegedly targeted by an online network linked to the dark web. The group reportedly instructed the girl to carry out acts of animal cruelty and self-harm, raising concerns about the growing risks of online exploitation involving children.
The incident highlights how cybercriminals can use social media platforms, messaging applications and concealed online identities to approach young people, manipulate them and pressure them into harmful activities.
Dark Web Exploitation in Pakistan: NCCIA Rescues 13-Year-Old Girl in Karachi
According to NCCIA Additional Director Tariq Nawaz, the agency launched an investigation after receiving information from a foreign intelligence agency about suspicious online activities linked to a group allegedly involved in child exploitation.
The agency received a tip-off containing an email address associated with the suspected group and relevant internet protocol (IP) addresses. Investigators traced the digital activity to Karachi and discovered that the person linked to the suspicious activity was a victim rather than a perpetrator. The agency then rescued the girl.
How Online Networks Target Children
According to Nawaz, individuals allegedly linked to the network contacted the girl through social media platforms and messaging applications. They reportedly used concealed online identities to communicate with her and assign tasks involving animal cruelty and self-injury.
Such cases demonstrate how online predators can exploit children’s trust and vulnerability. Offenders may use manipulation, intimidation or threats to pressure victims into following instructions. They may also attempt to isolate children from their families or discourage them from seeking help.
Not every case of online exploitation involves the dark web. Criminals can approach victims through mainstream platforms before moving conversations to private channels or hidden online services. This can make it difficult for parents to recognise the warning signs before a situation becomes serious.
What Is the Dark Web?
The dark web is a part of the internet that requires specialised software or configurations to access. While it has legitimate uses, criminals can also misuse hidden online services to conceal their identities, communicate privately and facilitate illegal activities.
Some online networks exploit these features to target vulnerable people or distribute illegal material. However, anonymity does not make users completely untraceable. Investigators can analyse digital evidence, IP addresses, online communications and other records to identify suspects and locate victims.
The Karachi case demonstrates the importance of digital investigations and cooperation between agencies. Information received from a foreign intelligence agency helped investigators trace suspicious online activity and identify a child who needed protection.
Online Blackmail and the Misuse of Private Photographs
Online exploitation can take several forms, including cyber blackmail, harassment, grooming and the non-consensual sharing of private photographs. Criminals may build trust with victims before using personal information or images to threaten them.
In some cases, offenders demand money, additional photographs, or compliance with other instructions. Others may threaten to share private material with family members or publish it online. Once such material spreads across multiple accounts and platforms, removing every copy can become difficult.
A recent court case in Islamabad has also highlighted the seriousness of online exploitation. Two men reportedly received 10-year prison sentences each for blackmailing a 12-year-old girl using objectionable photographs. The case underlines the legal consequences of exploiting children through digital platforms.
Although these incidents involve different alleged methods of abuse, they highlight a common concern: criminals can use digital tools to manipulate, threaten, and harm children.
How Parents and Siblings Can Protect Children
Parents, siblings and guardians have an important role in helping children stay safe online. Open communication can make it easier for children to report suspicious messages, uncomfortable interactions or threats without fearing punishment or blame.
Families should teach children not to share private photographs, personal information or account details with strangers. They should also encourage them to question requests from unknown online contacts, especially when someone demands secrecy or pressures them to complete disturbing tasks.
Privacy settings, strong passwords, two-factor authentication and age-appropriate parental controls can provide additional protection. Parents should also remain aware of the platforms and messaging applications their children use.
Most importantly, children must understand that they can seek help if someone threatens or manipulates them. Families should support victims rather than blame them for the actions of offenders.
How Victims Can Seek Help
If a child receives threatening messages or is pressured into harmful activities, families should preserve relevant evidence, including screenshots, usernames, account links and messages. They should report abusive accounts to the relevant platform and contact the appropriate authorities.
In Pakistan, suspected cybercrime can be reported to the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency. Families should avoid confronting suspected offenders directly, as doing so could increase risks or interfere with an investigation.
The rescue of the 13-year-old girl in Karachi highlights the need for stronger awareness of online exploitation and closer cooperation between families, technology platforms and law enforcement agencies.
As children’s lives become increasingly connected to the internet, protecting them requires more than monitoring their screen time. Families must help them recognise manipulation, feel safe reporting abuse and understand that support is available when someone targets them online.

items.content:

Pakistan’s 5G rollout is gaining momentum, with 1,782 5G sites deployed across 24 cities, according to details shared by Federal Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja.
Jazz is leading the deployment with 1,015 sites, followed by Zong with 640 and Ufone with 127. The figures reflect the operators’ reported network infrastructure as Pakistan gradually expands next-generation mobile connectivity.
The minister said 5G services were introduced after the country’s multiband 5G spectrum auction, with Next Generation Mobile Services (NGMS) licences signed on March 19, 2026. The four-phase rollout started on March 20, 2026, under a plan approved by the federal government.
The licensing obligations seek to improve existing 4G services alongside the phased introduction of 5G. All cellular mobile operators conducted technical 5G trials between 2020 and 2025, the minister added.
Which Cities Have the Most 5G Sites in Pakistan?
According to the minister’s reply, 5G services have been launched or are being consolidated in Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore, Rawalpindi, Faisalabad, Peshawar, Quetta, Multan, Gujranwala, Sialkot, Sheikhupura, Hyderabad, Abbottabad, Attock, Jhelum, Kasur, Kohat, Mardan, Rahim Yar Khan, Sahiwal, Sukkur, Swabi, Chitral and Gujrat.
Karachi has the highest reported number of deployed sites at 385, followed by Lahore with 373 and Islamabad with 276. Faisalabad has 144 sites, Peshawar 122, Rawalpindi 108, Multan 103, Sialkot 87, Quetta 65 and Sheikhupura 55.
Jazz leads deployment in Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad and Multan, while Zong has a stronger presence in Peshawar, Quetta, Sheikhupura and Sialkot. Ufone’s footprint remains comparatively limited at 127 sites across the reported rollout cities.
Under the first phase of the NGMS licence obligations, deployment in federal and provincial capitals is mandatory. Operators may expand into additional cities according to their respective business models.
However, deployed sites do not necessarily mean citywide 5G availability. Real-world network experience may vary by location and operator, as highlighted in PhoneWorld’s earlier coverage of 5G coverage and mobile network performance.
Affordable 5G Smartphones Remain a Major Challenge
While network deployment is expanding, the cost of compatible devices remains a barrier for many users. According to the minister, the cheapest locally available 5G-capable handset currently costs approximately Rs. 36,000.
The government reported that 607,093 5G-compatible handsets were locally assembled between January and August 2026. Local manufacturing could help improve access to more affordable devices, although the pace of adoption will also depend on consumer budgets and coverage.
PhoneWorld has previously reported on the country’s local mobile phone assembly trends and 5G production, underscoring the importance of device availability as networks expand.
The minister clarified that existing 4G SIM cards do not need to be replaced to access 5G. Consumers will still need a compatible handset and an active 5G signal from their mobile operator.
Although the rollout represents an important step for Pakistan’s digital connectivity, the government did not specify a definitive timeline for making 5G affordable for ordinary consumers. Wider coverage and the availability of lower-cost handsets will remain key factors as the next generation of mobile broadband reaches more users.
