items.content:
Two hot air balloons carrying smuggled cigarettes exploded after hitting power lines in central Lithuania on Wednesday, October 21. Police recovered nearly 20,000 packs of suspected contraband cigarettes from the two sites.
According to Lithuania’s fire and rescue service, the incidents occurred in the Kėdainiai and Kaišiadorys districts within 24 hours.
The first explosion occurred at around 6 a.m. in Padotnuvys village in the Kėdainiai district. Firefighters received a report of something burning on Draugystės Street, initially suspecting that a streetlight had exploded.
However, responders discovered that a balloon used to smuggle cigarettes had struck power lines and exploded. Its debris was burning along the roadside.
Police later found 10 packages tied with rope on the road. Preliminary estimates indicated that the packages contained around 15,000 packs of suspected contraband cigarettes. Authorities have not identified those responsible, and investigators handed the collected evidence to Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service.
Modestas Tvaravičius, head of the Dotnuva District, told local publication Rinkos aikštė that this was the first such incident in the area. He said the balloon had most likely landed on a farmer’s land, although he had not yet spoken to the landowner.
The second incident occurred at around 11 p.m. in Šakniai village in the Kaišiadorys district. Firefighters responded after residents reported an explosion and a fire in a field.
At the scene, crews found another cigarette-smuggling balloon that had hit power lines and caught fire. Authorities recovered approximately 4,900 packs of suspected contraband cigarettes.
Combined, the two incidents resulted in the recovery of around 19,900 packs of cigarettes.

The National Biosafety Committee (NBC) meets on Friday to consider a range of biosafety applications, including long-pending cases related to genetically modified (GM) corn technologies, according to a statement issued on Thursday.
The agenda follows the government's approval earlier this year of the National Agricultural Biotechnology Policy, which the government says will strengthen the regulatory framework for agricultural innovations. No decision on the pending applications has been announced.
CropLife Pakistan, an industry body representing seed and crop-protection companies, said approval of the pending GM corn biosafety licences would mark a milestone for agricultural biotechnology. CropLife Pakistan Executive Director Rasheed Ahmed said such a move could accelerate the adoption of advanced seed technologies, which he said would improve farm productivity, food security and the competitiveness of the sector.
GM corn has been cultivated commercially for more than two decades and is widely grown in major agricultural economies and across the Asia-Pacific region.
The committee's deliberations come against a separate constraint on the sector. Louis Dreyfus Company (LDC) Country Head and Head of Grains and Oilseeds Muhammad Daniyal told The Express Tribune last month that Pakistan produces excellent non-GMO corn, which commands a higher price globally, but that inadequate systems for drying, storing and transporting the crop mean Pakistani corn is often not purchased in international markets at all. Where a buyer is willing, he said, agreements are struck at prices 10% to 15% below prevailing market rates. Daniyal said the issue was directly linked to the absence of basic infrastructure, and that aligning harvesting, drying, storage and marketing with required standards could earn the country millions of dollars.

Key banks reported results for nine months of calendar year 2026 that were broadly in line with expectations. HBL posted earnings per share (EPS) of Rs36.84 (up 5% year-on-year) and a dividend per share of Rs18; Meezan Bank reported EPS of Rs41.02 (up 6% year-on-year) and dividend of Rs23.5 and MCB recorded EPS of Rs37.26 (flat year-on-year) with dividend of Rs27.
In a key geopolitical development, Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia signed an agreement in Doha to boost defence cooperation and strengthen defence capabilities. The "Badr MoU" is viewed as a signal of mutual interest in deepening partnerships. "Market bias remains to the downside below the 167,000-168,000 zone. Year-to-date, the index is down 5.82%, with week-to-date and month-to-date declines of 1.50% and 3.56%, respectively," AHL said.
Total market capitalisation stood at Rs18.17 trillion ($65.6 billion). Regular-market turnover was 367 million shares valuing at Rs18 billion. Leading gainers in terms of index contribution included Unilever Pakistan Foods, Thatta Cement and Airlink Communication, while the largest losers were PTCL, Nishat Chunian Power and Power Cement, AHL added.
Topline's market review noted that the KSE-100 index witnessed a sharp sell-off, shedding 2,007 points (-1.21%), as escalating geopolitical tensions and rising international oil prices weighed on investor sentiment. The benchmark initially touched the intra-day high of 249 points before plunging to the low of 2,148 points, reflecting heightened volatility and mounting selling pressure.
Persistent geopolitical uncertainty, coupled with concerns over rising oil prices and their potential implications for Pakistan's economic outlook, kept investors on the defensive. ENGROH, UBL, HUBC, HBL and PTC emerged as the major laggards, collectively dragging the index down by 752 points and amplifying the market's downward momentum, Topline said.
Overall trading volumes were recorded at 367.09 million shares compared with the previous session's tally of 379.91 million. The value of shares traded during the day was Rs18 billion.
Shares of 494 companies were traded. Of these, 101 stocks closed higher, 355 fell and 38 remained unchanged.
Pakistan Refinery was the volume leader with trading in 25.88 million shares, losing Rs4.76 to close at Rs95.12. It was followed by Cnergyico Pk with 23.19 million shares, losing Rs0.17 to close at Rs12.35 and WorldCall Telecom with 22.16 million shares, losing Rs0.03 to close at Rs0.90. items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
The government should transfer energy-sector management and decision-making to the private sector to promote competition, improve efficiency, attract investment and reduce costs, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali said, identifying energy, taxation and state-owned enterprises (SOEs) as the three areas most in need of reform.
Addressing the CEO Summit Islamabad 2026, organised by CEO Club Pakistan, he said high power costs undermined the competitiveness of domestic industries and stressed the need for affordable, reliable and sustainable energy supplies.
He presented a framework called TRUST, focused on targeting sectors where Pakistan has competitive strengths, implementing sustainable reforms, unlocking private capital, scaling up exports and developing talent. Sectoral priorities should be determined through five considerations: proven strength, the ability to deliver with existing institutions and infrastructure, global demand, employment generation at scale and foreign-exchange earnings. Applying these criteria, he identified agriculture, textiles and information technology (IT) and digital services as offering opportunities for employment creation, higher economic output and export growth.
Pakistan's agricultural sector, he said, needed a new wave of development focused on improving crop yields, storage facilities, processing and value-added exports, building on the gains of the Green Revolution of the 1960s. In textiles and apparel, the country needed to move beyond yarn and fabric production towards finished garments, brands and technical fabrics to increase value addition and competitiveness in international markets. Pakistani youth were already serving international clients through freelance work, and better organisation of the sector and stronger digital skills could help capture growing global demand.
On taxation, he emphasised documenting the economy to broaden the tax base and distribute the burden more fairly, saying too few taxpayers were carrying a disproportionate share.
He said Pakistan had faced severe economic challenges during 2022 and 2023, including fiscal constraints, low productivity, production curtailments, high inflation and elevated interest rates. "We cannot go through that sort of test again," he said. "So we need to do something to avoid it in the future."
Citing international examples, he said China had built on its agricultural strengths after launching reforms in 1978, South Korea had developed textiles and plywood in the 1960s, Vietnam had transformed from a rice importer into a major exporter, and Bangladesh had developed its garment industry by capitalising on existing strengths.
"These countries did not try to do everything at once," he said. "They started from what they could already do well and built upon it." Sustained effort and policy continuity had enabled long-term progress. Federal Minister for Board of Investment Qaiser Ahmed Sheikh told the summit that investment was essential for generating employment, introducing modern technologies, enhancing productivity, expanding industrial capacity and increasing exports, and that Pakistan needed both domestic and foreign investment to build a more resilient and competitive economy.
He identified IT, agriculture and agro-processing, mining and minerals, energy, manufacturing, infrastructure and tourism as sectors offering substantial investment opportunities, and said the Board of Investment was committed to facilitating investors, removing unnecessary hurdles and improving coordination among government departments. Investors required policy consistency, clear regulations, timely decisions and a predictable business environment for long-term commitments, he said.
Referring to China's three decades of double-digit growth, the minister said Pakistan could draw lessons on promoting investment, expanding productive capacity and maintaining a long-term focus on economic transformation. He said the private sector was a central partner in the country's economic transformation and that regular engagement between policymakers and business was essential for effective policy.
Sheikh said Pakistan's strengths included a young population, a large domestic market, natural resources and a strategic location, and that realising them required encouraging entrepreneurship, promoting innovation and strengthening competitiveness. Overseas Pakistanis, he said, could contribute beyond remittances through direct investment, business partnerships, technology transfer and access to international markets.
Muhammad Ali also thanked CEO Club Pakistan President and Founder Ijaz Nisar for convening the summit, saying such forums allowed meaningful discussion of economic challenges and growth prospects. WITH ADDITIONAL INPUT FROM APP

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
The World Bank projected on Thursday a moderate 4.2% economic growth for Pakistan in the year before general elections in 2029 but urged the government to implement a plan to stay on course of macroeconomic stability in the election year.
In its Pakistan Development Outlook, the Washington-based lender said rupee-dollar parity was not "freely" responding to market conditions and a fully flexible exchange rate would better serve Pakistan's interests. The report discussed in depth Pakistan's current exchange rate policy, implying that such stability led to three macroeconomic crises in the recent past and adjustment was needed to arrest appreciation of the real effective exchange rate.
The report projected 4.2% economic growth in fiscal year 2027-28, which would be the second last year of the government, and 4.4% during the election year. It underlined that Pakistan's current-to-medium-term growth rate was not enough to create jobs for 3.6 million people entering the market every year.
"With the current International Monetary Fund programme ending in September 2027 and national elections scheduled for early 2029, developing, publishing and effectively implementing a medium-term fiscal plan that preserves macroeconomic stability is critical to maintaining confidence," said the World Bank.
The lender emphasised the need for preserving macroeconomic stability due to past episodes of loosening fiscal purse during the election year. For the current fiscal year, the World Bank projected 3.8% growth, slightly lower than the government target of 4%.
"The growth rate in the medium term does not seem going beyond 4.5%, which is too low to create enough jobs," said Sebastian Essl, Lead Author of the report. The report underlined growth-enabling reforms that were urgently required to reverse recent increases in poverty from 22% in 2019 to 29% in 2025 and create sufficient jobs for 3.6 million Pakistanis reaching working age every year.
The World Bank said that under a baseline scenario with continued sound macroeconomic management and limited structural reform progress, growth was projected to remain broadly stable at 3.8% this fiscal year. Elevated commodity and energy prices were expected to weigh on services and industry, it added. "The macroeconomic outlook assumes that Pakistan's economy will continue to be affected by the conflict in the Middle East through end-2026, with a gradual de-escalation over the course of 2027," said the lender.
"Pakistan has made real progress in restoring stability and markets have taken notice," said Bolormaa Amgaabazar, World Bank Country Director for Pakistan. But real per capita growth – the rate at which the income of an average Pakistani increases – remains stuck at around 1.6% and reforms to drive faster growth are now urgently needed, according to Bolormaa.
The report showed that a more prolonged and intense conflict in the Middle East remained the most significant risk to Pakistan's near-term macroeconomic outlook. A longer or deeper conflict would sustain elevated energy prices and increase Pakistan's import bill while weighing on export demand and disrupting trade routes.
These effects could widen the current account deficit and add pressure to reserves. Intensified domestic demand-management measures to contain energy shortages could deepen the drag on domestic activity, while sustained higher input costs would renew pressure on inflation and household purchasing power.
The report found that such growth was possible if Pakistan followed the path taken by other successful countries in pursuing ambitious economic reforms. Reforms that upgrade policies and institutions to the quality seen in the average middle-income country could drive sustained growth of up to 6.2-6.9% per annum, sufficient for Pakistan to reach Vietnam's current level of income by 2050.
The World Bank commented extensively on Pakistan's exchange rate policy, suggesting that it had issues with the current policy. "The central bank exchange rate intervention creates temporary stability but leads to disruptive adjustments, deterring investment and undermining confidence," it stated.
"Stability in the face of these shocks suggests that the exchange rate is not responding freely to market conditions. A fully flexible, market-determined exchange rate would better serve Pakistan's economic development needs: it would buffer external shocks, support private sector confidence and prevent a gradual erosion of competitiveness."
The World Bank said that the rupee remained stable against the dollar, but the real exchange rate appreciated due to higher inflation, weighing on competitiveness. The average exchange rate in FY26 was Rs280.4 per dollar, compared to Rs279.4 the previous year. With higher inflation, deteriorating terms of trade and exchange rate stability, the real effective exchange rate (REER) appreciated 10% between end-June 2025 and July 2026, it added.
The World Bank said that over the past two fiscal years, its standard deviation was below Rs2, about 0.6% of its longer-term average. This stability was held through a series of terms-of-trade shocks from FY25, including lower rice export prices and sharp increases in import prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It said that cross-country evidence demonstrated that exchange rate rigidity had increased macroeconomic risks. Among 50 emerging markets over 1980-2011, less flexible regimes were associated with greater vulnerabilities and more frequent crises. Rigid regimes also absorb shocks less well: in developing countries, negative terms-of-trade shocks cause larger output losses under fixed regimes than under flexible ones.
The World Bank said that the current account deficit was projected to widen in the current fiscal year as recovering demand kept import growth faster than exports, but remittances would remain a key offset. It said that external financing needs were estimated to average around 5% of GDP over the near term, reflecting continued reliance on external debt rollovers and remittance-financed current account deficits. Tighter global financial conditions could raise borrowing costs and reduce capital flows to emerging markets, complicating the rollover of financing at a critical juncture.

— Pakistan Embassy US (@PakinUSA) October 22, 2026
Emphasising the longstanding relationship between Pakistan and the United States, he said cooperation between the two countries had produced results beyond their bilateral relationship.
“Each time Pakistan and the United States have come together, we have produced results, and results not only for ourselves in the bilateral domain, but results for the whole world,” he said.
Sheikh called for a shift in bilateral priorities from traditional security concerns to technological cooperation, saying closer ties in information technology could pave the way for a mutually beneficial partnership.
Read: Ambassador Sheikh calls for stronger Pakistan-US tech collaboration
“A key goal is to make a transition in the bilateral relationship from ‘CT to IT’, moving from counterterrorism to information technology,” he said, adding that this would yield a mutually rewarding partnership in the future.
Describing the current period as the “Pakistan moment”, the ambassador said the country’s potential was particularly evident in the digital domain.
The ambassador also highlighted Pakistan’s role in regional and global stability.
“Over the past 16, 17 months, we have seen the best of Pakistan's defense and diplomacy. We have emerged as a factor of stability as well as a stabilizing agent, a stabilizing force, a stabilizing nation,” he noted.
Sindh Governor Syed Nehal Hashmi, who attended the forum, said US enterprises were looking for reliable partners capable of delivering long-term value.
He urged Pakistani technology companies to translate their digital capabilities into concrete business opportunities, pilot projects and high-value contracts.
PSEB Chief Executive Officer Faisal Jeddy, Ignite CEO Bilal Abbasi and OPEN Global DC Chapter President Hassan Khalid also highlighted the expansion of Pakistan’s technology sector.
They said Pakistan had substantial technical talent, while the US market offered opportunities for companies seeking to expand their businesses and develop scalable solutions.
Discussions at the forum focused on the need for Pakistani technology firms to move beyond routine IT services and labour arbitrage towards developing proprietary intellectual property and scalable products.
Also Read: Ambassador Sheikh urges Pakistani-Americans to drive 'mutually rewarding' economic engagement
The shift, participants noted, could help position Pakistani companies as higher-value partners in the global technology industry.
Concluding the event, Sheikh reiterated that Pakistan had arrived on the global technology stage and praised the participating companies as representatives of the country’s capabilities.
Inviting international partners to “come and profit from the promise of Pakistan”, he said competitive costs could attract businesses initially, while the performance of Pakistani technology professionals could help sustain long-term partnerships.
He urged participants to use the platform to help redefine and promote Pakistan’s image internationally.
The event was organised by the Embassy of Pakistan in collaboration with the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, OPEN Global and the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB) to facilitate direct engagement between Pakistani technology firms and their American counterparts.
The forum brought together representatives of 16 Pakistani technology companies working in areas such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data analytics, financial technology and healthcare technology. Representatives of US technology and financial firms, multilateral institutions, government agencies and the Pakistani-American business community also attended the event.
The initiative aimed to develop commercial partnerships in enterprise solutions, digital transformation, product development and strategic IT collaboration through executive discussions and business-to-business meetings.

Scientists have administered artificial intelligence-designed viruses to a human patient for the first time in an experimental treatment aimed at fighting a serious bacterial infection, according to a report by The New York Times.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Scientists have administered artificial intelligence-designed viruses to a human patient for the first time in an experimental treatment aimed at fighting a serious bacterial infection, according to a report by The New York Times.
The treatment uses specially designed viruses called bacteriophages, or phages, which infect and kill bacteria. Researchers hope the AI-generated viruses can eliminate an E. coli infection that has resisted antibiotics and existing phage treatments.
The viruses were developed by US biotechnology startup Radical Numerics, which announced the treatment on Tuesday, October 20.
However, the company has not disclosed details about the patient or the doctors involved, citing confidentiality requirements.
How AI Designed the Viruses
Radical Numerics developed the treatment using its AI model, Omnii, which can analyze DNA sequences, protein structures, and other biological information.
The company created modified versions of a virus called T7, which specifically targets E. coli bacteria.
Researchers used Omnii to redesign the virus’s leg-like structures, allowing it to attach to bacterial strains that existing phages could not infect.
After generating the new viral genomes, scientists produced the corresponding DNA and inserted it into bacteria. Laboratory testing showed that the modified viruses could infect and kill the targeted bacteria.
The researchers then conducted safety checks before providing the viruses to doctors treating the patient.
FDA Authorizes Treatment
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) authorized the experimental treatment.
However, Radical Numerics has not revealed whether the patient has recovered or whether the treatment successfully cleared the infection.
The company’s technical findings have also not undergone peer review or been published in a scientific journal.
Earlier AI Research
The development builds on research conducted at the Arc Institute in California.
In 2025, researchers developed an AI model called Evo 2, trained on millions of DNA sequences, including those from viruses.
The model generated approximately 700,000 viral genomes. Researchers selected 285 designs for laboratory testing and found that 16 produced viable viruses.
Three researchers from the project, including Dr. Eric Nguyen, later established Radical Numerics.
In June 2026, the company introduced Omnii, an AI system designed to work with multiple forms of biological data.
Besides designing viruses, the company is exploring applications in cancer vaccine development and identifying potential pandemic risks.
Faster Treatment for Resistant Infections
Radical Numerics believes AI could significantly reduce the time required to develop personalized treatments for antibiotic-resistant infections.
Traditional phage therapy can involve lengthy searches for viruses capable of attacking a specific bacterial strain.
By using AI to design suitable viruses, researchers hope to shorten the process to a matter of days.
Eric Nguyen, the company’s chief executive, said the team believes it could eventually create personalized treatments within days.
However, researchers still need clinical evidence to establish whether AI-designed phages can safely and effectively treat infections in humans.
The treatment represents an early clinical application of AI-designed viruses, but its effectiveness remains unconfirmed.

items.author: Sher Alam
items.content:
Lithuanian police have uncovered one of the largest synthetic drug laboratories in the Baltic region, seizing more than 500kg of methamphetamine, over 300kg of amphetamine, and thousands of liters of chemicals during a three-day operation near Vilnius.
Authorities suspect that a Dutch national of Turkish origin ran the laboratory with the help of three Lithuanian nationals. Investigators believe the group operated an international drug supply network and produced synthetic drugs on an industrial scale.
“[Drugs] were being produced on an almost industrial scale,” Saulius Briginas, Deputy Chief of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told journalists on Wednesday.
Police recovered more than 3,000 liters of BMK, a chemical used to manufacture amphetamines, along with over 500kg of methamphetamine, more than 300kg of amphetamine, and around 4.5kg of the synthetic drug 3-CMC. According to Briginas, the seized substances could produce more than 4 million individual doses.
The drugs have an estimated wholesale value of more than €2 million. However, their combined street value could be ten times higher, Briginas said.
Authorities believe the group intended to supply markets across Europe rather than Lithuania alone. The Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, and the Czech Republic were among the potential destinations.
Investigators also traced the group’s procurement of laboratory equipment and chemicals to China, India, and several European countries. The group reportedly purchased some uncontrolled substances from specialist suppliers in Lithuania.
Police found 380 hydrogen cylinders originating from China at the site. Hydrogen is used in synthetic drug manufacturing, while the group reportedly bought sulphuric acid in shipments of one ton per transaction.
The investigation also led police to intercept a shipment bound for the Czech Republic. Officers discovered 17kg of amphetamine crystals hidden in two plastic containers inside cargo handled by a Lithuanian logistics company.
Under Lithuanian law, illegal production, possession, and smuggling of particularly large quantities of narcotic or psychotropic substances can result in prison sentences of up to 18 years.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
The US Pentagon has authorized the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a military-grade heat ray weapon for potential use along the US-Mexico border, according to a memo obtained by CNN.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed the memo in September, allowing DHS to borrow the weapon for seven months and develop tactics for its possible deployment during border operations.
The weapon, known as the Active Denial System (ADS), uses invisible electromagnetic waves to create an intense burning sensation on human skin without physical contact.
How the Heat Ray Works
The Active Denial System is a nonlethal weapon developed by the US military. It can project an invisible beam of electromagnetic energy over a distance of slightly more than half a mile.
According to military officials, the beam creates a burning sensation similar to opening a hot oven. The resulting tingling sensation can last between 10 and 15 minutes and creates a strong urge to move away.
The system is designed to disperse people without using conventional weapons.
Pentagon Approves Testing
The Pentagon has authorized DHS to borrow one Active Denial System for seven months, beginning in September 2026.
Under the agreement, DHS will be responsible for operating the weapon and developing procedures for its potential use. Pentagon personnel will not operate the system.
The memo does not specify where testing will take place or how the weapon might eventually be deployed.
DHS can also request an extension after the seven months if additional testing or deployment is required.
Previous Deployment Plans
According to CNN, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officials have previously considered using the weapon to control crowds and discourage unauthorized border crossings.
In 2018, officials discussed deploying the system against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen rejected the proposal.
The weapon was also considered during protests following George Floyd’s killing in 2020.
The US military previously deployed the system to Afghanistan but never used it during combat operations.
Safety and Legal Concerns
The proposed use has raised concerns about safety, legality, and the potential risks to migrants.
Former border officials warned that people attempting to escape the heat ray could enter dangerous areas, including rivers, increasing the risk of drowning.
Officials also questioned whether the weapon could be directed at people who had not yet crossed into US territory.
Meanwhile, some Border Patrol agents have questioned the need for the technology, citing declining border crossings and increased staffing.
A CBP spokesperson told CNN that the agency continues to evaluate new technologies to improve its operational capabilities.
For now, DHS has permission to test the system, but authorities have not confirmed whether it will be deployed at the US-Mexico border.

items.title: EU awards fresh funds to ramp 6G drive
items.summary:
A body charged with pushing 6G-related developments in the European Union selected a quintet of projects to share €22 million in its latest funding award, including undertakings on connected devices and improving data for AI-native networks.
The European Smart Networks and Services Joint Undertaking (SNS JU) explained the initiatives selected were intended to help address key needs for the next phase of 6G development.

The partly EU-funded organisation noted now was a “crucial point for Europe’s 6G ambitions” given intensified global competition in next-generation communications.
Those chosen this time around are 6G-AID, Hemes-6G, EUnicon-6G, EU-India-6G-Bridge and SNS Impact.

items.author: Chris Donkin
items.content:
A body charged with pushing 6G-related developments in the European Union selected a quintet of projects to share €22 million in its latest funding award, including undertakings on connected devices and improving data for AI-native networks.
The European Smart Networks and Services Joint Undertaking (SNS JU) explained the initiatives selected were intended to help address key needs for the next phase of 6G development.
Its aim with the newly-backed projects is to help researchers and businesses in the region advance promising technologies to large-scale tests and real-world adoption.
The partly EU-funded organisation noted now was a “crucial point for Europe’s 6G ambitions” given intensified global competition in next-generation communications.
Those chosen this time around are 6G-AID, Hemes-6G, EUnicon-6G, EU-India-6G-Bridge and SNS Impact.
6G-AID is focused on building a European data foundation for AI-native 6G networks; Hemes-6G will bring together eight testbeds across the EU on a shared platform for larger-scale work; EUnicon-6G seeks to identify opportunities for connected devices outside of smartphones; as the name suggests EU-India-6G-Bridge deepens collaboration with India; and SNS Impact is set to support cross-project collaboration.
Executive director of the SNS JU, Erzsebet Fitori, said for industry the projects would mean: “better access to the data, testbeds, technologies and partnerships needed to turn 6G research into products and services” while for citizens it helped “the foundations for more secure, reliable and capable connectivity in the years ahead”.
“These proposals are about making sure that Europe helps shape the technologies and standards that will define the future.”
The five selected come from the organisation’s sixth call for proposals which closed earlier this year.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Pakistan recorded the second-highest number of advertising bids linked to an Israeli spyware delivery operation, according to an October 15 report by Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto.
The investigation found that an Israeli company called Discover-Tech used online advertisements to deliver malicious code capable of infecting devices without requiring users to click on the ads.
Citizen Lab identified the technique as “AdFection” and linked the operation to spyware developed by another Israeli company, Candiru, now known as Integrity Labs.
Pakistan Records 139 Million Ad Bids
Citizen Lab examined nearly four billion advertising bidding records from Discover-Tech’s system between March and June 2026.
Researchers found that approximately 19% of the bids involved advertisements containing scripts capable of delivering attack code to selected devices.
Pakistan ranked second globally with around 139 million such bids, behind Yemen, which recorded approximately 457 million.
The researchers also found that the advertisements appeared more than 100,000 times on Pakistani technology website WhatMobile.com.pk.
Additionally, Pakistan was among the countries where these advertisements appeared on government-operated networks. However, the report did not identify the Pakistani networks involved.
Al Jazeera Devices Targeted
According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech acted as an intermediary between spyware developers and online advertising platforms.
The company allegedly used advertising infrastructure to distribute spyware developed by Candiru.
Researchers found that at least 45 devices belonging to Al Jazeera were targeted through this method during 2024 and 2025.
Citizen Lab attributed the attacks to Candiru with high confidence.
Pakistani User Identified
The investigation also identified a user named “Pindi” who accessed Discover-Tech’s control platform exclusively from Pakistan.
However, Citizen Lab could not establish whether the account was connected to any spyware company.
Researchers also identified two other unattributed users who accessed the platform from India and Italy.
The report clarified that login locations only indicate where users accessed the system and do not establish whether individuals in those countries were targeted.
Ad Exposure Does Not Confirm Infection
Citizen Lab clarified that displaying a suspicious advertisement does not automatically mean a device was hacked.
The researchers said an ad impression alone cannot establish whether a user was specifically targeted or infected with spyware.
Similarly, the bidding records do not identify individuals in Pakistan who may have been selected for surveillance.
However, the researchers warned that the large number of suspicious advertisements highlights potential security risks and called for investigations to determine whether devices on affected networks were compromised.
Global Networks Also Exposed
The investigation found that Discover-Tech’s advertisements also reached networks associated with NATO, the United Nations, the European Parliament, and government ministries in several countries.
Citizen Lab warned that the wider online advertising system could allow spyware companies to identify and monitor users without their knowledge.
Following the investigation, Google removed Discover-Tech from its advertising platforms, while IAB Europe removed the company from its approved vendor list. Other advertising companies also restricted its access.
The researchers stressed that the findings demonstrate weaknesses in the online advertising industry and the need for stronger safeguards against spyware attacks.

The Peshawar High Court (PHC) on Thursday suspended a government notice ordering the inactive Deputy Speaker of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Assembly Suraiya Bibi to vacate her official residence, allowed her to continue living there and directed law-enforcement agencies not to arrest her.
A two-member bench comprising Justice Ijaz Anwar and Justice Faheem Wali issued the written order arising from the previous hearing. Advocate Yasir Khattak appeared on behalf of the petitioner, the inactive Deputy Speaker.
In its detailed order, the court noted that the relevant presidential ordinance makes no mention of the offices of Speaker or Deputy Speaker. Similarly, the administrative directive requiring vacation of official residences contains no reference to these constitutional posts. The judges therefore found sufficient ground to stay the eviction process pending further examination of the legal position.
Read: PHC stays arrest of K-P Assembly deputy speaker, orders de-sealing of official
items.author: Yasir Ali
items.content:
The Peshawar High Court (PHC) on Thursday suspended a government notice ordering the inactive Deputy Speaker of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Assembly Suraiya Bibi to vacate her official residence, allowed her to continue living there and directed law-enforcement agencies not to arrest her.
A two-member bench comprising Justice Ijaz Anwar and Justice Faheem Wali issued the written order arising from the previous hearing. Advocate Yasir Khattak appeared on behalf of the petitioner, the inactive Deputy Speaker.
In its detailed order, the court noted that the relevant presidential ordinance makes no mention of the offices of Speaker or Deputy Speaker. Similarly, the administrative directive requiring vacation of official residences contains no reference to these constitutional posts. The judges therefore found sufficient ground to stay the eviction process pending further examination of the legal position.
Read: PHC stays arrest of K-P Assembly deputy speaker, orders de-sealing of official residence
During arguments, counsel for the petitioner contended that the K-P Assembly Speaker and Deputy Speaker Act 2026 confers a clear legal right on the Deputy Speaker to occupy the official residence for the duration of her term. He further argued that law-enforcement agencies are barred from conducting any raid or taking coercive action against the residence while the office-holder remains in position.
Opposing the petition, the Advocate General submitted that an emergency empowers the provincial government to reclaim official residences allotted to ministers, advisers and the Deputy Speaker. He also apprised the court that a criminal case under Section 406 of the Pakistan Penal Code has already been registered against the Deputy Speaker on the complaint of the Deputy Commissioner of Chitral.
After hearing both sides, the bench suspended the notice to vacate the residence, expressly authorised the petitioner to remain in occupation and ordered that she should not be arrested. The matter will be taken up again on the next date of hearing.
The ruling provides immediate relief to the inactive Deputy Speaker and places the burden on the provincial authorities to justify the eviction drive in light of the statutory protections available to the holder of the office.

Update | October 22, 19:35 IST
Jio Platforms’ ₹30,213 Cr IPO ended the second day of bidding with 5.57X subscription, receiving bids for 110.03 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data.
Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) led demand, bidding for 65.15 Cr shares against 4.90 Cr shares reserved for the category, taking subscription to 13.29X. The non-institutional investor (NII) portion was subscribed 5.97X, with bids for 21.76 Cr shares.
Within the NII category, the portion reserved for applications exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 6.76X, while the segment for applications above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 4.38X.
The retail portion was subscribed 1.54X, receiving bids for 13.11 Cr shares against 8.50 Cr shares reserved for the category.
Meanwhile, the employee and shareholder portions were subscribed 2.10X and 4.05X, respectively.
Original | October 22, 12:28 IST
Reliance Industries’ digital services arm Jio Platforms’ IPO was subscribed 3.65X on the second day of bidding, with institutional investors leading demand and the retail portion crossing full subscription.
Investors bid for 72.05 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer as of 12:03 IST, according to BSE data.
The qualified institutional buyers’ (QIBs) portion was subscribed 9.42X, receiving bids for 46.16 Cr shares against an allocation of 4.91 Cr shares. Domestic financial institutions, including banks and insurance companies, accounted for 25.92 Cr shares, followed by foreign institutional investors at 16.18 Cr shares and mutual funds at 3.19 Cr shares.
The non-institutional investors’ (NIIs) portion was subscribed 2.85X, getting bids for 10.38 Cr shares against 3.64 Cr shares reserved for the category. Within this, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 3.06X, while that for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 2.43X.
Retail investors bid for 9.39 Cr shares against an allocation of 8.50 Cr shares, translating to 1.10X subscription. The employee and shareholder portions were subscribed 1.71X and 2.38X, respectively.
On its first day of bidding yesterday, the public issue was subscribed 3.15X, driven by strong demand from institutional investors.
India’s Largest Public Offering
Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065-₹1,119 per share for the IPO, which closes tomorrow. The ₹30,213 Cr (about $3.2 Bn) offering is set to surpass Hyundai Motor India’s ₹27,870 Cr issue as India’s largest IPO.
At the upper end of the price band, Jio Platforms would be valued at around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr (about $108 Bn).
Ahead of the public offering, the company raised ₹8,109.8 Cr from anchor investors, allotting 7.25 Cr shares at ₹1,119 apiece. Domestic mutual funds acquired around 2.48 Cr shares through 95 schemes, while insurance companies and pension funds picked up 97 Lakh shares.
The anchor book also included Fidelity, Allianz, BlackRock, the Government of Singapore, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, and Goldman Sachs.
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, with no offer-for-sale component. Jio plans to use ₹27,500 Cr of the proceeds to prepay certain borrowings of its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd (RJIL), and deploy the remaining funds for general corporate purposes.
The proposed repayment covers three external commercial borrowing facilities worth a combined ₹29,971 Cr, raised from a consortium of Indian and international lenders, including SBI, Bank of America and First Abu Dhabi Bank. The loans funded 5G infrastructure deployment and spectrum acquisition, with repayments scheduled between March and June 2028 and interest rates ranging from 1.40% to 5.13% per annum.
The IPO comes as Jio expands beyond telecom connectivity into fixed broadband, cloud services, enterprise solutions, and AI. RJIL had 533.3 Mn customers as of June 30, 2026, while its fixed broadband subscriber base stood at 28.6 Mn.
Jio Platforms reported a 9.2% increase in consolidated net profit to ₹7,764 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹7,110 Cr a year earlier. Operating revenue rose 11.8% YoY and 2.4% QoQ to ₹39,173 Cr.
For FY26, operating revenue rose nearly 15% YoY to ₹1.47 Lakh Cr, while net profit increased 15.1% YoY to ₹30,049 Cr.

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Early backers Kae Capital Fund II and Kalysta Capital Fund II bagged 38.3X returns on shares sold through manufacturing company Zetwerk’s IPO, emerging among the biggest gainers in its offer for sale (OFS).
At ₹151 apiece, the upper end of the IPO price band, the sale price was 38.3 times the two funds’ weighted average acquisition cost of ₹3.94 per share.
Kae Capital Fund II pocketed ₹196.3 Cr by selling around 1.3 Cr shares, while Kalysta Capital Fund II received ₹63.3 Cr from the sale of 41.9 Lakh shares.
Both investors retain sizeable holdings after the sale. Kae Capital Fund II holds 4.3 Cr shares valued at ₹649.3 Cr at ₹151 apiece, while Kalysta Capital Fund II holds 1.4 Cr shares worth ₹211.4 Cr.
The payouts come after Zetwerk’s IPO closed with 3.06X subscription, attracting bids for 56.62 Cr shares against 18.50 Cr shares on offer. The company’s shares are scheduled to list on the exchanges tomorrow.
Meanwhile, Peak XV and Lightspeed sold shares through multiple investment vehicles, with returns varying across their funds.
Peak XV pocketed a combined ₹359.3 Cr through two vehicles – Peak XV Partners Investments V and Peak XV Partners Growth Investments III. Peak XV Partners Investments V sold around 1.8 Cr shares for ₹271.8 Cr, clocking a 23.9X return multiple. It retains 12.2 Cr shares valued at ₹1,842.2 Cr at the IPO price.
Peak XV Partners Growth Investments III received ₹87.5 Cr from the sale of around 58 Lakh shares, realising a 3.3X return multiple. It retains 4 Cr shares worth ₹604 Cr. Together, the two funds held a 12.1% stake in Zetwerk before the OFS.
Lightspeed, which invested through three vehicles, collectively pocketed around ₹440 Cr.
Lightspeed Venture Partners Select IV Mauritius sold around 1.4 Cr shares for ₹211.4 Cr, while Lightspeed India Partners II, LLC sold 1.2 Cr shares for ₹181.2 Cr. Lightspeed India Partners III, LLC received ₹47.5 Cr from the sale of 31.5 Lakh shares.
Lightspeed India Partners II recorded the highest return multiple among the three vehicles at around 10.9X.
Among other selling investors, Accel clocked a 19.5X return. However, Creovate Innovation sold shares at 0.9X its acquisition cost, taking a loss on the stake sold.
Zetwerk Cofounders Pocket ₹423 Cr
Zetwerk cofounders Amrit Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan collectively pocketed around ₹423 Cr through the OFS, selling approximately 1.4 Cr shares each for ₹211.4 Cr apiece.
Following the sale, Acharya retains 10.1 Cr shares worth ₹1,525.1 Cr at the IPO price, while Ramakkrushnan retains 11.4 Cr shares valued at ₹1,721.4 Cr.
Cofounders Rahul Sharma, Vishal Chaudhary, and Ankit Fatehpuria also sold shares through the OFS. The RHP categorised the three under “individual selling shareholders”.
Sharma and Chaudhary each pocketed around ₹26 Cr by selling approximately 17.2 Lakh shares, while Fatehpuria received ₹34.3 Cr from the sale of 22.7 Lakh shares.
The shareholder payouts formed part of Zetwerk’s ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO, comprising a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end of the price band.
Founded in 2018, Zetwerk operates a manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories.
It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to manage manufacturing orders across sectors including renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation.
Ahead of the issue, Zetwerk raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors. Domestic mutual funds, including SBI Mutual Fund and ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, accounted for around 46% of the anchor book. Global investors, including Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, also participated.
On the financial front, Zetwerk’s operating revenue from continuing operations rose 55.4% to ₹4,117.9 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹2,649.4 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr.
Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr came from discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included ₹803.2 Cr in exceptional charges from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
The federal government on Thursday decreased the price of petrol by Rs1.60 per litre while increasing the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.64 per litre for October 23.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs377.71 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs391.75 per litre for Friday.
The latest revision comes a day after the government decreased the price of petrol by Rs2.71 per litre while increasing the price of diesel by 31 paisas per litre, for October 22.
Read: Oil jumps on escalating Middle East conflict
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Also Read: Govt mulls $2b LNG import decision
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices climbed about ​3% to a five-month high on Thursday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy ‌supplies from the key exporting region.
Brent futures rose $3.51, or 3.2%, to $112.33 a barrel at 1:05 p.m. EDT (1705 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude rose $2.14, or 2.2%, to $99.29.
"Reports ​of Middle East crude oil exports exceeding pre-conflict levels are more than countered by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the ​Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and on its oil infrastructure," PVM Oil analyst Tamas Varga said.
Morgan Stanley analysts estimated that Middle East crude oil exports were around 17 million barrels per day last week. Crude exports from the region averaged about 18 million bpd in the 12 months before the start of the Iran ​war, according to Kpler.

items.content:
Motilal Oswal Financial Services and Calliope Capital Advisors have applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares in Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr rights issue against entitlements transferred by two promoter group entities.
The electric two-wheeler maker said in an exchange filing that Motilal Oswal Financial Services applied for 1.28 Cr shares against rights entitlements renounced by ANI Technologies. Calliope Capital Advisors applied for another 1.10 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by Indus Trust.
Calliope Capital Advisors LLP is an investment vehicle owned by Navin Agarwal, group MD of Motilal Oswal Financial Services.
Both investors submitted their applications before 11:00 IST on the opening day of the issue, covering the full entitlements transferred to them.
Renouncing a rights entitlement means transferring the right to subscribe to new shares to another investor.
ANI Technologies, which operates the Ola Cabs business, and Indus Trust held 3.47% and 2.98% stake, respectively, in Ola Electric as of June 30, according to the company’s letter of offer. Ankush Aggarwal, brother of founder Bhavish Aggarwal, serves as the trustee of Indus Trust.
Meanwhile, CMD Bhavish has committed to subscribing to his full rights entitlement. Promoter group members have also committed to subscribing to their entitlements or transferring them within the permitted categories, including to specified investors.
Earlier this month, Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in Ola Electric to fund his participation in the rights issue.
Another Round Of Fundraising
The rights issue, which closes on October 30, comprises up to 37.03 Cr partly paid-up shares priced at ₹27 apiece. Investors must pay ₹16.20 per share on application and the remaining ₹10.80 through a subsequent call.
Ola Electric plans to allocate ₹350 Cr towards repaying or prepaying borrowings, including accrued interest and applicable prepayment penalties, and ₹400 Cr towards organic growth. The remaining net proceeds will fund general corporate purposes.
The fundraise follows the company’s ₹780.24 Cr qualified institutional placement (QIP) in June, with some proceeds from earlier capital raises yet to be deployed.
As of September 20, 2026, ₹139.21 Cr of IPO proceeds allocated towards debt repayment, organic growth, and general corporate purposes remained unutilised. Another ₹190.77 Cr from the QIP remained unutilised across these common objects, according to the letter of offer.
The fundraise comes at a time when Ola Electric is stepping up investments in its battery cell manufacturing and battery energy storage system businesses.
On the financial front, its consolidated net loss narrowed 22% YoY to ₹336 Cr in Q1 FY27. However, operating revenue plunged 45% YoY to ₹455 Cr. Sequentially, revenue rose 72% from ₹265 Cr, while loss narrowed from ₹500 Cr.
Shares of Ola Electric ended today’s trading session 3.21% lower at ₹31.94 apiece on the BSE.

items.content:
When telecoms pull out of markets, data protection and human rights commitments often disappear
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Akil Mazumder via Pexels. Used under a Pexels license.
By Jie Zhang
This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.
In March 2022, just over a year after Myanmar’s military coup, Telenor, the Norwegian telecommunications giant, sold its subsidiary in the country to M1 Group, bringing nearly eight years of operation to an end. But leaving Myanmar did not end the controversy surrounding its departure. Instead, the hasty exit came back to haunt the company over the next four years.
Since then, criticisms, lawsuits and litigation by civil society and affected people have continued to follow the company. The scrutiny also reached a crescendo this September, when Norwegian authorities opened criminal investigations into Telenor over allegations of aiding crimes against humanity in the country and transferring sanctioned surveillance equipment during the sale. Within days, a court in Norway also green-lit a class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of a group of Telenor’s former customers in Myanmar.
Telenor reiterated its position upon the investigation, arguing that any alternatives would have endangered the employees’ lives. Yet the company’s trouble raises a broader question that many telecommunication multinationals may have to confront one day: When a company decides to exit a “high-risk market,” where does its responsibility end?
Leaving is not just a business decision
Under military rule, Telenor faced government demands to facilitate surveillance, hand over the personal data of dissidents and activists, and restrict access to information. In a market like this, staying may cease to be viable. For a telecom operator, the matter is not simply to make a choice between remaining in the market or leaving, but whether it can exit in a way that minimizes further harm to users, without leaving them more vulnerable. Unfortunately, Telenor failed to do so.
In a conventional asset sale involving multinational companies, the transaction may center largely around physical and commercial assets, such as factories, equipment, and inventory. Selling a telecom subsidiary is another story.
As gatekeepers of internet access and digital information, telcos control sensitive user data, including location records and device logs. They also serve as key intermediaries for interception systems and have the technical capacity to cut off network access. In a sale, the company hands over not just infrastructure and commercial assets, but also systems and data that can expose the movements and footprints of millions of users.
Without rigorous buyer scrutiny and assessments of the risks associated with the transfer, a corporate sale may lead to grave harm to users, who might be watched, tracked, or even silenced in authoritarian contexts.
What followed in Myanmar showed that the risk was anything but hypothetical. It also revealed why powerful companies cannot simply shed their responsibilities by selling their business, when people depending on their services are left to bear the consequences.
A global pull back is underway
This matters because Telenor’s withdrawal from Myanmar is hardly an isolated case. After the debacle, the telecom giant began systematically pulling back from its Asian markets. In 2022, the company combined its Malaysian subsidiary Digi with local telecom service Celcom. In Thailand the following year, it merged its local business dtac with True Corporation before later selling down most of its stake in the entity. It also completed its sale of Telenor Pakistan to PTCL at the end of 2025, with further plans to dispense with its remaining Asian assets.
Zooming out, multinational telecom operators are shrinking the overseas footprints they spent decades building. MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, announced its plan to “orderly exit” from the Middle East in 2020 amid geopolitical risks. The company has ended its operations in Syria, Yemen, and Afghanistan by 2025. MTN also completed the sale of its operations in Guinea-Bissau and Guinea-Conakry in 2024, citing unsustainable costs.
Aiming to refocus on a small group of more profitable core markets — Britain, Brazil, Germany, and Spain — Spanish telecom giant Telefónica also accelerated its retreat from Spanish-speaking Latin America. In 2025 alone, it sold its subsidiaries in Argentina, Peru, Uruguay, and Ecuador, followed by exits from Colombia, Chile, and Mexico in early 2026.
The reasons for telecoms’ departure vary from geopolitical tensions to high costs. However, we should ask the critical question: what changes for the customers after a telecom operator leaves them behind?
What gets lost in the handover
While the network will continue to provide service to users, the transparency practices and internal procedures and protocols for data safeguards may change after a sale. This is where the risks of market exit are less visible. Telenor, MTN, and Telefónica have all developed sophisticated governance systems, including formal human rights policies, data-protection and security procedures, and regular transparency reporting. Research shows they are among the strongest performers on transparency and accountability in the telecom industry.
Those transparency reports provide a useful window into how telcos handle government demands. The reports describe the procedures in place to respond to government requests for user data, content restrictions, and network disruptions, and publish data on such requests across different markets. Although transparency alone cannot prevent abuse, it creates a public record of how governments exert pressure on companies.
However, we found that transparency reporting mostly does not survive ownership changes. Once a multinational operator leaves a market, it naturally stops reporting in that country. Disappointingly, its successors overwhelmingly fail to maintain the same level of transparency.
Millicom, a recurring buyer of Telefónica’s Latin American assets, acquired its operations in Uruguay and Ecuador, and a controlling stake in Colombia. Millicom does publish law-enforcement disclosures, but the data are aggregated by region rather than by country. Moreover, as of September 2026, only the 2024 report is publicly available. Elsewhere, the picture is even bleaker: None of the other recent buyers appeared to publish transparency reports or commit to continuing their predecessors’ transparency practices.
The discontinuation of transparency reporting removes the opportunity for the public to scrutinize whether or not the volume of the government demands changed after each ownership transition. It also hides from view how those demands are handled internally.
Transparency reporting, however, is only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath it lies a much broader mechanism of user data protections, institutional norms, and governance safeguards, such as risk escalation channels, legal and human rights checks, and many more.
In authoritarian states, multinational telcos are no less likely to face government pressure to shut down networks, block websites, or hand over user data. While these companies may also have limited room to resist, they usually operate under more institutional oversight than state-controlled ones. They are also exposed to more scrutiny from the international press and civil society, greater reputational risk, and often stronger regulatory frameworks established by their home countries.
By contrast, many operators who succeeded these businesses might be more closely connected to governments and more deeply embedded in the local political and regulatory environment. Facing fewer external constraints from society, media, and NGOs, they also have less willingness and fewer resources to challenge governments.
What a more responsible exit might look like
Since safeguards may weaken or even disappear with ownership shift, the essential duty to protect users’ rights should not be treated as an afterthought to a market exit. It must be a key element of the transaction.
For telecom companies, a responsible exit should begin well before a buyer is even selected. Before entering Myanmar in 2014, Telenor commissioned a human rights impact assessment (HRIA) for its planned market entry. The company also states that it considered human rights and data privacy as it prepared for its departure. But there is no public record showing that Telenor conducted a standalone assessment of the human rights risks of the exit itself.
Companies should commission a mandated, exit-specific human rights impact assessment, evaluating what user risks the sale itself might create, the concerns of stakeholders and users, how the data might be used or transferred in the future, and which groups of users would be most exposed to the risks it identifies.
Buyer due diligence should go beyond financial stability to examine the buyer’s human rights record, its capacity to govern sensitive data, and whether existing safeguards can survive under new ownership.
Moreover, a responsible exit from any politically risky market should also ask a basic question: What should not be transferred in a sale? Should every piece of user data be handed over to the next owner? Telecom companies should evaluate if any sensitive data can be segregated, anonymized, or even deleted whenever feasible, particularly when transferring such data could expose high-risk users.
Similarly, some technical infrastructure, such as surveillance equipment, interception systems, and other network-control capabilities, should not be bundled into a sale automatically as ordinary infrastructure. Norwegian authorities are now probing whether Telenor transferred sanctioned surveillance equipment as part of the sale of Telenor Myanmar without the required authorization from the Norwegian government.
A new test for the next exit
If Telenor offers a lesson for everyone about what can go wrong in a reckless departure from a high-risk market, MTN’s unfinished exit from Iran may offer a test about whether companies can approach their next departure differently.
MTN still holds a 49 percent stake in Irancell. The current U.S. sanctions on Iran also complicate any attempt to exit. Earlier this year, MTN also protested after the CEO of Irancell was ousted by the Iranian authorities over delaying an internet blackout order during the domestic protest. This arguably makes MTN’s position in Iran even more difficult than Telenor’s trajectory in Myanmar. When MTN is finally able to withdraw from the country, can it exit in a more responsible way?
Written by Ranking Digital Rights

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Binny Bansal-backed AI startup ShopOS has launched Sloosh, a self-service platform that makes the image and video generation technology it uses for enterprise clients available to individual creators and small businesses.
Speaking to Inc42, ShopOS cofounder Ajay PV said Sloosh targets creators, designers, photographers, video editors and small businesses who want to generate visual content using AI tools without engaging its enterprise creative team.
“ShopOS owns the outcome for mid and large brands. Sloosh goes after a much bigger market: anyone who makes visual content needs creatives every day,” he said.
The platform is being opened to users globally, with paid subscription plans starting at $19 per month.
Launched today, the platform operates on a subscription model, with paid plans starting at $19 per month globally.
Ajay said the decision to build a self-service product followed interest from smaller brands and individual creators who could not afford ShopOS’ enterprise retainers.
“Some of our smaller brands couldn’t afford the retainers and asked us to turn the technology into a product they could use. The idea had been brewing for a while, and over the last three months, we worked on packaging the image and video orchestration engine we had built to generate millions of creative assets for our brands into a product called Sloosh,” the cofounder added.
Sloosh brings third-party AI image and video models into a single platform, allowing users to generate content from prompts and templates. It also offers reusable workflows called Spaces and a visual canvas, Spacelab, for building or modifying these workflows.
Spaces allow users to repeat a creative task with different inputs without rebuilding prompts and settings each time. The platform also supports batch generation, enabling users to produce multiple images and videos through the same workflow.
Users can also access human creative experts for more complex projects, according to the startup.
Sloosh supports connections with AI assistants through model context protocol (MCP), allowing users to request image and video generation from compatible tools. The startup said it is also launching an Adobe After Effects plugin and plans to add more integrations.
To attract users, ShopOS plans to work with creators and build communities across markets. Users will also be able to publish and share their Spaces.
Sloosh is currently part of ShopOS, but the team is open to exploring a restructuring depending on the platform’s growth, Ajay said.
ShopOS Eyes Global Expansion
Founded in 2025 by Sai Krishna V K and Ajay, ShopOS builds AI tools and services for ecommerce brands across catalogue operations, category management, pricing, promotions, recommendations, and marketing.
The cofounders previously built augmented reality and AI commerce startup Scapic, which Flipkart acquired in 2020.
ShopOS raised $20 Mn from Binny Bansal’s investment vehicle 3STATE Ventures in June last year to develop its products, onboard brand partners, and expand its team.
Under its managed services model, ShopOS delivers finished creative assets, with its team reviewing and refining AI-generated content before handing it over to clients.
Ajay said the startup currently serves around 30-40 brands in India and a few in the US. It has also secured US contracts worth around $500,000.
Over the next year, ShopOS aims to expand its enterprise customer base to more than 100 brands in India and 40-50 brands in the US.
Its clients include Kareena Kapoor-backed Fizzy Globlet, Van Heusen, among others. The startup claims its services have reduced clients’ production budgets by nearly 90%.

items.title: Nvidia boss criticises 'cheap' AI doomsday warnings
items.summary:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia's boss Jensen Huang said on Thursday that warnings that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity were "cheap" attempts to grab headlines.
"When you say that it will be the end of the human civilisation, first of all, it's not true," he told a conference organised by his company in Berlin.
While such statements generate "headlines", they were "made up" and "cheap", added Huang, whose visit to Berlin is the final stop of a European tour.
After incidents of the technology getting around controls during tests, there has been a heated debate about whether AI presents an existential risk to humanity.
In September, a researcher resigned from Anthropic with a stark warning that leading AI labs were "gambling with our lives", and the bosses of Anthropic and fellow industry giant OpenAI have called for a slowdown.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia's boss Jensen Huang said on Thursday that warnings that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity were "cheap" attempts to grab headlines.
"When you say that it will be the end of the human civilisation, first of all, it's not true," he told a conference organised by his company in Berlin.
While such statements generate "headlines", they were "made up" and "cheap", added Huang, whose visit to Berlin is the final stop of a European tour.
After incidents of the technology getting around controls during tests, there has been a heated debate about whether AI presents an existential risk to humanity.
In September, a researcher resigned from Anthropic with a stark warning that leading AI labs were "gambling with our lives", and the bosses of Anthropic and fellow industry giant OpenAI have called for a slowdown.
Read: DeepSeek wrapping up $15b fundraising to fuel AI race, sources say
Huang, however, is firmly in the opposing camp, and has advocated for development of the technology to move full steam ahead.
Speaking in Berlin, he urged the world to approach AI with "responsible optimism".
"If you care about the future, past our own lives, if we care about the future of sustainability, this is the perfect time -- build AI," he said.
"Don't try to stifle AI."
US regulators are seen as unlikely to intervene when it comes to AI development.
President Donald Trump opposes strict regulation and said in September that the US government would rename the technology "super intelligence" in official communications.
During Huang's European tour, Nvidia pledged nearly $10 billion in investments in the continent's technology sector and urged Europe, which is lagging behind in the AI race, to move faster.

items.content:
France on Thursday reported the first ‌human case of the Shamonda virus, usually found in livestock, in a patient who later died, with authorities adding there was no risk to the general population at this stage.
It is suspected that the victim was bitten by ​a midge carrying the virus in eastern France, where it had circulated among animals ​this spring and summer, the government said in a statement.
The UN's World Health ⁠Organisation said it was in contact with French authorities about the outbreak.
The patient died in early ​October and had been receiving treatment for a serious illness that made them more susceptible to infection ​than the general population, the Stockholm-based European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said in a statement.
Read: Govt swings into action after new polio case in Karachi
The victim was a man in his 60s living in the Lyon area, local newspaper Le Progres reported.
"Based on current information and knowledge ​of the transmission of closely related viruses, this is an isolated human case, and it is ​unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time," said the Geneva-based WHO, which coordinates responses to international ‌public health ⁠issues and emergencies.
The French government also said no health risk to the general population had been identified.
Virus spreading in animals in Europe
Shamonda is transmitted by biting midges and most commonly found in cattle, though it has also been found in horses, alpacas, sheep and goats, according to the World Organisation for ​Animal Health (WOAH).
It is not classified ​as a disease ⁠under the EU Animal Health Law and is not subject to official surveillance or control measures.
Read more: Australia confirms first H5N1 bird flu case on sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island
Identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, Shamonda was first confirmed in ​Europe in late July after genomic tests on sick cattle in southern ​Germany, Switzerland and ⁠eastern France.
France's weekly animal health surveillance bulletin said it had also been detected in Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and the UK's Jersey.
The virus has several effects on ⁠animals, with affected cattle ​showing diarrhoea, weakness, loss of appetite and, less often, ​fever, French animal health authorities said. A study of nine French dairy farms found milk production fell by up to 75%.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Update | October 22, 16:51
Delhi-based B2B travel tech startup TravClan has raised a $5 Mn funding round comprising a mix of equity and debt. While Walmart-owned ecommerce major Flipkart and Singapore-based investment firm August One subscribed to the equity portion of the round, Trifecta Capital provided the debt financing.
“The next generation of travel software will not just help sellers search faster. It will increasingly execute work for them. Our ambition is to make TravClan the infrastructure that any travel business can build on instead of having to recreate the entire travel stack itself. This capital allows us to invest aggressively behind that opportunity,” said TravClan CEO and cofounder Arun Bagaria.
Original | October 5, 18:51
Walmart-owned Flipkart picked up a minority stake in Delhi-based B2B travel tech startup TravClan to bolster its international travel offerings, expand holiday packages offered by subsidiaries Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel as well as enhancing on-ground support across.
The ecommerce giant also aims to leverage the partnership to expand its own curated international leisure offerings by tapping into TravClan’s technology and partner network.
On the other side of the table, the fresh capital infusion will support TravClan’s team expansion in business development, engineering, and destination operations, as well as allow for further investments in global supply, technology, and destination expansion.
“Travellers today are looking for more than a flight or hotel booking. They want a holiday that is curated around their interests and supported throughout the journey. TravClan’s supplier network and destination capabilities will help us build that experience across Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel,” said Nishant Verman, Flipkart’s SVP, Corporate Development and Partnerships.
Founded by Arun Bagaria, Chirag Agrawal, and Ashish Thapliyal in 2018, TravClan assists travel agents to build and grow online businesses. It works with over 15,000 travel agents to customise and book real-time packages, hotels, and activities.
The startup’s cap table also includes angel investors like Cars24 cofounders Vikram Chopra and Mehul Agrawal and Trip.com’s Travis Katz, as well as institutional investors like Leo Capital.
Flipkart’s Diversification Push
For Flipkart, the travel tech investment adds on to its push to build out its other business verticals beyond its flagship ecommerce platform.
While the company has been eyeing new entries in the food delivery and the event ticketing industry, it has been aggressively doubling down on its quick commerce arm, Flipkart Minutes.
Ahead of its annual Big Billion Days, the ecommerce giant announced that it has expanded its dark store network to nearly 1,200 Flipkart Minutes microfulfillment centres across 150-plus cities. The company is now expected to add another 1,000 dark stores by mid-2027 or the Big Billion Days sale of 2027.
In recent years, it has also expanded its in-house Flipkart Travel beyond flight booking services into bus bookings and hotel bookings. Cleartrip, an online travel aggregator which Flipkart acquired in 2021, also later expanded into corporate travel.
Besides, Flipkart made some additional investments in AI startups last week. Its investment arm Flipkart Ventures backed Alive, an AI-powered platform for live consumer experiences, and Keploy, a native-AI software testing platform.
To date, Flipkart has made over 20 startup investments via Flipkart Ventures across AI, consumer internet, fintech, e-commerce adjacencies and logistics tech.
It claims to support portfolio ventures with strategic mentorship, operational expertise and access to its ecosystem in order to help them scale, besides the capital they get.
