items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
Omnichannel furniture and home furnishings brand Chapter Homes has raised ₹63 Cr ($6.6 Mn) in a strategic funding round through a mix of debt and equity. The fundraise valued the startup at nearly ₹1,000 Cr (around $106 Mn).
The round saw participation from Bessemer Venture Partners, Stride Ventures, comedian Tanmay Bhat and a clutch of family offices. The brand claims to have also received further commitments from undisclosed backers for a future fundraise.
In a statement, the startup said that it plans to utilise the fresh capital to strengthen product development, expand into newer categories and invest in technology and brand building. A chunk of the capital will also be used to scale its omnichannel distribution network and set up its initial offline footprint.
“… Consumers are increasingly looking for better-designed products, trusted quality, strong functionality and a superior overall experience – online and in store – and we see a meaningful opportunity to build for those needs. That is why we are building focused brands for each category across home and kitchen,” said Chapter Homes cofounder Nitin Chugh.
Founded in 2025 by former PharmEasy executives Chugh, Akarsh Bharadwaj, Shrey Mittal, Dhiraj Jain and Dheeraj Goyal, Chapter Homes claims to be building multiple consumer brands across categories for home and kitchen needs of Indian consumers. It has already launched a home furnishing brand under HOKIPO.
Going forward, it plans to leverage synergies across supply chain, content, technology and distribution to expand into adjacent categories such as cookware, home décor and small kitchen appliances. The startup also said that it plans to leverage AI across cataloguing and demand forecasting to product assortment and customer retention to launch faster and rein in costs.
Notably, Chapter Homes is not the first home improvement startup to emerge from the PharmEasy stable. Earlier this year, AllHome, founded by PharmEasy cofounders, raised ₹200 Cr in its Series B round led by Bessemer Venture Partners.
The fundraise comes amid continued investor interest in the home improvement and home decor segment. In August, home decor marketplace Vaaree raised ₹65 Cr in its Series A round co-led by Hero Enterprise and Cap Alpha Ventures. Prior to this, D2C homeware startup HomeEssentials also raised ₹70 Cr in its pre-Series B round led by 360 ONE Asset.
Even the adjacent kitchen tech segment is seeing healthy adoption among masses due to LPG shortages. Many Indians are now buying induction cooktops, AI-powered smart appliances and electric rice cookers and air fryers. It is this segment that Chapter Homes plans to target going forward.
But for now, Chapter Homes is eyeing a piece of the Indian home furnishing and decor market, which is projected to become a $45.5 Bn opportunity by 2031.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Apple has warned customers that the new iPhone Duo may be difficult to buy in stores on launch day due to limited stock and strong demand. The foldable smartphone will go on sale on Friday, October 23, 2026, but customers planning to purchase it without a pre-order may face difficulties.
According to Apple, demand for the iPhone Duo has been extraordinary since pre-orders opened last week. The company expects the limited stock available for walk-in customers to sell out quickly.
The warning means buyers who have not secured a pre-order may need to reserve a device online or wait for additional stock.
Apple Confirms Limited Walk-In Availability for iPhone Duo
Apple will offer limited walk-in stock in the United States, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Mexico, Germany, the Netherlands, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United Kingdom.
Some Apple Stores in Italy will also offer the device to walk-in customers, although the company has not identified the locations. In Macao, walk-in purchases will be available only on launch day, with limited inventory.
However, customers in France, China, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates will not be able to purchase the iPhone Duo as walk-in buyers on launch day.
Instead, customers in these markets will need to book a pickup time through Apple’s online store. The store has currently advised customers to check again on Saturday, October 24, leaving some uncertainty about whether pickup reservations will become available on launch day itself.
Apple Takes Steps to Control Demand
Apple’s restrictions appear aimed at managing crowds and limiting purchases by resellers who may try to buy devices in large quantities and sell them at higher prices.
The company has also limited iPhone Duo purchases to two units per customer. This measure is intended to give more buyers a chance to purchase the foldable phone rather than allowing a small number of customers to acquire large quantities.
There is some positive news for customers who have already placed pre-orders. Apple has moved up estimated shipping dates for many buyers after delivery estimates previously extended as far as January 2027.
The change suggests that some customers may receive their devices sooner than initially expected, although availability will depend on their individual orders.
iPhone Duo Specifications and Features
The iPhone Duo is Apple’s new foldable smartphone and comes with two LTPO OLED displays. Its inner screen measures 7.6 inches and offers a resolution of 1,878 x 2,670 pixels, while the 5.4-inch cover display has a resolution of 1,398 x 2,034 pixels. Both screens support a 120Hz refresh rate.
The device runs on Apple’s A20 Pro chipset and includes 12GB of RAM. Buyers can choose configurations with up to 2TB of internal storage.
For photography, the phone features a 48MP main camera with sensor-shift optical image stabilisation and a 48MP ultrawide camera. It also includes a 12MP selfie camera on the cover display and a 4MP under-display camera on the inner screen.
The iPhone Duo packs a 4,883mAh battery and supports 25W MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging. Other features include an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance and Apple’s iOS 27.1 software.
iPhone Duo Price
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the United States. Its starting price is €2,299 in Germany and £1,999 in the United Kingdom.
With strong demand and limited walk-in availability, customers who want the foldable iPhone may need to act quickly. Those who have not placed a pre-order should check Apple’s online store for pickup reservations and future stock updates before visiting a retail location.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
North Korean hacking group Lazarus is using post-quantum cryptography to deliver malware in a new cyberattack campaign targeting South Korean organizations. The operation combines older malware tools with new techniques designed to make attacks harder to detect.
Cybersecurity researchers at Kaspersky have named the campaign FlashHole. Their investigation found that the hackers use a standardized post-quantum encryption mechanism to secure communication between infected systems and their command-and-control (C2) servers.
Lazarus Hackers Use Post-Quantum Cryptography to Deliver Malware
The attacks reportedly began in July 2025. Researchers identified at least three affected companies operating in the software, construction, and wired communication equipment manufacturing sectors in South Korea. However, they believe the campaign may have targeted more organizations.
How the FlashHole Campaign Works
The attackers use phishing pages to direct victims to specially designed GitHub pages. These pages load JavaScript code from external domains, starting a complex infection process that allows the hackers to install malware on targeted systems.
The attack chain also abuses INISAFE CrossWeb EX, a security tool commonly used in South Korea. The tool’s process launches a legitimate Windows executable called fsquirt.exe, which the attackers use to execute malicious code.
This process installs TechHub, a downloader that retrieves additional malware from private GitHub repositories.
The campaign also uses ClientHub, a malware loader that supports communication through Dropbox and direct data exchange with LPEClient. This helps the attackers deliver additional malicious components to compromised systems.
Multiple Malware Tools Used in Attacks
LPEClient plays a central role in the campaign. The malware collects information about infected systems, receives encrypted payloads, and helps the attackers avoid security monitoring.
Another tool, called Cubridge, is a modular backdoor that gives attackers several ways to control compromised computers. It supports file management, command execution, system reconnaissance, screenshot capturing, and the installation of additional malware.
Kaspersky also identified tools designed to steal sensitive information from Chromium-based browsers. These tools can target account credentials, cookies, and browsing history.
Researchers noted that much of the malicious code runs directly in system memory instead of being stored as files on the device. This technique can make detection more difficult because security tools may have fewer files to examine. However, some components still leave files on infected systems to maintain access.
Why Post-Quantum Cryptography Matters
One of the most notable features of FlashHole is its use of ML-KEM-1024, a standardized post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism approved by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).
Post-quantum cryptography is designed to protect communications against attacks from future quantum computers. It can also help address the risk of attackers collecting encrypted information today and attempting to decrypt it later when more powerful technology becomes available.
In the FlashHole campaign, Lazarus uses ML-KEM to establish shared cryptographic keys between its malware and command-and-control infrastructure.
According to Kaspersky, LPEClient receives data containing four ML-KEM-1024 public keys from the C2 server. It then generates four separate pairs of shared keys and ciphertexts. The malware encrypts the ciphertexts using the GOST algorithm and sends them back to the server through ClientHub.
The resulting shared secrets provide key material for the Threefish encryption algorithm. This allows LPEClient to decrypt the server’s response, which contains configuration information and an executable payload.
The final payload is Cubridge, which LPEClient loads directly into the system’s memory.
Kaspersky believes this combination of post-quantum cryptography and in-memory execution helps Lazarus conceal its subsequent payloads and reduce the chances of detection.
Links to Earlier Lazarus Operations
Researchers have placed FlashHole within the broader Cascade Hole activity and linked it to the earlier Operation SyncHole campaign with medium-to-high confidence.
The findings highlight how advanced hacking groups are combining established malware with newer cryptographic methods to improve their attacks. While post-quantum encryption is being developed to strengthen cybersecurity, its use in this campaign shows that malicious actors can also adopt modern security technologies to protect their own communications and conceal malware delivery.
The discovery reinforces the need for organizations to strengthen phishing defenses, monitor suspicious application behavior, and investigate unusual activity involving trusted software and online services.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
OnePlus is putting a fan inside a phone. The company has confirmed that the OnePlus Ace 7 Pro and Ace 7 launch in China on October 29 at 7 PM local time, which is 4:00 PM in Pakistan.
OnePlus calls the Ace 7 Pro its “most powerful Ace ever” and the first OnePlus phone with an active cooling fan.
What OnePlus has confirmed
The Ace 7 Pro runs on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a 3 nm chip with an Adreno 840 GPU. The fan is the headline feature, with two air paths: one cools the chip, and the other cools the back panel.
The company says the design lowers temperature by up to 10°C in long gaming sessions. The air intake sits away from where fingers rest, and hot air leaves through the top of the phone.
OnePlus also claims maximum frame rates at maximum graphics in all games. In one example, it says the Ace 7 Pro beats rival phones with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 in Delta Force at 185 fps.
These are company claims, not independent tests. Earlier leaker posts described the rival in that test only as an unnamed 2nm flagship, which hit 165 fps, so the exact comparison phone is unclear.
What is still a leak?
OnePlus has not confirmed the rest of the specifications.
Detail
Status
Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, Adreno 840, two-path fan
Confirmed by OnePlus
6.78-inch 1.5K OLED flat display, 185 Hz
Leaked
200MP Samsung HP5 main camera
Leaked
50MP 3.5x periscope telephoto (Pro)
Leaked
About a 9,000 mAh battery
Leaked
120W wired charging
Leaked
Ace 7 with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 V Series variant
Leaked
Leaks also say the main camera will use OPPO’s flagship camera processing. Pricing has not been announced. Whether the standard Ace 7 gets a fan is also unclear. There is no certainty yet that it will have the cooling fan found on the Pro.
Why a fan matters
Most phones slow down in long gaming sessions as the chip heats up. This is called thermal throttling, where the processor cuts speed to protect itself. Vapour chambers and heat spreaders delay the effect. A fan pushes heat out of the body, which is a more direct fix.
The trade-off is physical. A fan needs openings, which raises questions about dust, water resistance, noise and long-term durability. OnePlus has said none of this so far.
Editorial view
A cooling fan is a clear selling point, but the evidence offered so far is thin. OnePlus’s Delta Force result is a single game, and “max frame rates in all games” is a marketing line, not a measurement.
If the claims hold, the Ace 7 Pro could set a template for mid-priced performance phones. If the fan proves noisy or fragile, it will stay a niche feature. Price will decide how many people ever find out.

items.content:
Government of India (GoI) has announced the sale (re-issue) of two dated securities for a notified amount of ₹33,000 crore as per the following details:
Sr No Security Date of Repayment Notified Amount
(₹ Crore) GoI specific Notification Auction Date Settlement Date
1 6.53% GS 2031 Sep 07, 2031 19,000 F.No.4(1)-B(W&M)/2026 dated October 19, 2026 October 23, 2026
(Friday) October 26, 2026
(Monday)
2 7.71% GS 2066 May 18, 2066 14,000
  Total   33,000      
2. GoI will have the option to retain additional subscription up to ₹2,000 crore against each security mentioned above.
3. The securities will be sold through Reserve Bank of India Mumbai Office, Fort, Mumbai – 400001. The sale will be subject to the terms and conditions spelt out in the ‘Specific Notification’ mentioned above and the General Notification F.No.4(2)–B(W&M)/2018, dated March 26, 2025.
4. The auction will be conducted using multiple price method. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system) on October 23, 2026 (Friday). The non-competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 a.m. and 11:00 a.m. and the competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. The result will be announced on the same day and payment by successful bidders will have to be made on October 26, 2026 (Monday).
5. Bids for underwriting of the Additional Competitive Underwriting (ACU) portion can be submitted by ‘Primary Dealers’ from 09:00 a.m. up to 09:30 a.m. on October 23, 2026 (Friday) on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
6. The securities will be eligible for “When Issued” trading for a period commencing from October 21, 2026 – October 23, 2026.
7. Operational guidelines for Government of India dated securities auction and other details are given in the Annex.
Ajit Prasad          
Deputy General Manager
(Communications)    
Press Release: 2026-2027/1354
ANNEX
Type of Auction
1. For multiple price-based auction, successful bids will get accepted at the respective quoted yield/price for the security. For uniform price-based auction, bids will get accepted at the cut off yield/price accepted in the auction.
2. The auction will be yield based for new security and price based for securities which are re-issued.
3. In case of a Floating Rate Bonds (FRB), the auction will be spread-based for new security and price based for securities which are reissued. At the time of placing bids for new FRB, the spread should be quoted in percentage terms.
Minimum Bid Size
4. The securities will be issued for a minimum amount of ₹10,000/- (nominal) and in multiples of ₹10,000/- thereafter.
Non-Competitive Segment
5. In all the auctions, Government security up to 5% of the notified amount for sale of individual security will be allotted to the eligible individuals and institutions under the Scheme for Non-competitive Bidding Facility in the Auctions of Government Securities. Individual investors can also place bids as per the non-competitive scheme through the Retail Direct portal (https://rbiretaildirect.org.in).
6. Each bank or Primary Dealer (PD) on the basis of firm orders received from their constituents will submit a single consolidated non-competitive bid for individual security on behalf of its constituents in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
7. Allotment under the non-competitive segment will be at the weighted average rate of yield/price of the successful bids that will emerge in the auction on the basis of the competitive bidding.
Submission of Bids
8. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
9. Bids in physical form will not be accepted except in extraordinary circumstances.
Business Continuity Plan (BCP)-IT failure
10. Only in the event of system failure, physical bids will be accepted. Such physical bids should be submitted to the Public Debt Office, Mumbai through (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 022-22603457, 022-22603190) in the prescribed form which can be obtained from RBI website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx) before the auction timing ends.
11. In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team should be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415).
12. For other auction related difficulties, IDMD auction team can be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-22702431, 022-22705125).
Multiple Bids
13. An investor can submit more than one competitive bid in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
14. The aggregate amount of bids submitted by an investor in an auction should not exceed the notified amount of auction.
Decision Making Process
15. On the basis of bids received, the Reserve Bank will determine the minimum price/maximum yield up to which tenders for purchase of Government Security will be accepted at the auctions.
16. Bids quoted at rates lower than the minimum price/higher than the maximum yield determined by the Reserve Bank of India will be rejected.
17. Reserve Bank of India will have the full discretion to accept or reject any or all bids either wholly or partially without assigning any reason.
Issue of Securities
18. Issue of securities to the successful bidders will be by credit to Subsidiary General Ledger Account (SGL) or to Constituents’ Subsidiary General Ledger Account (CSGL), maintained with Reserve Bank of India.
Periodicity of Interest Payment
19. Interest on the Government Security will generally be paid half-yearly other than in case of securities with non-standard maturities. The exact periodicity of coupon payment is invariably mentioned in the specific notification for the issue of security.
Underwriting of the Government Securities
20. The underwriting of the Government Securities under auctions by the ‘Primary Dealers’ will be as per the “Revised Scheme of Underwriting Commitment and Liquidity Support” announced by the Reserve Bank vide circular RBI/2007-08/186 dated November 14, 2007 as amended from time to time.
Eligibility for Repurchase Transactions (Repo)
21. The securities will be eligible for Repurchase Transactions (Repo) as per the conditions mentioned in Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Repurchase Transactions (Repo)) Directions, 2025 as amended from time to time.
Eligibility for ‘When Issued’ Trading
22. The securities will be eligible for “When Issued” trading in accordance with the guidelines on ‘When Issued transactions in Central Government Securities’ issued by the Reserve Bank of India vide circular No. RBI/2018-19/25 dated July 24, 2018 as amended from time to time.
Investment by Non-Residents
23. Investments by Non-Residents are subject to the guidelines on ‘Fully Accessible Route’ for Investment by Non-residents in Government Securities and other related guidelines as issued by the Reserve Bank from time to time.

items.content: Mumbai: In just about six weeks, the Reserve Bank of India has drained banking system liquidity from a peak surplus of ₹11 lakh crore to ₹48,303 crore. How did the central bank withdraw this liquidity and what was the market impact of this? ET explains.Why was there a sudden gush in system liquidity?The banking system was suddenly flushed with liquidity after banks attracted $133 billion dollars from overseas Indians under the FCNR(B) scheme. Banks exchanged these dollars with the RBI through a swap facility, receiving rupee funds in return. Thus, system liquidity, which stood at a surplus of about ₹3.5 lakh crore in August, went up to over ₹11 lakh crore in September.What was the impact of this sudden liquidity surplus?The overnight rates, the weighted average call rate (WACR), went as low as 4.93% in mid September, or 30 bps below the repo rate. The WACR is supposed to be closely aligned with the RBI repo rate. However, crude oil prices were also beginning to rise, fuelling expectations of a rate hike by the RBI to contain inflationary pressures. But for a rate hike to translate into tighter monetary conditions, liquidity would ideally need to be neutral or in deficit, with WACR at the repo rate. The banking system, however, was flush with surplus funds, kept overnight rates below the repo rate and potentially diluting the impact of monetary tightening.Read more: Sundaram Mutual Fund announces launch of Equity Ex-Top 100 Long Short Fund through its SIF platform SelectWhat measures did the RBI take to absorb liquidity?The Reserve Bank of India was draining liquidity via temporary variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions. But the WACR was still lower than the repo rate. The central bank also conducted sell-buy swaps of at least $10 billion in September in an effort to drain the excess cash.Lastly, the RBI increased banks daily cash reserve ratio (CRR) to 99%, from 90%. Raising the daily minimum to 99% reduced banks' flexibility to use those funds, helping Reserve Bank of India absorb surplus liquidity and keep overnight rates closer to its intended policy rate.With the RBI maintaining a calibrated tightening stance, the persistently large liquidity surplus and overnight rates trading below the repo rate were at odds with its policy stance. The central bank therefore needed to absorb excess liquidity to align money-market conditions more closely with its tightening stance.Read more: Jio Platforms' IPO-linked inflows boost rupee; elevated oil prices spur cautionAfter withdrawing a substantial amount of surplus liquidity, why did the RBI announce a variable rate repo (VRR) operation to inject funds ?The liquidity drain had pushed the WACR higher, with the rate rising to 5.75% last Friday, 25 basis points above the 5.50% repo rate on Friday. The WACR remains elevated at around 5.65% on Wednesday.To prevent overnight rates from rising too sharply as liquidity tightens, the RBI has temporarily infused funds through VRR operations. It conducted a ₹1 lakh crore VRR auction on Monday and a ₹50,000 crore operation on Friday.

But concerns over elevated valuations are beginning to catch up as investors evaluate whether the broader risk-off sentiment could impact future returns.Over the past two years, the midcap and smallcap indices have each entered correction territory three times. This perception could be slowly shifting with valuations rising."What is perceived as a safe space can gradually become unsafe as valuations go up. We are seeing corrections even in midcap and smallcap stocks, although this may not yet be visible at the index level," he said.Read more: Jio IPO Day 1: Issue subscribed 3 times on strong QIB push; retail portion booked 68%. Check GMPOf the 97 stocks in the midcap index that have hit 52-week highs so far in 2026, two have fallen 40-45% from their peaks, 18 have declined 30-40%, 35 have lost 20-30%, and 42 are down 1-20%.In the smallcap segment, 172 stocks have hit 52-week highs so far this year. Of these, seven have fallen 40-50%, 23 have declined 30-40%, 64 have lost 20-30%, and 70 are down 1-20%.Even after the recent declines, valuations are still at a premium over large-caps. The mid-cap index is currently trading at a 42% premium to the Nifty, compared with its five-year average of 40%. The small-cap index is trading at a 45% premium, below its five-year average of 75%, analysts said."Small and mid-cap valuations have come off from very high levels but remain on the higher side," said Atul Bhole, executive vice-president and fund manager at Kotak Mahindra AMC. items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Agentic AI startup Karta AI has raised $3 Mn (around ₹28 Cr) in a seed funding round led by PeerCapital and Cedar Hill Capital. The round also saw participation from Wyser VC, CDM Capital and Seedstars.
The startup intends to use the fresh capital to expand its go-to-market (GTM) strategy and distribution over the next two years. A portion will also help it expand its product development, particularly capabilities around emerging AI technologies such as self learning, cofounder and CEO Vijaypal Singh told Inc42.
Founded in 2024 by former Razorpay executives Vijaypal Singh and Abhishek Kushwaha, Karta AI offers an omnichannel customer communication platform spanning voice, chat, email and WhatsApp.
The startup focuses primarily on voice-based interactions, targeting complex inbound queries that require coordination across multiple enterprise systems rather than routine frequently asked questions.
It claims to handle around 2 Mn customer conversations a month across more than 25 languages. According to Singh, it has 10-12 paying customers, including PhonePe, Pine Labs, Bajaj and Aavas.
Karta AI deploys its AI agents across customer servicing and retention workflows at financial institutions.
The startup claims its agent resolves around 70% of borrower queries end to end without human intervention, reducing the cost per query by approximately 50%. These queries include requests for loan disbursal updates, statements of account, foreclosure statements and the release of property documents.
It focuses on inbound interactions, where customers contact businesses to resolve issues such as failed payments, blocked cards, loan-related queries and insurance claims. Unlike outbound calls, which businesses typically initiate for a specific purpose, inbound conversations can involve multiple queries and require AI agents to retrieve information and execute actions across several systems.
Singh said he and Kushwaha began working on Karta AI after leaving fintech major Razorpay, where they had worked on internal AI automation. The startup initially focused on chat-based automation before expanding into voice in August 2025.
Karta AI targets level 2 (L2) and level 3 (L3) queries, which require AI agents to interpret multiple customer intents, retrieve information from different systems and execute workflows. This differs from level 1 (L1) queries, such as basic FAQs or requests that can be resolved through a single API call.
For instance, a borrower may call a lender to check loan disbursal status and request a foreclosure statement in the same conversation. The agent must identify both intents, retrieve the relevant information and initiate the required workflows.
Singh said Karta AI has achieved 70-80% end-to-end automation in its inbound proof-of-concept (PoC) deployments and has won all such PoCs so far.
The focus on complex queries reflects their disproportionate cost. According to Singh, L1 queries account for 30-40% of customer service volumes but only around 10% of costs. L2 queries contribute another 30-40% of volumes, while L3 queries make up the remaining 10-20%. Together, he estimates, L2 and L3 queries account for around 80% of customer service costs.
The platform does not automate every interaction. Queries involving fraud or other high-risk matters, along with processes lacking clearly defined standard operating procedures (SOPs), are routed to human agents. Customers can also request a human representative.
How Karta AI’s AI Tech Works
Karta AI’s proprietary context engine is designed to help its agents manage multi-intent conversations. While conventional voice AI systems typically convert speech to text, process the query through a large language model (LLM) and generate a spoken response, Karta AI adds a layer that identifies customer intent and retrieves relevant enterprise data before generating an answer.
The engine draws on SOPs, knowledge bases, previous conversations and API data. This allows an agent to handle follow-up requests within the same call without treating each query in isolation.
Karta AI integrates with enterprise systems to execute customer-facing and back-office workflows. It uses models from OpenAI and Google’s Gemini family, alongside open-source models such as Kimi and Gemma, Singh said.
Its voice platform supports around 25 Indian languages, while its chat offering supports more than 200 languages. The voice system is designed to accommodate Hindi-English code-switching, regional accents and dialects, though performance varies across languages.
Given its focus on financial services, the startup has built compliance measures and guardrails into the platform. Singh said agents are tested by Karta AI’s team, customers and AI-based testing systems before deployment.
Karta AI primarily serves Indian businesses in banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI), where high customer interaction volumes and complex back-office processes offer opportunities for automation. It plans to develop reusable, industry-specific capabilities before expanding into international markets.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Healthtech startup CureBay raised around ₹100 Cr ($10.6 Mn) in a pre-Series C funding round, comprising over ₹69 Cr in equity led by IvyCap Ventures alongside existing investors and around ₹30 Cr in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners.
CureBay cofounder and CEO Priyadarshi Mohapatra told Inc42 that the round came amid strong investor interest. The startup will use the proceeds to expand geographically, strengthen its delivery network and invest in its AI and technology capabilities.
The healthtech startup, which currently operates in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar, plans to enter Telangana and Andhra Pradesh markets next. It aims to grow its network of rural clinics from 250 to 800 over the next two to three years.
CureBay connects patients in underserved areas with healthcare providers through a combination of rural clinics, local community health workers and a digital platform linking patients to doctors, hospitals, diagnostic laboratories and pharmacies. It also uses AI-assisted screening and care coordination to support patient care.
The startup is also investing in GPUs and training AI models to screen patients and assess health risks. Its existing AI products cover areas such as skin conditions, dental health and haemoglobin screening, with plans to expand these capabilities.
“We have a full suite of AI products for areas like skin, dental, and haemoglobin. We will keep adding more products and continue investing in width as well as depth,” Mohapatra said.
CureBay also runs Kavach, a subscription programme designed to encourage preventive care by offering consultations and support for medicines, diagnostics and certain hospitalisation-related costs.
The startup claims to have served over 12 Lakh patients and connected more than 270 doctors and 1,000 healthcare professionals across 4,500 pincodes.
Prior to this round, CureBay had raised over $34.6 Mn from investors including Bertelsmann India Investments, British International Investment and Elevar Equity.
While the startup is yet to file its audited FY26 financial statements, Mohapatra said it closed the fiscal year with an annual recurring revenue (ARR) of nearly ₹170 Cr. It aims to double this figure by the end of FY27.
“We broke even at an operating EBITDA level in FY26. Currently, our monthly run rate is about ₹20 Cr, and we expect the number to grow almost 50% from now till March,” he told Inc42.
Mohapatra attributed the growth to customers spending more on CureBay as they increasingly view it as a trusted healthcare partner, alongside the expansion into new markets.
However, the startup remains loss-making at the company level. Mohapatra said entering new markets entails fresh expenditure, while profitability would depend on reaching a more stable operating scale.
“When we stop expanding and we reach a stable state, we will be net positive at a company level. So the important metric for us to track is operating EBITDA,” he said.

items.author: Malka Older
items.content:
Protest helps close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we actually have
Originally published on Global Voices
Image via Canva Pro.
This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Democracy is often presented as an orderly, structured system of representation and deliberation, colorless and linear like an organizational version of the faux-classical architecture so many democratic countries adopt for their government buildings. Voting leads to representatives, debates lead to votes on laws, participation leads to action, like columns leading to a pediment.
But democracy is not actually about cushy debating chambers or political speeches — or not only about that. Democracy means rule by the people, and in most of the systems we call democracies today, the people’s role is for the most part narrowed to voting, and often a curtailed, difficult, limited vote that does little for accountability or expressing preferences on specific issues.
Protest is one of the ways we close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we have. With protest, the people can express general emotional responses or very specific policy proposals; we can punctuate the long intervals of electoral cycles to influence government outside of the voting booth; and perhaps most importantly, we build coalitions and solidarity, forming a collective consciousness of our democratic responsibilities.
Voting is a single, standardized, and fairly isolated action. Protest, on the other hand, unfolds in dozens, if not hundreds, of permutations, letting us — the people — express our creativity along with our civic engagement. One of the wonderful things about this spotlight has been seeing the sheer range of capacity and ingenuity as people use protest to inspire others, express anger or determination, and pressure governments and other decision-makers.
Maybe the most obvious example of this in the spotlight is the collaborative article on protest music, with its examples of not just different songs, but different styles and approaches and even understanding of what it means to use music for advocacy. In Japan, young people are finding new paths into activism, like handing out placards, while the Cockroach Janta Party in India has used memes and online jokes to mobilize young people right from the start of the movement.
Severe oppression requires more creativity, as this article about the evolution of street art in Russia points out. Similarly, Russians — many of them in exile — used allusion and wordplay in online videos to get their messages across.
That raises the question, ably explored in this piece, about whether online and offline protest are equally effective, and what their different strengths and weaknesses are. And, if the digital world has enabled new forms of protest, it has also activated new means of repression. Our friends at Ranking Digital Rights contributed this well-researched article about the complicity of telecoms in internet shutdowns in Africa. This piece, from AlgorithmWatch, details the Russian surveillance software being used against protesters in Georgia. And the virtual world can be used to hijack, undermine, or redirect protest energy, as this case study from Funky Citizens in Romania details.
As vibrant as protests are in the moment, though, it’s also important to ask about the long-term impact, the consequences, both good and bad. The protests in Bangladesh two years ago were successful in the sense that they led to a change of government; this article asks whether that change of government led to a meaningful difference in democratic accountability. And this powerful piece from Nepal follows up with those involved in the Gen Z protests there last year, tracking the long-term impacts of injuries and trauma.
As with all our monthly spotlights, this one is in many ways about showing the common threads that link all of our countries, as well as the exceptions that can open us to new ideas or inspire us to a different kind of action. This spotlight is, then, a form of protest in its own right: a way of reasserting that protest is legitimate, important for democracy, and everywhere.
Written by Malka Older

The Chair the Local Organising Committee of the flag off of All Progressives Congress(APC) 2027 Presidential Campaign and the Deputy Governor of Kaduna State, Dr Hadiza Balarabe, has said that Kaduna is set to receive President Bola Tinubu on Saturday.
Dr Balarabe disclosed this to journalists after, she and members of her team inspected facilities at the Kaduna Township Stadium, the venue of the flag off, on Wednesday evening.
‘’I’m comfortable with what has been done so far; we have the holding area, the conveniences are ready, the pavilions are ready. What remains is the markings for the different states,’’ she added.
The Deputy Governor said that the LOC has deliberated extensively about security before, during and after the presidential rally, with seasoned security professionals at both state and federal levels.
Dr Balarabe said that people will be screened before gaining access into the stadium and she assured everyone of their safety in the arena.
According to her, the LOC envisages a large turnout of party members and supporters from across the country because the North West is an APC stronghold.
Also speaking, the Commissioner of Information and Culture, Malam Ahmed Maiyaki disclosed that mobilisation is still ongoing, adding that hotels and service apartments have been fully booked within Kaduna metropolis.
The Commissioner said that Kaduna State is privileged and honoured to host the flag off of the Presidential Campaign and its citizens are eager to welcome President Tinubu.
Maiyaki pointed out that hosting the maiden campaign rally in Kaduna is an opportunity for the people of the state to demonstrate their support for the president and APC.
He said that in the last three and half years, Kaduna State has benefitted from the APC-led administration in terms of projects and appointment of its citizens at the federal level.
He listed the conversion of Federal College of Education Zaria to a university, the recent conversion of Kaduna Polytechnic to a Federal University of Technology and the 122km Mando-Birnin Gwari road and proposed Kaduna Light Rail Project.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Serial entrepreneur Ajeet Singh, who previously cofounded unicorns such as Nutanix and ThoughtSpot, has announced the launch of his third venture, called Different.
Emerging out of stealth mode, the AI-powered martech startup has now raised $48 Mn (nearly ₹453 Cr) in its seed funding round led by General Catalyst. The round also saw participation from Lightspeed Venture Partners.
Meanwhile, former Asana executive Abhishek Pani and former chief technology and product officer (CTPO) at PharmEasy, Abhinav Yajurvedi, have also joined Singh as cofounders at Different.
“Different is an AI marketing system that runs demand generation end-to-end for lean B2B marketing teams,” Singh said in a post on LinkedIn. The startup has teams in San Francisco and Bengaluru, per its website.
Different aims to address enterprise bottlenecks such as hiring specialised talent, engaging multiple external agencies and managing disparate software tools. The startup’s AI platform plans, creates, executes and scales personalised content across channels in accordance with the business context, strategy, audience, and other parameters specified by the user.
It also learns from the results and adjusts accordingly to optimise performance. Prior to its public launch, Different tested its services with early corporate customers, including software firms Descope and Motif.
An alumnus of IIT Kanpur and IIM Calcutta, Singh has previously worked at companies like Oracle, Honeywell and PwC. Notably, this is not the first time that Singh is setting up his own business.
He previously also cofounded Nutanix in 2009, a hybrid cloud unicorn that went on to list on the Nasdaq in 2016. Singh stepped down from the company in 2012 to launch AI-powered analytics platform ThoughtSpot that same year. ThoughtSpot has raised over $670 Mn to date and was last pegged at nearly $4.5 Bn.
The development comes at a time when a growing number of founders are starting new ventures. Last month, Livspace founder Saurabh Jain and former executive Lalit Mittal banded together to launch a new venture, Gravity.
In May, Zeta founder Bhavin Turakhia launched a new AI startup, Neo, with a personal investment of $30 Mn. Prior to this, Healthians founder Deepak Sahni also said that he was building a new healthtech venture UN:BLOC.
Earlier this year in April, Inc42 reported exclusively that BharatPe cofounder Shashvat Nakrani was set to join Dubai-based luxury ecommerce platform Luxury For You as its cofounder and CEO.

Hon. Bashir Saidu, former Chief of Staff to Governor Nasiru El-Rufai, has denied betraying the former governor who is currently in detention.
Saidu, who was among the former allies of El-Rufai that announced that they had parted ways with him, spoke in an interview with RFI Hausa.
Daily Trust had reported how El-Rufai recently said some people he stood by during difficult times had abandoned him, a comment which sparked further controversies.

He said, “We were the first to suffer before him. I was taken to prison on New year eve. I spent 50 days there. I was moved from one court to another, until the judge who agreed to attend the trial revoked my bail. I was taken back to prison again where I spent 54 days. Is there any night I have not seen?
“I also spent the last Eid-Adha in prison. It is an outright lie to say we abandoned him. We only left when the betrayal became apparent. We learnt the person we submitted to did not value us. We moved where we are valued.

Saidu argued that he was among those who brought El-Rufai into politics.

items.author: Guest Contributor
items.content:
Emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control
Originally published on Global Voices
An aerial view showing destruction in Rafah, Gaza Strip, on January 21, 2025. Photo by Ashraf Amra on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO).
By Jalal Abukhater
This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.
For Palestinians, the relationship between technology and authoritarianism is a lived reality, rather than predictions or science fiction. Israel’s settler-colonial regime has long fused military force with legal, economic and technological mechanisms to dominate Palestinian life.
Surveillance, data harvesting, facial recognition, telecommunications blackouts, digital censorship and algorithmic systems are now woven into this architecture of control. The genocidal war on Gaza has exposed the consequences with devastating clarity, where technologies built to collect, process and classify information have been absorbed into systems that surveil, target and kill Palestinians.
But Palestine is also a warning about what comes next. Technologies developed, tested and refined under occupation do not stay there. They become products, expertise and business models that circulate globally. What emerges is a political economy in which military and intelligence institutions, technology companies, investors and governments converge around the extraction and processing of data as a means of exercising power.
This is one of the central arguments of Digital Domination, a publication of The Arab Center for the Advancement of Social Media’s Maryam Abu Daqqa Fellowship, which brings together five studies on artificial intelligence, surveillance, data extraction and corporate power in Palestine and beyond. The fellowship is named after Maryam Abu Daqqa, a Palestinian journalist murdered by Israel in Gaza in August 2025 while documenting life under siege. Across different cases, the research points to the same transformation, showing how emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control. It is becoming their infrastructure.
Intimate ties
Israel’s surveillance industry shows this plainly. It operates through intimate ties between military and intelligence institutions, private companies, venture capital and international markets. Tools tested on Palestinians are refined, repackaged as commercial products and exported to the world as security solutions. This is no accident of a thriving tech sector. It is a political and economic system in which security technologies gain value precisely because of their capacity to monitor, classify and control populations.
The violence these systems enable is increasingly literal. Investigations into Israel’s AI-assisted targeting systems, including Lavender, The Gospel and Where’s Daddy, have documented how machine-learning systems and mass surveillance data have been folded into the identification and targeting of Palestinians in Gaza.
A new film, NAZA, produced by The Guardian and built on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, details the secret systems used to select people for bombing in their homes at night, in the knowledge that their families would be killed, too. At a military conference in London in late June, an executive from the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems presented a slide crediting its digital command system with 850,000 “real-time intel targets” across Gaza and Lebanon between October 2023 and the end of 2025. The company has since tried to recast the figure as aggregate system activity, a claim that sits uneasily with the slide itself.
The significance is not that an algorithm has replaced human violence. It is that these systems increase the scale, speed and bureaucratic distance at which violence is organised, while cloaking life-and-death decisions in the appearance of technical objectivity. In June, Amnesty International and more than 100 other signatories warned that systems such as Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy dilute human responsibility and obscure international crimes behind a veneer of algorithmic objectivity.
Digital erasure
The same architecture extends beyond weapons. At 7amleh, we have documented how platforms suppress Palestinian speech, how state-linked actors use commercial platforms to shape information environments, and how Meta profits from content and accounts tied to illegal settlement expansion and violent rhetoric against Palestinians.
Two studies in Digital Domination make the point from different angles. One examines the Israeli government’s use of Google advertising to place its preferred narratives in front of people searching for information. Another examines algorithmic voice surveillance, showing how Palestinian speech itself is captured as data for systems of control.
This is where digital erasure becomes inseparable from physical violence. The destruction of Gaza also threatens the evidence and memory through which Palestinians can establish what was done to them. Platforms have removed or restricted documentation of Israeli violence, while physical archives, cultural records, cemeteries and the evidence beneath Gaza’s rubble have been destroyed or put at risk.
The UN refugee agency UNRWA ran a covert 10-month operation to smuggle millions of documents out of Gaza and East Jerusalem, amid fears that the originals, and even their digital copies, could be seized or destroyed. This September, the UN Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, Francesca Albanese, warned that Israel’s clearance of Gaza’s rubble could destroy evidence of atrocity crimes, and called it unacceptable that Gaza’s reconstruction be conditioned on the erasure of its past and the evidence needed to secure justice for its victims.
The problem, therefore, goes far beyond whether a post stays online. It concerns who retains the power to document reality, preserve history and establish evidence after violence has taken place. We have described this wider process as platformicide: the destruction and denial of the digital spaces through which Palestinians communicate, organise, document and preserve collective memory.
Epistemic power
Now the same problem is entering the systems through which people increasingly access knowledge.
Large language models and AI agents are becoming intermediaries between people and information, yet they are acutely vulnerable to manipulation. Microsoft’s security researchers have documented “AI recommendation poisoning,” in which companies embed hidden instructions that plant persistent biases in AI assistants’ memory, with 31 companies across 14 industries identified.
Salesforce researchers found that web-search agents fed authoritative-looking false content will reproduce it as fact: in controlled tests, around 80 percent of queries returned the attacker’s preferred answer, and in more realistic conditions, with poisoned documents buried among more than 100,000 clean ones, nearly one in four did.
For Palestine, this is not hypothetical. Drop Site News reported that Israel awarded a USD 46.5 million contract to Brad Parscale’s firm Clock Tower X to build networks of websites and blog posts aimed at shaping what chatbots tell users about Gaza, content written for machines rather than readers. Journalists have since put leading chatbots to the test to see how far the campaign has reached.
A society already subjected to censorship, propaganda, data extraction and the destruction of evidence is now entering an information environment in which people increasingly depend on AI systems to tell them what is true, what happened and what matters, and in which the party responsible for the violence is paying to shape those answers.
The danger is not only inaccurate information. It is the concentration of epistemic power in systems whose training data, retrieval mechanisms and decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Information manipulation can move from suppressing a Palestinian post to shaping what an AI system retrieves, remembers, or presents as knowledge.
A warning to heed
Meanwhile, the technologies and companies enabling these systems are becoming embedded in public life elsewhere. In the UK, Palantir’s GBP 330 million National Health Service (NHS) contract led a parliamentary committee to call the company’s growing public-sector role “an unacceptable point of weakness”, and the government is now reviewing the contract amid pressure to use a break clause in 2027. In the United States, Amnesty International has documented how technology from Palantir and Babel Street is used to monitor and target migrants and people speaking out for Palestinian rights.
These developments should be understood as part of a wider transformation in how power is organised. Palestine shows what happens when data, surveillance infrastructure, artificial intelligence and corporate power are integrated into systems of domination. It also shows how quickly technologies developed in one context travel into another, stripped of the political conditions of their making and repackaged as innovation, efficiency, security or digital transformation.
The authoritarianism of the digital age does not require every state to build its own surveillance apparatus. It can purchase one. It does not require governments to control every source of information. It can outsource the infrastructure through which information is filtered, ranked and delivered. It does not require violence to disappear from public view. It can make violence more scalable, more automated and harder to attribute.
Palestinians are already living with the consequences. The rest of the world should heed the warning before these systems become too deeply embedded in its own institutions to challenge.
Jalal Abukhater is a human rights advocate based in Jerusalem and Policy Manager at 7amleh, The Arab Center for the Advancement of Social Media.
Written by Guest Contributor

items.content:
Five Imams from Dorowa-Babuje, Luggere and Jol communities in Barkin Ladi Local Government Area of Plateau State have raised concerns over what they described as “security threats” affecting their areas in recent times.
The Islamic clerics are from the five Juma’at Mosques in the communities.
This development comes amid heightened tensions in Barikin Ladi, Mangu, Bokkos and Riyom LGAs where the state government has imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew to restore order following killings and attacks in the area.
Worried by the security situation in their areas, the clerics, including Imam Bashir Khamis, Imam Salihu Muhammad, Imam Idris Usman, Imam Aliyu Mahmud and Imam Yahaya, called on the government to take action to address the problems before they get out of hand.
Gov. Yusuf celebrates Kwankwaso at 70
‎Alert Group wins Fastest-Growing financial services group of the year at 2026 BAFI awards
They said the current situation was a source of concern, hence the need to draw the attention of the state and federal governments to threats capable of disrupting peace in the region.
Speaking during a visit to the Daily Trust office in Jos on Tuesday, the Imams led by Imam Yahaya of the Juma’a Mosque in Luggere, said the current situation in the area is alarming.
He said, “We are in difficult times in these communities. Unlawful arrest of our members without any cogent reason is the order of the day. Our social media team who help to share what we are going through with the world are being arrested and some threatened. Destruction of property by security personnel and rampant killing of both humans and animals are a daily occurrence. Communities are attacked and houses burned without any reason.”
According to the Imams, they are not opposed to any lawful investigation or to security agencies carrying out their duties, but they said the agencies should be impartial and treat them equally with their neighbours.
He said, “We appeal to be treated equally with our Christian neighbours and that no one should be spared if found guilty, irrespective of their ethno-religious background. We also appeal that security personnel should stop vandalising our properties and burning our houses. We also need security in our communities and in our places of worship during Juma’at prayers, and security agencies should allow cattle to graze.”

items.title: Anthropic Lost $80.7 Billion in Just Six Months
items.summary:
Anthropic recorded a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, sharply wider than its $13 billion loss during the same period last year, according to a draft IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters.
Most of the loss did not come from Anthropic’s day-to-day operations. The figure included a $72 billion accounting charge caused by an increase in the estimated value of bonds that can eventually convert into Anthropic shares.
Anthropic is expected to go public in November, while some investors are now considering a lower valuation of around $1.5 trillion following its latest financial disclosures, Reuters reported last week.
Computing Spending Nearly Quadrupled
Anthropic’s infrastructure costs also increased significantly as it continued investing heavily in AI development.

Computing Spending Nearly Quadrupled
Anthropic’s infrastructure costs also increased significantly as it continued investing heavily in AI development.
The company spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure during the first half, compared with $2.3 billion during the same period last year, according to the S-1 filing.
Anthropic has committed to spending at least $518 billion over 10 years on cloud services, computing and infrastructure.
The figures highlight the enormous cost of developing advanced AI systems as investors increasingly question whether spending on chips, data centers and computing infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
Anthropic did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
Revenue Reached $16.8 Billion in Third Quarter
Anthropic told prospective IPO investors at an October 14 meeting that its third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The growth eased some concerns about the company’s rising expenses, but some investors were disappointed by the slower sequential growth.
Anthropic’s revenue had more than doubled between the first and second quarters, reaching $11.6 billion in Q2.
A weaker-than-expected reception for Anthropic’s IPO could also affect sentiment across the wider AI market, with investors closely watching the offering ahead of rival OpenAI’s potential listing next year.
Anthropic Lost $42 Billion in 2025
Reuters previously reported that Anthropic posted a $42 billion net loss in 2025, with most of that figure also resulting from an accounting charge linked to convertible notes.
As Anthropic’s valuation increased, the estimated fair value of those notes tripled compared with the previous year.
Excluding that charge, Anthropic reported an operating loss of around $8.1 billion on $4.6 billion in revenue in 2025.
The company has benefited from growing demand for Claude Code, its coding assistant used by developers to write software and build applications.
The latest figures show that Anthropic’s revenue is growing rapidly, but its computing, infrastructure, and financing-related costs remain extremely high as it prepares for one of the most closely watched AI IPOs.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Meta has suspended the conversation-sharing feature in Muse AI after security researchers found that public DNS records could expose thousands of shared chat links.
Security researchers at Claroc discovered the issue over the weekend. Ars Technica first reported on the findings, while Meta later confirmed to Benzinga that it had paused the feature while reviewing the report.
Researchers Found Around 6,800 Shared Chats
Claroc said Muse created shared conversation URLs using a predictable structure that included the title of each conversation.
Those addresses were also written into public domain name system records. As a result, researchers could use passive DNS searches, which examine archived DNS activity, to discover shared conversations.
Claroc said one such search returned thousands of links and identified approximately 6,800 shared Muse conversations.
Researchers accessed some of those chats and found sensitive information, including meeting details involving a major AI lab, a small-business loan application, a bank fraud alert containing partial account information, a company vacation calendar and internal business documents.
Meta Suspends Muse Sharing
Meta said the Muse bug bounty program was created so security researchers could identify issues and help improve the product.
The company noted that when users shared a Muse conversation, the feature generated a webpage that anyone with the link could access.
However, Meta said it had now paused the sharing functionality while reviewing Claroc’s findings and considering changes to how those links can be discovered.
Following Meta’s update, Claroc said researchers could no longer access a sample of the previously available links.
“We are glad to see it closed this quickly,” Claroc said.
Muse Has Faced Previous Privacy Concerns
The incident follows another privacy-related controversy involving Muse.
In September, Inc. technology columnist Jason Aten alleged that Muse accessed private messages on his Mac even though he had not enabled the system’s “Full Disk Access” permission.
Meta spokesperson Andy Stone rejected the claim at the time, saying Muse can access Apple’s Messages app only when users explicitly opt in.
Meta Is Betting on Muse as a Major AI Product
The issue comes just before Meta is scheduled to report its third-quarter financial results after the market closes on Wednesday.
Analysts expect revenue of $63.36 billion, up from $51.24 billion a year earlier. Meta has beaten revenue estimates for more than 10 consecutive quarters.
Tech analyst Dan Ives expects Meta to monetize its roughly 3.5 billion-user base through the Muse AI agent, including through Facebook and Instagram.
Truist, according to market strategist Shay Boloor, estimates that Muse could generate around $29 billion in revenue by 2030, including approximately $11 billion from subscriptions.
Meta shares closed Tuesday at $694.25, down 1.59%, before rising 0.11% to $695 in after-hours trading.

The Senate Standing Committee on National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination has directed the health ministry to conduct a fresh inquiry into complaints regarding the MDCAT 2026 examination within one week.
PMDC officials informed the committee that no irregularities or anomalies had been found during the examination.
The committee also expressed concern over the PMDC's practice of collecting question booklets from candidates after the examination and not allowing them to retain copies. Members questioned why the paper had not been made public, stressing that transparency in the question bank and examination process was essential to safeguarding merit.
PMDC officials said the question booklets were collected to protect the question bank and prevent candidates appearing in subsequent years from gaining an unfair advantage. The committee, however, rejected the justification.
The committee also questioned the PMDC's recently introduced policy requiring students intending to pursue medical education abroad to take the MDCAT, which was subsequently withdrawn following the committee's intervention.
Expressing dissatisfaction with the inquiry report, the committee directed the Ministry of National Health Services to conduct a fresh inquiry into the complaints within one week and submit its findings to the committee.

items.content:
Xiaomi has revealed more details about the upcoming Redmi K100, confirming that the phone will feature a massive 10,000mAh battery, the largest ever used in a Xiaomi smartphone.
The Redmi K100 will launch in China on October 27 alongside the Clip Neo earbuds.
Design and Display
The Redmi K100 features a 6.83-inch display with a 165Hz refresh rate and up to 3,500 nits of peak brightness. It supports a 480Hz multi-finger touch reporting rate and a 3,500Hz instantaneous touch sampling rate.
Xiaomi says more than 40 games support 165fps natively, while over 100 titles support frame interpolation.
The phone has a metal frame, a centered punch-hole display, and a horizontal rear camera module. It will also be available in a new Firefly Green color.
Internals and Software
The Redmi K100 is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite processor alongside a dedicated D2 gaming display chip designed to improve graphics and frame rates.
It will run HyperOS 4 and feature Bose-tuned audio hardware.
Battery and Charging
The biggest highlight is the 10,000mAh Jinshajiang battery. Xiaomi says it uses 28% silicon-carbon content and provides an energy density of 957Wh/L. The battery is also designed to maintain stable performance at temperatures as low as -20°C.
According to Xiaomi president Lu Weibing, the Redmi K100 can deliver more than 29 hours of Douyin playback, over 24 hours of live streaming, more than 47 hours of music, over 18 hours of navigation, and more than 46 hours of reading.
Xiaomi also claims the phone can handle up to 1,000 short drama episodes on a charge.
The device supports 100W wired charging and 27W wired reverse charging. It also includes bypass charging, which is designed to reduce heat while gaming. The Redmi K100 will officially debut in China on October 27.

items.author: Shraddha Goled
items.content:
A private key meant to vouch for the security of websites around the world turned out to be the number 4.
That was one of the weaknesses researchers found in eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates issued by Bengaluru-based eMudhra.
The discovery prompted Google, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft to block the affected certificates, triggering a wider effort to protect browsers, applications, and enterprise systems. The incident also rattled investors and eMudhra shares hit their 20% lower circuit at ₹431.55 on the BSE today.
The immediate concern is whether software still trusting the compromised keys could accept fraudulent certificates. A related challenge is replacing legitimate certificates affected by browser makers’ decision to withdraw trust in a parent certificate.
A digital certificate acts as a digital identity that allows a browser to verify a website’s authenticity. Certificate authorities issue these certificates and vouch for their authenticity. eMudhra is among the certifying authorities licensed by India’s Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA).
The incident goes beyond one company. It shows how much of the internet’s security rests on a chain of trust that one weak link can undermine, raising questions about how India oversees companies that participate in this global infrastructure.
What Happened
On October 17, a researcher named Wayne notified the Chrome Root Program, which forwarded the report to Mozilla, and also contacted eMudhra and the Apple and Microsoft root programmes, reporting that he had obtained the private keys corresponding to eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. He demonstrated control of each key by signing a message with it “We have a problem here – Wayne”.
The full details of how the flaw was discovered and fixed have now been published by Dennis Jackson, a cryptographic engineer at Mozilla.
Intermediate CAs can issue certificates that websites use to establish their identity. Anyone holding the corresponding private keys could potentially issue fraudulent certificates for websites they did not control, allowing affected clients that still trusted those CAs to accept the certificates.
The keys were not stolen, but the researcher found that they had been generated with insufficient randomness, making them easy to reconstruct from the public certificates.
Six of the eight intermediates were intended for website security through TLS, while two were intended for software signing. Chrome, Apple, Microsoft, and Firefox blocked the affected TLS intermediates.
What eMudhra Says
In a statement on its website, eMudhra said it was investigating the incident and reviewing its security controls and operating procedures. The company said the eight intermediate CAs were created during a key generation ceremony on April 30, 2025, and the hierarchy entered browser trust lists in mid-2025. It said its roots and issuing CAs had undergone independent audits in each of the previous two years, but did not identify the auditors or disclose the scope of those audits.
eMudhra said only one of the eight affected intermediates had been deployed in production and that none had issued end-entity certificates. It said it revoked all eight intermediates and was working with affected customers and root programmes to address the incident.
The company also said the incident did not affect its Indian Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) and eSign businesses, which operate on infrastructure separate from its global TLS business. On October 21, eMudhra said the affected global TLS business accounted for around 1% of its revenue.
India faced a similar trust-related incident in 2014, following the misissuance of certificates for Google domains by the National Informatics Centre. At the time, Google restricted the India CCA root certificate in Chrome to a limited set of domains, including gov.in and nic.in.
eMudhra has been a licensed certifying authority under India’s IT Act since 2008. The company has also worked with public- and private-sector organisations, including banks and government agencies.
The company provides digital identity, authentication and security solutions to businesses, financial institutions and governments. Its services include digital signature certificates (DSCs), electronic signatures and tools that help organisations secure digital transactions and manage identities.
In India, its DSCs are used for activities such as filing documents with government portals, including GST, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and income tax systems. Its eSign services also support paperless digital workflows.
Many critical government websites, including the Aadhaar issuer UIDAI as well as websites of the Indian postal services and the income tax filing portal, use eMudhra certificates or other technology developed by the company.
Why It Matters Beyond eMudhra
Browsers and operating systems rely on lists of trusted certificate authorities. A compromised intermediate CA can therefore threaten trust beyond the authority’s direct customers.
With the compromised keys, an attacker could potentially issue fraudulent website certificates to impersonate legitimate sites and intercept traffic, provided the affected systems still trusted those certificates and the attacker’s other technical requirements were met. The two code-signing intermediates also raised concerns about malicious software being presented as coming from a trusted publisher on systems that accepted their signatures.
“When news like this comes out about a company that supports our PKI infrastructure, it raises concerns about both the company’s reputation and the country’s reputation. Even a relatively small mistake or a gap in the validation process can affect confidence in the wider industry. People may start to question whether PKI infrastructure provided by Indian companies can be trusted,” said Abhijeet Zilpelwar, cofounder and chief technology officer at pi-labs.
The Long Tail: Software And Devices
Updated browsers received protections quickly. The harder problem is software and devices that do not receive the same updates or reliably check certificate revocation.
Applications, programming languages, package managers and build pipelines can use their own certificate bundles or the operating system’s trust store. Some do not reliably check revocation status, meaning they may continue to accept certificates unless their trust configuration or software is updated.
Embedded devices can be harder to update. Routers, cameras, payment terminals and industrial controllers running old firmware may continue to trust affected certificate chains if their software does not receive the relevant protections.
For Indian enterprises, exposure does not depend solely on whether they bought certificates directly from eMudhra. The company says none of the eight affected intermediates issued certificates to end users, and Google found no certificates chaining to the six website-security intermediates in public Certificate Transparency logs before blocking them.
However, systems that continue to trust the affected intermediates may remain exposed if they lack effective revocation checks or have not received relevant security updates.
Potentially affected systems include backend applications, servers and devices running outdated software, including those operated by organisations that use another certificate provider. Banking, fintech, e-governance and other businesses relying on certificate-based authentication should assess their exposure, though the incident does not establish that these sectors have been disproportionately affected.
“Mid-sized organisations, SaaS providers and those with lots of vendor-managed systems are most exposed as they often do not keep track of their certificates,” said Rajesh Chhabra, general manager for India and South Asia at global cybersecurity giant Acronis.
The Ministry of Electronics and IT has issued a statement saying that the impact of this incident on Indian websites and applications have been very limited and for a very short interval. Additionally, the department has also formed a special team to investigate the matter and is engaging with relevant stakeholders.
According to CERT-In’s advisory issued on October 21, organisations should update browsers, operating systems and applications, ensure servers and devices receive current trust lists and revocation information, identify affected certificates and services, and replace them where necessary. CERT-In also advised organisations to verify certificate details and not bypass certificate warnings or disable certificate checks.
Venkata Satish Guttula, former director of security at Rediff.com India, said the eMudhra incident raised wider concerns about security audits. “Titles keep getting bigger while the people holding them get more junior. Audits look clean on paper, but the skill behind them is thin,” he posted on X, describing what he called an “illusion of competence” in security audits.

items.summary:
Poco has quietly launched the Poco X8s in Vietnam, making it the fifth smartphone in the X8 series.
The new model joins the Poco X8 Pro, X8 Pro Max, X8, and X8 Power.
Design and Display
The Poco X8s features a compact 6.35-inch 1.5K LTPO OLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate and up to 3,500 nits of peak brightness.
The display has slim 1.18mm bezels.
The phone uses a metal frame, measures approximately 8.06mm thick, and weighs around 187 grams.
It also carries an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. The available colors are White, Black, and Blue.
Internals and Software
The Poco X8s is powered by the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 chipset.
It comes with either 8GB or 12GB of LPDDR5X RAM and 256GB or 512GB of UFS 4.0 storage.
The phone runs Android 16 with HyperOS 3.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
San Francisco-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith has raised $66 Mn in a Series C funding round led by Sequoia Capital, bringing its total funding raised till date to $125 Mn. Premji Invest and existing investors Peak XV Partners, Google Ventures, and Y Combinator also participated in the round.
The startup raised the fresh capital at an unicorn valuation of $1 Bn, doubling in just over two months. It was valued at $550 Mn when Peak XV led its $45 Mn Series B funding round in August.
In a statement, the startup shared plans to bolster its compute infrastructure and expand its technical engineering team. It says that it currently manages nearly 10 MW of compute footprint across data centers in the United States and Europe.
It shared plans to expand its total capacity by 5X in 2027 to meet growing enterprise demand.
“Even at the start of this year, we underestimated how much code people would be shipping. We expect that volume to only keep increasing as models get better and more engineers embrace AI codegen tools. We’re building Blacksmith to help developers merge code faster and feel confident about what they’re shipping,” Aditya Jayaprakash, Blacksmith’s cofounder and CEO, wrote in a post on LinkedIn.
Founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, Blacksmith operates a specialised cloud platform designed for automatically building and testing software code. It claims to serve more than 10,000 corporate customers worldwide, including high-growth tech firms such as Mercury, Granola, Supabase, and LangChain.
As AI agents accelerate the speed at which code is written, the bottleneck for shipping software is moving from writing the code, to validating and testing code before deploying it – a step known as continuous integration (CI).
Blacksmith claims its platform is tailor-made to absorb the spiky nature of CI demand with zero operational overhead, compared to general-purpose cloud infrastructure.
According to the company’s blog post announcing the latest funding round, weekly CI jobs processed on Blacksmith jumped to over 90 Mn from 5 Mn back in January, driving a 17X jump in ARR over the same period.
The post Peak XV-Backed AI Startup Blacksmith Nets $66 Mn At A Unicorn Valuation appeared first on Inc42 Media.
