items.author: Akshit Pushkarna
items.content:
Eternal, the parent company of Blinkit and Zomato, reported a consolidated net profit of ₹125 Cr for the second quarter of FY27, up 92% YoY from ₹65 Cr in the previous year quarter. On a sequential basis, profit surged 36% from ₹92 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Operating revenue for the quarter zoomed 78% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,138 Cr. Including other income of ₹351 Cr, total income stood at ₹24,489 Cr. Eternal’s adjusted revenue increased 76% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,621 Cr. On a like-for-like (LFL) basis, adjusted revenue grew 58% YoY.
The difference reflects Blinkit’s shift towards an inventory-led model, under which revenue includes the full value of goods sold directly to customers rather than only marketplace commissions. The like-for-like calculation excludes the cost of goods sold from Blinkit’s own inventory and Hyperpure’s non-restaurant revenue.
Total expenses for the quarter rose 75% YoY to ₹24,166 Cr, while tax expenses came in at ₹198 Cr. Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA almost tripled YoY, surging 197% to ₹666 Cr.
However, the company’s cash balance at the end of September dipped by ₹1,813 Cr to ₹16,475 Cr.
The decline was driven by seasonal net working capital requirements, including building Blinkit’s inventory ahead of the festive season and quarter-end timing in Zomato’s weekly restaurant settlement cycle that temporarily lowered payables.
Besides, Eternal’s board also approved exchanging its entire stake in adtech startup AdOnMo for shares in Mygate ahead of a proposed merger between the two startups. Eternal will eventually own around 4.4% of the merged entity, with the holding currently valued at ₹156 Cr.
The board also approved transferring the India going-out business housed directly in Eternal to wholly owned subsidiary Zomato Entertainment Pvt Ltd for around ₹130.76 Cr, subject to adjustments, through a slump sale. The business housed in two other subsidiaries will subsequently be consolidated into the same entity to streamline operations.
Here’s how Eternal’s key businesses performed during the quarter:
Blinkit Accelerates Store Expansion
Blinkit remained Eternal’s largest revenue contributor, with operating revenue increasing 94% YoY and 22% QoQ to ₹19,152 Cr. On an LFL basis, revenue grew 84% YoY.
The quick commerce business reported a segment profit of ₹488 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA stood at ₹184 Cr, compared with a ₹156 Cr loss in the year-ago quarter.
Blinkit’s net order value (NOV) rose 79.3% YoY and 22.2% QoQ to ₹20,940 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA margin improved for the sixth consecutive quarter to 0.9% of NOV.
The company added 308 net new stores in Q2 FY27, taking its network to 2,751. Eternal now expects Blinkit to cross 3,500 stores by March 2027, raising its earlier target of 3,000, and reach around 5,000 stores by March 2028.
CFO Akshant Goyal said the accelerated expansion was supported by improving performance in smaller cities and newer categories, with new stores meeting the company’s margin and payback expectations.
Eternal expects Blinkit’s adjusted EBITDA margin to continue improving through the expansion, with profitability gains at mature stores and cities offsetting the initial drag from new outlets. Its mature cities already report adjusted EBITDA margins exceeding 5%, while cities contributing around 70% of NOV are adjusted EBITDA positive.
Although annual NOV growth moderated to around 79% owing to a higher base, management expects growth to pick up as new stores open and scale. Blinkit is tracking ahead of its three-year guidance of 60% NOV compound annual growth, but Eternal said it was too early to revise the target upwards.
Zomato’s Growth Regains Pace
Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal reiterated the company’s long-term expectation of more than 20% annual growth in food delivery, following a recovery over the past two quarters.
Zomato’s food delivery NOV increased 21.5% YoY to ₹11,445 Cr. Operating revenue rose 37% YoY to ₹3,396 Cr.
Adjusted EBITDA increased 25% YoY to ₹627 Cr, although its margin declined marginally to 5.5% of NOV. Average monthly transacting customers grew 16% YoY to 28 Mn.
Goyal attributed part of the previous year’s slowdown to some ordering occasions shifting to quick commerce as the segment expanded. That shift now appears to have stabilised, he said.
Recent growth has been driven by more customers ordering food online and placing orders more frequently. A growing share of new users are ordering food online for the first time, including many outside Zomato’s top eight cities.
“There is still a lot of headroom. Restaurant food is a small part of how India eats. As cities grow, incomes rise and more young people live away from home, we think the food delivery market can keep compounding at 20%+ for many years,” Goyal said.
District Retains Breakeven Timeline
District’s NOV increased 58% YoY and 1.3% QoQ to ₹3,259 Cr. Operating revenue grew 61% YoY to ₹304 Cr, although it declined 4% sequentially.
Its segment loss narrowed to ₹55 Cr from ₹61 Cr in the preceding quarter. Adjusted EBITDA loss remained broadly flat QoQ at ₹64 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA margin improved to -2% of NOV from -3.1% a year ago. CFO Goyal said District remained on track to achieve adjusted EBITDA breakeven within the four-to-six-quarter timeline outlined in January 2026.
Annual NOV growth is running above 50%, ahead of the 30%+ compound annual growth assumption built into its FY30 plan. Eternal retained its FY30 targets of ₹28,000 Cr in NOV and ₹1,400 Cr in adjusted EBITDA.
However, management flagged AI agents that transact on consumers’ behalf as a potential longer-term disruption to parts of the business. Eternal said it is building physical infrastructure and operations that could help District deliver a differentiated customer experience.
Hyperpure Turns EBITDA Positive
Restaurant supplies business Hyperpure reported operating revenue of ₹1,154 Cr, up 13% YoY. On an LFL basis, revenue increased 22.7%.
Its segment profit stood at ₹19 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA turned positive at ₹10 Cr, as against a loss of ₹5 Cr a year ago.
Hyperpure now serves around 85,000 restaurants, up from 62,000 a year ago.
Management said two-hour deliveries, greater adoption of organised procurement, and services such as kitchen setup were supporting growth. Around 25% of its orders are delivered within two hours.
The others segment, which includes Bistro and Nugget, reported revenue of ₹132 Cr, up 39% from ₹95 Cr in the preceding quarter. Its adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to ₹91 Cr from ₹94 Cr sequentially.
Shares of Eternal ended Wednesday’s trading session 2.71% lower at ₹311.75.
The post Eternal’s Q2 Profit Surges 92% YoY to ₹125 Cr appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.content:
Bitcoin for treasury, stablecoins for payments. That rule fits most of what a business does with either asset, and it fails in two places. It treats Bitcoin’s volatility as a one-way risk, and it treats a stablecoin as a permanent hedge against the naira.
Bitcoin swings in both directions, and the naira has gained about 9% on the dollar over the past 12 months. Below are the four differences that matter, the job each asset fits, and a way to skip the choice.
Bitcoin vs stablecoins: 4 differences that matter to a business
The comparison runs on four dimensions: price stability, accountability, settlement, and risk. Each is easier to judge with numbers than with adjectives.
Bitcoin
Fiat-backed stablecoin (USDT, USDC)
Price
Set by open-market supply and demand
Designed to track $1, can briefly lose the peg
Accountability
No issuer, rules enforced by the network
Named issuer, reserves, redemption terms
Settlement
One chain, a block about every 10 minutes
Minutes, around the clock, several networks
Main risk
Market risk
Counterparty and reserve risk
Price stability, and what “stable” costs
Bitcoin’s price moves a lot. It peaked near $126,000 in October 2025 and traded at about $81,400 on October 20, 2026, a fall of roughly 35%.
The same swing shows up at day scale. A poster on a Nigerian Bitcointalk thread said an employee paid in Bitcoin “could lose 3-5% of its value within a day.” A second poster replied that the payment “could also gain extra 2 to 5%.” Neither figure is measured data, but both describe the mechanism: you don’t know what the payment is worth until you convert it.
A fiat-backed stablecoin such as USDT or USDC is designed to track the US dollar at roughly 1:1. Circle says USDC’s reserves are cash and short-duration US Treasuries. For a business choosing between the two, USDC or USDT is its own decision.
Stable does not mean risk-free. In March 2023, Circle disclosed that $3.3 billion of USDC reserves, about 8% of the total, sat at the failed Silicon Valley Bank, and USDC briefly lost its dollar peg. Stable means lower volatility, not zero risk.
Who’s accountable: no one, or a named company
Bitcoin has no issuer. A decentralized network of nodes and miners enforces its rules through proof of work, which is the mechanism behind the Bitcointalk line that “Bitcoin is trusted.” For stablecoins, the same poster wrote, “that trust is placed [on]the people that introduced it.”
A stablecoin’s soundness depends on its issuer, reserves, reporting, and redemption terms. In the US, the GENIUS Act requires covered issuers to publish a monthly reserve report, examined by a registered accounting firm and certified by the CEO and CFO. That is an attestation, which is narrower than a full audit.
Control is the other difference. On April 23, 2026, Tether froze $344 million in USDT across two addresses, in coordination with OFAC and US law enforcement. OFAC sanctioned the same two wallets the next day as property of Iran’s central bank. Bitcoin has no issuer to flip that switch.
With a stablecoin, a business trusts both the blockchain and the company running it. With Bitcoin, trust sits with the network. These are different dependencies, and neither is lighter.
Settlement speed and what it does to reconciliation
Bitcoin payments can appear almost instantly, but they are final only once included in a block, and blocks arrive about every 10 minutes. Businesses often wait for several confirmations on large payments. Lightning is faster, but most counterparties don’t use it by default.
Stablecoins settle in minutes, including weekends and bank holidays, across several networks. Breet’s crypto payment API, for example, accepts USDT and USDC on TRC20, ERC20, Solana, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Arbitrum, and Base.
Tax reconciliation differs too. In Nigeria, individuals pay income tax of 0% to 25% on crypto gains, measured in dollars between purchase and sale. A dollar-pegged stablecoin usually produces little or no dollar gain, and sales of USDT and USDC are exempt from the 1% withholding that applies to Bitcoin and Ether.
A Bitcoin payment can create a taxable gain between the day you receive it and the day you sell. Companies follow separate corporate rules, so confirm treatment with your accountant.
Risk profile: market risk vs counterparty risk, not “risky vs safe”
Bitcoin’s main risk here is market risk. The payment’s value can rise or fall before you sell, and the same move produces either a loss or a gain.
A stablecoin moves the risk instead of removing it. The concerns become counterparty and reserve risk: whether the issuer holds what it claims, how transparent the reserves are, how fast holders can redeem, and whether the issuer can freeze an address.
Stablecoins also come up for paying teams. Payroll brings legal, tax, and labor questions outside this comparison.
When your own currency is the one gaining
A stablecoin protects a business from local-currency depreciation only while the local currency is depreciating. Over the past year, the naira has not been.
USD/NGN traded at ₦1,330.43 on October 20, 2026, and the naira has strengthened 9.23% against the dollar over 12 months. It has been flat for the last month (0.02%). Trading Economics’ model expects ₦1,308.80 in 12 months, so treat further gains as a forecast.
A Bitcointalk poster flagged the mechanism in September, when the rate sat near ₦1,370. Holding 500 USDT loses naira value if the rate falls to ₦1,200, and “the only time that the USDT will be preferable is when the rate of naira is [depreciating].”
Run the numbers on a business that converts ₦13.3 million into $10,000 of USDT at ₦1,330 and holds it. At the forecast ₦1,308.80, the position is worth ₦13,088,000, about ₦212,000 less before fees. If the naira slid back to ₦1,500 instead, the same $10,000 would be worth ₦15 million, ₦1.7 million more. Both outcomes are a bet on direction.
This leaves the case for stablecoins as a payment rail intact. If a customer pays in USDT and the business converts right away, the naira’s direction tomorrow barely matters. The exposure appears when stablecoins sit as a standing treasury position.
Which one, for which job
“Bitcoin or stablecoin?” is four separate decisions.
Paying a supplier abroad: stablecoin, in most cases. If the supplier invoices in dollars, a dollar-pegged stablecoin removes the exchange-rate gap between invoice and payment, and it settles outside banking hours.
Holding treasury float: depends on currency direction. If your currency is depreciating, dollars preserve purchasing power. If it is strengthening, holding dollars costs you, as the ₦212,000 example above shows. Check the direction before defaulting to “hold stablecoins for safety.”
Accepting a customer’s payment: either works. What matters is the next step. If you convert on arrival, the asset the customer sent never becomes treasury.
Wanting long-term Bitcoin exposure: Bitcoin, on purpose. The price of that upside is drawdowns like the 35% fall above, which can land when you need cash. Hold only money you can leave untouched through one.
You don’t have to pick a side to settle the transaction
None of those four jobs requires holding either asset, as long as the payment converts to fiat when it lands. For many businesses, the need is simple: the customer wants to pay in Bitcoin or a stablecoin, and the business wants naira, cedis, or dollars in its account.
Settle automatically, in fiat, the moment either asset lands
With our Crypto and Stablecoin Payment API, a customer’s deposit of Bitcoin, USDT, USDC, or another supported asset is detected on-chain and converted. With auto-settlement on, it is paid to a linked bank account. With it off, it sits as a USD, NGN, or GHS balance until you withdraw. You can set this per wallet address or business-wide.
A webhook fires the moment a transaction is detected on-chain, so your system can fulfill the order without anyone checking a dashboard. The platform has 100+ verified businesses, 3M+ transactions settled programmatically, and a 99.9% uptime SLA.
Access dollars through stablecoins without carrying a treasury position
A business that needs dollars for a supplier does not have to hold USDT or USDC in between. The API gives import and export teams an interface to convert NGN, USD, or GHS to USDT or USDC and back for supplier payments, bypassing dollar scarcity and the parallel market.
For large trades, our OTC desk locks the rate before execution, so the market can’t move against you mid-trade. Settlement lands the same hour in NGN, GHS, USD, USDT, or USDC. Settling in USDT or USDC is the option for businesses that want dollar-denominated float. The desk is built for large volumes, not routine top-ups, and minimum sizes depend on the asset and currency.
Reconcile the same way no matter which asset shows up
If one customer pays in Bitcoin and another in USDT, finance should not need two processes. The API generates a wallet address per customer or per transaction, with bank details and a label attached at creation. Deposits to that address auto-settle to the right account.
That means no manual matching and no guessing which invoice a payment belongs to, whichever asset landed.
Check the direction, then convert
Bitcoin carries market risk. A stablecoin carries issuer and reserve risk, plus currency-direction risk when you hold it against a strengthening naira. Neither label, “risky” or “safe,” tells you what to do with a payment.
Start with this today: pull your last 90 days of crypto payments. For each one, note how long it sat before conversion and what the rate did in that window. If the gap is days and the rate moved against you, turn on auto-settlement.
Two limits apply. We convert crypto and don’t custody it, so Bitcoin you want to hold for years belongs in your own wallet or with a custodian. And Breet is not a payroll platform.

items.author: Press Release
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Zong has won four prestigious awards in the Telecommunication category at the Asian Innovation Excellence Awards 2026, held in Singapore on 20th Oct. The recognition underscores Zong’s position as Pakistan’s Leading Technology Services Enterprise and its ability to translate advanced technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and home-grown engineering expertise into meaningful outcomes for customers, business partners, and Pakistan’s digital ecosystem. Across brand, network, consumer services, and business operations, Zong continues to demonstrate how innovation can strengthen customer experience, create differentiated value, and enable a more intelligent and connected digital future.
Zong won the Pakistan Brand Innovation of the Year award for its AI-powered 5G launch campaign, “AIsa Hai Future”. Blending artificial and augmented intelligence with Pakistani creativity, the campaign reimagined the nation’s digital future through a distinctive, customer-focused brand narrative. Challenging conventional telecom advertising, it positioned AI as both the creative medium and the central message, bringing the promise of future-ready technology closer to consumers. The campaign helped narrow the brand equity gap, achieve parity in unaided 5G brand association, and strengthen brand differentiation through enhanced uniqueness and memorability.
Extending this innovation from brand promise to network performance, Zong received Pakistan Technology Innovation of the Year for its AI-driven Self-Intelligent Radio Access Network (RAN) Optimization platform, reiterating the advancement toward autonomous, AI-enabled network operations. Developed in-house, the platform autonomously detects network congestion, identifies and implements corrective actions, and verifies outcomes. By enabling faster issue resolution and intelligent network optimization, the solution enhances network responsiveness and performance, particularly during periods of high demand, supporting delivering a more consistent and reliable customer experience.
Translating customer needs into practical service innovation, Zong won Pakistan Consumer Service Innovation of the Year award for its “My5 – Family Sharing Package.” Designed around the evolving connectivity needs of households, My5 offers a flexible family connectivity solution complemented by value added benefits, including embedded insurance coverage, lifestyle perks and digital streaming access. By bringing connectivity and lifestyle benefits together in one offering, the package provides families with greater flexibility, convenience, and value, including an alternative to traditional home broadband services. The award recognizes Zong’s customer-first approach to developing relevant, accessible, and future-ready solutions that address everyday needs and enrich connected living.
Complementing these customer-facing innovations, DI-CAPE, Zong’s digital commission governance engine, won Pakistan Financial Innovation of the Year. Through intelligent automation, the platform strengthen business governance, improves process efficiency and transparency, and enhances partner enablement across Zong’s distribution ecosystem. This recognition highlights how digital innovation can create value beyond the customer interface by enabling more efficient, transparent, and reliable business processes for partners.
Commenting on this international recognition, Zong’s Head of Strategy & Company Spokesperson, Nabila Yazdani said:
“Winning four prestigious honors at the Asian Innovation Excellence Awards 2026 validates Zong’s technology leadership and commitment to translating 5G, AI, and home-grown digital innovation into meaningful impact. From AI-driven network intelligence and customer-centric connectivity to transparent business processes and a distinctive 5G brand promise, we are turning innovation into tangible value for customers, partners, and society. These wins reflect our strategic focus on delivering an ultimate customer experience while advancing Pakistan’s digital transformation toward a more connected and future-ready digital ecosystem.”
Aligned with its “Aisa Hai Future” brand promise, Zong continues to advance its strategic priorities of Ultimate Customer Experience, Diversified Products & Services Portfolio, and AI Enablement. Through sustained investment in 5G, AI, digital platforms, and in-house technical capabilities, the company is translating technology leadership into smarter networks, more efficient operations, and innovative digital experiences that deliver meaningful value to customers and partners while contributing to a more connected, inclusive, and future-ready Digital Pakistan.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
BYD Pakistan will lean on imported cars when it begins selling and plans to build up domestic production over time. The Chinese electric vehicle maker’s long-term aim, according to partner Hub Power Company Limited (HUBCO), is a local share of 80 percent in vehicle production.
The two statements describe a long road. Imports come first, localisation later, and the second step is not guaranteed.
What HUBCO says
HUBCO, BYD’s partner in its Pakistan business plan, says the goal is to reduce reliance on imports, bring down production costs and strengthen the domestic side of the auto industry.
It also sees spill-over effects. Higher local production could create investment openings in parts manufacturing, supply chains and related industrial sectors.
The target comes with conditions. HUBCO says progress will be phased and will depend on investment, production capacity and the industrial and policy environment.
Imports have a job in the meantime. Continued sales of imported vehicles in the early stage, HUBCO says, will help BYD stay available to buyers and move its business expansion forward.
Where BYD already stands
BYD is not starting from zero. Its Pakistan business is nearing local production at a $150 million assembly plant in Gharo, Sindh, which is expected to assemble about 25,000 vehicles a year once operational. The plant is undergoing equipment installation and commissioning.
BYD Pakistan also received its largest shipment so far, more than 2,000 vehicles, on a roll-on/roll-off vessel. Imported vehicles are meant to support deliveries and dealer stock until local production starts.
On infrastructure, HUBCO Green Private Limited and BYD Pakistan have set up 19 public DC fast-charging stations along a 1,300-kilometre corridor between Karachi and Peshawar.
Stage
What has been reported
Now
Imported vehicles continue to be sold.
Next
Gharo plant, 25,000 vehicles a year at full capacity
Later
80 percent local share in production (HUBCO target, conditional)
Why localisation matters for price
Assembly at home changes the cost equation. Fully imported vehicles face relatively high import duties, so local assembly gives a cost advantage and may improve affordability.
That is also why 80 percent is a bigger commitment than assembly alone. Duties apply to the car as a whole, but a high local share requires batteries, motors and components to be made or sourced in Pakistan, which takes much more investment than putting vehicles together from kits.
How far the gap is
In July 2025, a company executive said the plant would begin by assembling imported parts, with some non-electric components produced locally. A plant that starts this way sits well below 80 percent.
HUBCO’s statement gives no year for reaching the target, no figures for the local share at the start and no investment amount tied to it. Those are the numbers that would show how steep the climb is.
The Pakistan angle
The statement lands as the government talks up EV adoption. Haroon Akhtar Khan, Advisor to the Prime Minister for Industries and Production, said on October 13 that Pakistan aims for a 30 percent EV share by 2030 and that the forthcoming Auto Policy would give electric vehicles particular weight.
The policy’s content will matter to BYD. HUBCO ties its localisation goal to industrial and policy conditions, so incentives, duty structure and support for suppliers could decide whether 80 percent is reachable.
Bottom Line
Starting with imports is a sensible way to test demand while a plant comes online. The real test is whether Pakistani suppliers can meet the quality and volume a global EV maker requires.
Parts makers need orders large enough to justify new lines, and orders depend on vehicle volumes that, for now, remain modest. That circular problem has limited localisation in Pakistan’s car industry before.
The 80 percent figure is best read as an aspiration with conditions, not a commitment with a date. A published timetable, interim local-content milestones and named supplier agreements would turn it into something readers can measure.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
A trip to a NADRA office has long meant arriving early and joining a queue. The National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) now wants citizens to book a NADRA appointment through the Pak ID mobile app before they leave home.
The authority has urged people to use the facility to choose a registration centre and a time that suits them. Once the slot is booked, they can reach the centre shortly before it and get the service they need without waiting in a long line, NADRA says.
How the booking works
Citizens select their preferred NADRA registration centre in the Pak ID app, then pick an appointment time. According to NADRA, they should arrive a little ahead of that time and observe the schedule.
Earlier reporting described the steps as downloading or updating the app, logging in, then choosing a centre and time slot. The Pak ID app was already in use for online CNIC applications and biometric login, so most users will not need a new application.
A rollout that started small
The idea is not new. NADRA first announced it in July 2025, when the feature was slated for 43 designated registration centres in a first phase. Those included mega centres in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad, Peshawar and Quetta.
More recently, NADRA released an updated version of the app that covers online complaints and digital identity services alongside appointments. The announcement this week reads as a push to get citizens to use what already exists.
Why queues are the target
Crowded registration centres are a daily problem for people applying for or renewing identity documents. Long waits cost a working day, particularly for those travelling from outside a city.
NADRA says the facility is meant to make services easier to reach, save time and reduce crowding. An appointment system helps because it spreads demand through the day instead of concentrating it at opening time.
Earlier NADRA messaging also asked people to arrive about ten minutes early. That guidance came with the aim of improving crowd management.
What the statement leaves open
The announcement does not say what happens to people who arrive without an appointment. It does not report how many bookings have been made, how many slots a centre releases per day, or whether waiting times have fallen at centres already using the system.
Access is another question. Booking requires a smartphone, a working internet connection and some comfort with apps. Many of the people who queue longest at NADRA offices may be those least likely to have all three.
Bottom Line
An appointment system only reduces queues if two things hold: enough slots, and a clear rule for people without bookings. If slots fill within hours, the line moves from the pavement to the app. If walk-ins are still served first come, first served, the benefit for those who booked disappears.
For now, the advice is practical: update the app, check that your centre offers bookings, and arrive on time.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Supreme Court of Pakistan has quashed a Rs. 4.79 billion tax demand against the Universal Service Fund (USF), ruling that payments made to telecom operators for expanding connectivity in underserved areas are not subject to tax deduction under Section 153(2)(b) of the Income Tax Ordinance.
The decision marks a significant legal victory for USF, which plays a key role in extending broadband and telecommunication services to remote and underserved regions of Pakistan.
According to official USF sources, the Fund presented detailed facts, supporting evidence, and legal arguments during the proceedings to establish its position regarding the tax treatment of payments made to telecom companies.
After considering the case, the Supreme Court ruled in favour of USF and annulled the tax order issued by the revenue authorities.
The judgment provides clarity on the application of the relevant tax provision to USF payments made to telecom operators for connectivity projects in underserved areas.
What Does the Supreme Court’s Decision Mean for Digital Connectivity?
The ruling is particularly important for USF’s ongoing efforts to improve telecom infrastructure in areas where commercial operators may find network deployment financially challenging.
USF supports projects aimed at extending mobile coverage, broadband connectivity, and digital infrastructure to communities that remain outside reliable telecommunication networks.
With the Rs. 4.79 billion tax demand set aside, the Fund intends to focus on accelerating network deployment activities across unserved and underserved regions.
According to USF sources, the judgment represents an important milestone toward achieving the government’s Digital Pakistan and Digital Nation objectives.
The Fund reiterated its commitment to improving access to high-speed broadband and telecom services in remote parts of the country, where connectivity remains essential for education, business opportunities, and access to digital services.
USF also acknowledged the support of the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) and the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) throughout the legal proceedings.
The decision removes a significant tax dispute for USF and could provide greater certainty for its connectivity initiatives. However, the pace of future network expansion will continue to depend on project approvals, available funding, and implementation by telecom operators.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Her Startup, an accelerator for women-led technology startups in Africa, has opened applications for the second cohort of its programme.
The Her Startup initiative, a partnership between the KSH Foundation, Tomorrow Foundation and EHA Impact Ventures, will select 10 early-stage women founders and help them build investment-ready tech businesses. The training component will be delivered by Founder Institute, which bills itself as the world’s largest pre-seed startup accelerator.
Women-founded startups continue to struggle for funding in Africa. According to Disrupt Africa’s latest Diversity Dividend report, only 9.6 per cent of ventures funded in 2025 were led by a female CEO.
Her Startup was set up to tackle that gap by giving women entrepreneurs training, capital and networks through a single, integrated programme.
Selected founders will take part in a 12-week intensive training programme with Founder Institute, with fees covered by Her Startup, and will receive a monthly stipend so they can commit to the programme full-time.
They will also get the chance to pitch to Her Startup’s investment committee for funding through convertible revenue-based financing, as well as 12 months of sector-matched mentoring and access to Founder Institute’s global network.
The programme is open to women founders or CEOs aged between 18 and 35 who run a tech-enabled business that has been operating for at least six months and generates at least US$500 in monthly gross revenue. Founders from Francophone Africa are strongly encouraged to apply for the 2026/2027 cohort.
The second cohort follows a 2024/2025 pilot that drew more than 200 applications from 18 African countries. Ten founders were selected for training, and three ventures won funding at the programme’s Pitch Day in Lagos in April 2025. Alumni have since gone on to win grants and awards and attract investor interest.
One of them is Nigerian healthtech startup Dynalimb Technologies, which makes affordable 3D-printed prosthetics.
“Since Her Startup, we’ve seen a steady rise in customer adoption and product sales, as more amputees experience the comfort and mobility that Dynalimb’s affordable 3D-printed prosthetics provide,” said Blessing Aniefiok, the startup’s COO.
Her Startup’s funding model sets it apart, with repayments on its convertible, revenue-based financing linked to each company’s revenue.
“It’s not enough to just give these companies financing. It’s about giving them financing that will truly help them succeed. We chose a convertible, revenue-based loan, an innovative financing mechanism that is just starting to enter the market. It is incredibly founder-friendly, and it will help the women in this programme succeed,” said Evelyn Castle, co-founder of Her Startup and co-founder of EHA Impact Ventures.
Applications are open here until October 26.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
vivo appears to be preparing another major addition to its premium smartphone lineup, with fresh leaks revealing key specifications of the upcoming vivo X500 Ultra. The device is tipped to feature a next-generation Snapdragon processor, a 144Hz AMOLED display, and an ambitious camera setup.
While the company has not officially announced the device, reports suggest that the vivo X500 Ultra could debut in March or April 2027. For Pakistani consumers, the bigger question is whether this premium flagship will reach the local market and how much it might cost.
The latest information, attributed to Chinese tipster Digital Chat Station, suggests that the handset could feature Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. The processor is reportedly based on a 2nm process, with leaks pointing to CPU clock speeds of up to 5.01GHz and an Adreno 850 GPU.
If these specifications prove accurate, the device could deliver substantial performance improvements for demanding applications, gaming, and AI-powered features. However, its configuration and performance have not been officially confirmed.
On the front, the vivo X500 Ultra is tipped to feature a large 6.85-inch flat AMOLED display supplied by BOE. The panel could offer 2K resolution and a 144 Hz refresh rate, slim bezels, and an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor.
Triple 200MP Cameras and a Larger Battery Expected
Photography could remain the biggest selling point of the upcoming Ultra model. Earlier leaks have suggested a triple-camera configuration featuring 200MP sensors for the primary, periscope telephoto, and ultrawide cameras.
Such a setup would represent a significant hardware upgrade, particularly for ultrawide photography. However, these camera details remain speculative, and there is no confirmation that all three 200MP sensors will appear in the final commercial device.
Battery capacity could also increase to around 7,000mAh, according to reports. Fast charging is expected, although the company has not confirmed charging specifications. The previous X300 Ultra’s reported 100W charging is a reference point, not a guarantee for the successor.
vivo X500 Ultra Expected Price and Release Timeline in Pakistan
The vivo X500 Ultra is currently tipped for an international debut around March or April 2027, although its official release schedule and market availability remain uncertain.
Preliminary unofficial market listings indicate an expected Pakistan price of approximately Rs. 364,999 for a possible 12GB RAM and 256GB storage version. Considering the Ultra series’ premium positioning, an indicative editorial estimate of Rs. 350,000 to Rs. 420,000 could be plausible if the model officially launches in Pakistan.
These are unofficial estimates, not announced prices. Final pricing would depend on variants, currency movements, applicable taxes, and vivo’s local distribution strategy.
Availability outside China is also uncertain. Pakistani buyers should treat the pricing and launch window cautiously until vivo makes an official announcement.
If the reported specifications materialize, the vivo X500 Ultra could become a notable camera-focused Android flagship in 2027. Its appeal will depend on real-world camera performance, software, pricing, and local availability.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
OpenAI has introduced a new Locked Chats feature in ChatGPT that lets users protect sensitive conversations from anyone who may access their device. The feature adds an extra layer of privacy by allowing users to secure individual chats with a four-digit PIN, Face ID, or Touch ID on supported devices.
Announced on October 20, 2026, the feature is for users who want to keep personal discussions private while sharing their phones or computers with friends, family, or colleagues.
ChatGPT Introduces Locked Chats to Keep Private Conversations Secure
For example, users can lock a conversation about a personal matter or a surprise gift before handing their device to someone else. They can then unlock the conversation whenever they need it.
Unlike Temporary Chats, which do not appear in regular chat history, Locked Chats remain available for users to access later.
How ChatGPT Locked Chats Work
Once users lock a conversation, ChatGPT moves it to a separate section called “Locked Chats.” These conversations remain separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and search results.
Users can protect their locked conversations with a four-digit PIN or biometric authentication, depending on the device and available security options.
The feature allows users to maintain access to important conversations without keeping them visible alongside their regular chats.
OpenAI says the feature is intended to provide additional privacy when someone else might use or view a user’s device.
Locked Chats Have a Separate Memory
The new feature also includes a separate memory system for users who have Memory enabled in ChatGPT.
According to OpenAI, Locked Chats can maintain their own shared memory across conversations within the locked section. New messages sent in these chats can update that separate memory but will not update the user’s regular ChatGPT Memory.
This separation is designed to prevent information shared in locked conversations from influencing regular chats through the standard Memory feature.
However, locking a conversation does not remove information that ChatGPT remembered before the user locked the chat. Users should keep this distinction in mind when discussing sensitive information.
Locked Chats Do Not Offer End-to-End Encryption
OpenAI has clarified that Locked Chats are not a separate encrypted vault and do not provide end-to-end encryption.
The feature also does not change how long ChatGPT retains conversations or modify the user’s “Improve the model for everyone” data setting.
This means the feature primarily helps restrict access to conversations within the app. It does not change the underlying data storage and privacy policies that apply to ChatGPT.
Users who want to manage how their conversations may be used to improve OpenAI’s models will still need to review their existing data controls separately.
Resetting the PIN Permanently Deletes Locked Chats
OpenAI has also outlined an important restriction related to PIN recovery.
Resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN. Users should therefore take care when managing their security settings to avoid losing conversations and associated files.
The Locked Chats option is also unavailable for certain conversation types, including Temporary Chats, archived chats, group chats, conversations created through shared links, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats containing meeting recordings.
ChatGPT Locked Chats Availability
OpenAI is rolling out Locked Chats across ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare.
The rollout began on October 20, 2026, but it may take time to reach all eligible users.
With this addition, OpenAI is giving users more control over who can access their personal conversations on a shared device. However, users should understand that locking a chat provides an additional access restriction rather than a replacement for broader data privacy and security measures.

items.title: Can India Capitalise On The AI Homecoming?
items.summary:

items.author: Ankush Das
items.content:
For decades, Indian engineers and researchers moved to Silicon Valley, joining global technology companies and contributing to products and research that shaped the industry. Now, the tides are turning. Indian talent with experience at some of the world’s most influential AI labs is making its way back home to build startups and research organisations of its own.
This emerging trend could signal a new wave of reverse brain drain. But what has changed to make India a more credible place to build AI companies for those who have worked at the world’s leading research labs? And why is this happening now? Let’s ponder in this edition of The AI Shift…
A Land Of Opportunities
The shift is being driven by a combination of entrepreneurial ambition and a changing Indian AI ecosystem. Experienced researchers are beginning to see an opportunity to build companies around their own research agendas, while India’s growing startup landscape and emerging AI infrastructure are making that ambition more achievable.
Shyamal Hitesh Anadkat, a former OpenAI researcher who returned to India to build Empirical Machines, a startup focused on accelerating scientific discovery, pointed to this change in an interview with Financial Express.
He cited growing momentum in the startup ecosystem, the emergence of companies such as Sarvam AI, and a stronger appetite for risk among researchers and founders. The sense that more talent was beginning to rally around India’s AI opportunity had also become an important factor.
Parth Sarthi, cofounder of Chariot, offers another perspective. After completing his masters from Stanford University, Sarthi joined Contextual AI and later Google DeepMind as a research engineer. His work at DeepMind included multimodal reasoning for Gemini Deep Thinking, involving systems that reason across text, numbers and images.
Sarthi had long felt that India needed to develop similar frontier research capabilities. Limited GPU access had previously constrained the research that could be conducted locally. The IndiaAI Mission’s call for proposals to develop indigenous foundation models made the prospect of building in India more tangible. He saw an opportunity to apply his experience to developing advanced AI capabilities in India rather than continuing to build similar systems for Western markets.
Government support is also helping make the proposition more credible. The IndiaAI Mission is expanding access to compute, supporting indigenous foundation models and providing assistance for AI startups. These initiatives do not eliminate the gap with global AI labs, but they can lower some barriers to experimentation and company formation. Not to forget, AI funding in India grew 235% YoY in Q3 2026, as per Inc42’s latest report.
From Global AI Labs To Indian Startups
Anadkat is among the clearest examples of this shift. After nearly four years at OpenAI, where he led the Applied Evals team, he returned to India in 2026 to build here. The startup aims to use AI to accelerate research involving molecules and materials.
According to Moneycontrol, Empirical Machines is in talks to raise around $15 Mn from Peak XV Partners and Bessemer Venture Partners at a reported valuation of approximately $80 Mn.
Sarthi’s Chariot is another example of experienced researchers attempting to build frontier AI capabilities from India. The company is developing speech-native foundation models and was among the teams selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop foundational models. His earlier research included RAPTOR, a retrieval technique for language models published at ICLR 2024 and subsequently incorporated into frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex.
The movement also extends to specialised AI infrastructure. Anish Das Sarma, a former Google engineering director, founded Reinforce Labs to build tools that evaluate, red-team and remediate enterprise AI systems. The startup was featured in Peak XV’s Surge cohort, reflecting demand for infrastructure that helps businesses deploy AI more reliably.
Meanwhile, Sarvam AI has drawn experienced researchers into its effort to build Indian foundation models. These examples represent different forms of talent movement: researchers returning to start companies, experienced technical leaders launching specialised ventures, and global researchers advising Indian startups. They point to a growing willingness to build AI capabilities outside traditional technology hubs.
Are Investors Following The Trend?
For venture capitalists, experience at OpenAI or Google DeepMind can signal familiarity with advanced research, model development and the challenges of taking AI systems into production. It may also help founders recruit specialist talent and establish credibility with customers and investors. But pedigree alone does not establish whether a company can succeed.
Sayantan Sarkar, principal at Stellaris Venture Partners, believes hands-on experience building models at frontier AI labs offers three distinct advantages. Researchers who have worked closely with advanced models can anticipate how the technology is likely to evolve, identify gaps in existing capabilities and spot opportunities to build products for emerging needs.
Their understanding of post-training techniques can also help improve models and develop better products. In addition, their credibility within the AI ecosystem can help attract high-quality researchers and engineers, including those from frontier labs.
Ultimately, Sarkar argues, the advantage is not simply having worked at a leading AI lab, but being able to translate that experience into a differentiated company.
Rahul Mathur, the vice president at DeVC and a pre-seed investor, approaches the question from the founder’s perspective. Mathur believes investors should start by understanding the founder: why they left their previous role, what motivates them to pursue the opportunity, and whether they have the resources and commercial judgement to build a sustainable business.
He also examines the team they have assembled and why its members are willing to leave comfortable or well-paying jobs to join the startup. For AI research ventures, Mathur asks a more fundamental question: what customer-backed research is being conducted, and who will pay for it? He is looking for a “resourceful & commercially sound founder”.
The two perspectives highlight the distinction between technical advantage and investment merit. A researcher may understand how to build an advanced model, anticipate the next wave of capabilities and recruit exceptional talent. But those strengths must translate into a product that solves a real problem and creates a defensible business.
That challenge is particularly acute in AI, where research can take years to translate into a commercial product, while compute, experimentation and specialist talent demand substantial investment. Investors must establish whether a founder can identify a market, prioritise the right research and build a sustainable business around the technology.
A strong research pedigree may open the door, but customer demand, execution and commercial judgement determine whether a company can endure.
For India, the more consequential shift would be one in which experienced researchers build organisations that generate proprietary research, train new talent and sell globally competitive products. The measure of positive reverse brain drain will not be how many researchers leave global labs but how many enduring AI businesses they build from here.
Top Stories From India & Around The World
RapidCanvas Nets $29 Mn: The startup raised $29 Mn in a Series B round led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India to expand go-to-market operations, grow its AI engineering team and strengthen enterprise AI deployment.
Confido Health Raises $12.5 Mn: The healthtech startup raised $12.5 Mn in a Series A extension led by Z47 to expand its AI-powered CareOS platform and automate more administrative workflows across healthcare providers.
Anthropic Opens Its Models To Safety Evaluators: Anthropic has given researchers at nonprofit METR employee-like access to assess its models, with the independent evaluator expected to publish risk assessment findings as the lab expands external scrutiny of AI safety.
Meta’s Algo Under Review: The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has asked Meta to review its content recommendation algorithms, renewing scrutiny of how AI-driven systems rank and distribute content.
SaaS Models Under Pressure: Zoho cofounder Sridhar Vembu has sparked a debate on AI economics, warning that rising server prices and token expenditure are pushing up operating costs as software companies grapple with shrinking margins and uncertain returns on AI-driven productivity gains.
The Weekly Buzz: Meta’s Muse Wonder Claims The Frontier
Recently, Meta launched Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, the first frontier-class models from its Superintelligence Labs. The company says the new models reach parity with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s top Claude variants on multistep reasoning, coding, and long-horizon agentic tasks, priced at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.
Wonder is positioned as Meta’s largest and most capable model yet, built specifically for agent workflows such as processing insurance claims or complex lease negotiations. It introduces Active Memory and Active Focus features that let the model carry context across conversations and persist through difficult multi-step work.
A companion open-weight release, Muse Spark Open (816 Bn parameters, nearly 42 Bn active), was optimised with Apple to run efficiently on the Mac Studio. The models power the paid tier of Meta’s Muse personal agent and mark the clearest sign yet that Meta intends to compete head-to-head with the closed frontier labs rather than remaining primarily an open-weights player.
Early independent benchmarks appear supportive of the parity claims, though full third-party verification is still underway.
With Muse already a consumer hit, the Wonder family gives Meta a credible path to monetise advanced agent capabilities at scale while keeping a strong open-source presence.
Startup In The Spotlight: Coreshield
Founded in 2023 by Chandan Singh Rathore, a former Indian Air Force squadron leader, Bhavya K, an ex-Palo Alto Networks executive, and Rana Amit K N, CoreShield Technologies is building AI-driven security systems to protect critical infrastructure and national assets.
India’s growing geopolitical complexity and rising threats to defence, energy and public infrastructure have made real-time security intelligence increasingly important. However, existing defence and civil protection systems often operate in silos, with cameras, sensors and communication networks functioning independently. This fragmentation can delay threat detection and response during emergencies.
Operating from IIT Delhi’s Research & Innovation Park, CoreShield develops indigenous platforms that integrate video and acoustic analytics, AI-based decision orchestration and secure data-flow monitoring. Its systems bring together intelligence from multiple sources to help defence and infrastructure agencies detect, analyse and respond to threats in seconds.
Designed for both military and civilian applications, the startup aims to improve situational awareness and enable faster, data-driven responses. Its focus on coordinating intelligence across disparate systems differentiates it from solutions that address individual security components in isolation.
With India’s defence tech market projected to grow from $7.6 Bn in 2025 to $19 Bn by 2030, rising defence modernisation and AI adoption could create opportunities for indigenous security platforms such as CoreShield.
Prompt Of The Week
What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work?
Here’s Priti Sawant, founder & CEO of JoulesToWatts Business Solutions, with a prompt she uses to turn a messy business situation into a clear decision.
“Here is the situation as I see it: [context].
These are the outcomes that matter: [outcomes].
These are the constraints and trade-offs: [constraints].
My current hypothesis is: [view].
First, reflect the problem back in my logic.
Then challenge my assumptions, draw relevant parallels across industries and markets, identify what I may be missing, and recommend the best path forward.
Finally, capture the reasoning in a reusable playbook.”
Editor’s Note: Some prompts may need to be adjusted by users for best results or may not work as intended for certain users.

items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
Apple India Rolls In Profits
Apple’s India story is no longer just about iPhone sales. In FY26, the smartphone maker’s local unit saw record growth in revenue and profit, while exports and launch of new services further deepened its foothold. So, as component shortages loom, can Apple sustain its India surge?
An Expanding Ecosystem: Apple India’s FY26 performance reflected strong demand across iPhones, Macs, iPads and other products. Revenue from traded goods drove most of the growth, while services such as AppleCare and maintenance contracts further added to the revenue mix.
Here is a quick look at Apple India’s FY26 numbers:
Net profit rose 66% YoY to ₹5,311 Cr
Operating revenue grew 31.4% YoY to ₹1.04 Lakh Cr
Total Expenses also rose 28% YoY to ₹96,224 Cr
The numbers show Apple is building a broader consumer technology business in India rather than relying solely on its flagship smartphone.
The Cost Conundrum: However, Apple’s growth came with a steep price tag. Inventory purchases remained its largest financial drain in FY26, while licensing fees more than doubled to ₹10,374 Cr. Employee costs and marketing expenditure also rose substantially as Apple expanded its operations and strengthened its presence in India.
The India Playbook: All said and done, Apple’s ambitions in India extend beyond sales. The country has become one of its largest production bases outside China, with iPhone exports crossing ₹2 Lakh Cr in FY26. At the same time, it is also expanding its services ecosystem in India.
The OEM has launched new offerings such as Apple Pay and Fitness+ in the past few months, which are expected to create new revenue streams for the iPhone maker going forward.
The Sombre Outlook: But Apple’s near-term momentum faces pressure due to chip and memory shortages. As such, the company expects supply chain constraints to impact iPhones, Macs and iPads globally, potentially influencing product availability in India.
With demand rising, manufacturing deepening and services entering the ecosystem, here is how Apple fared on the financial front in FY26…
From The Editor’s Desk
Flipkart’s Food Delivery Foray
The Walmart-owned ecommerce major plans to roll out its food delivery service, called Eat-in by Minutes, to the general public by October-end this year. The company is said to have expanded its internal pilot in Bengaluru to more than 8,000 employees.
Flipkart, which began piloting food delivery internally earlier this year, plans to expand the service to six cities by 2026-end. It has tapped the state-backed ONDC for restaurant onboarding and has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders via its logistics arm Ekart.
Flipkart’s planned launch comes as new rivals take on Zomato and Swiggy. Rapido is offering a zero-commission model to attract eateries to its new foodtech platform Ownly. Swish has also begun piloting food delivery survive in select Bengaluru pincodes.
New Twist In Satcom Saga
The Centre is considering developing a hardware device to oversee services offered by Starlink and other overseas satcom operators. All traffic will be routed via the proposed device, which will act as a control layer between users and satellite networks.
The government is considering involving public sector R&D units, while keeping participation by select private players open. With this, officials are looking to address risks associated with foreign satellite operators.
The plan comes right after Elon Musk accused certain Indian “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s entry into India. The Centre has denied allegations of preferential treatment, maintaining that all applicants are at the same regulatory stage.
IndiaMART Under CCPA Radar
The Central Consumer Protection Authority has pulled up seven ecommerce platforms, including IndiaMART and Justdial, for listing and selling unauthorised hazardous explosives such as ammonium nitrate, gun powder, picric acid and PETN.
The regulatory action resulted in the delisting of 3,940 sellers and listing entries, including 3.092 at IndiaMART and 206 at Justdial. The CCPA also imposed penalties worth ₹30 Lakh on two platforms namely Dial4Trade and ExportersIndia.
The development comes amid regulatory clampdown on new-age tech consumer brands. Just days ago, CCPA imposed a fine of ₹10 Lakh on Rapido over unfair trade practices. FSSAI has also issued notices to multiple D2C brands and quick commerce players.
Founder FY26 Salary Tracker
Twenty-two founders across 15 Indian new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹66.87 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 2.3% from ₹65.34 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Of these, 16 received increases in fixed pay and four saw reductions.
Honasa cofounder Ghazal Alagh saw her fixed remuneration soar 60% YoY to ₹2.4 Cr in FY26, while Delhivery cofounder Sahil Barua followed with a 21.4% YoY jump to ₹3.4 Cr. Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal’s salary fell 34.8% to ₹4.5 Cr.
MobiKwik’s Bipin Preet Singh and Upasana Taku were the most paid founders, drawing fixed remuneration of ₹6.3 Cr each in FY26. Lenskart cofounder Peyush Bansal followed at ₹5.7 Cr, down 1.7% from ₹5.8 Cr.
Decoding Burma Burma DRHP
Last week, the restaurant chain’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Limited, filed its DRHP with SEBI. The proposed IPO consists of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.79 Cr shares.
As per the draft IPO papers, Hunger Pangs has 110 shareholders. Cofounders Ankit Gupta and Chirag Chhajer each hold a 33.35% stake. Its cap table remains heavily concentrated, with top eight stakeholders collectively owning 83.19% in the company.
Negen Capital, via its two funds, holds about 10% stake in the company, while rubber and plastic manufacturing company Bbigplas Poly also owns a 2.72% stake. Venture Catalysts also holds around 1.88% stake in Burma Burma.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
How Protein Pantry Is Reimagining Vegetarian Protein
On-the-go snacking and quick meals are becoming the norm for the Indian urban milieu. On this front, choices remain very limited for vegetarians. To solve this, Protein Pantry is building a portfolio of clean-label, high-protein snacks and meals that are designed for quick preparation.
Protein For Daily Needs: Founded in 2025, Protein Pantry sells a range of ready-to-cook frozen foods such as soya chaap, kebabs, cutlets and falafels. The brand claims that its products are baked rather than fried, with no maida, preservatives or palm oil. Each item can be prepared in under three minutes, targeting users who want a protein-rich meal without lengthy cooking.
Healthy Early Traction: Protein Pantry claims to have so far served around 30,000 users and is currently clocking a revenue run rate of ₹7 Cr. It also operates a 10,000+ sq ft facility in Noida and sells its offerings through its website and quick-commerce platforms.
The Road Ahead: Backed by Sharrp Ventures and Indian Silicon Valley Capital, the startup plans to now focus on scaling manufacturing and expanding distribution. Currently operating in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, Protein Pantry plans to expand to more cities in the long-term.
With the Indian frozen food market projected to become a ₹64,364 Cr opportunity by 2034, can Protein Pantry make high-protein food a daily habit for Indians?

India’s condiment game is getting a glow-up. From pudina chutney and chilli oil to peri-peri mayo and dips, homegrown D2C brands are leaving no stone unturned to grab a pie of the thriving Indian condiment market. So, which startups are adding the extra tadka to our plates…

items.author: ProPK Staff
items.content:
The prime suspect in the murder of a teenage orphan in Multan has been killed in an alleged encounter with Punjab’s Crime Control Department (CCD) near Bahawalpur.
The suspect, identified as Tauqeer Niaz, was wanted in connection with the killing of 15-year-old Waseem Abbas. The teenager was allegedly chased and deliberately run over by a car in Multan.
According to police, Tauqeer was the main accused in the case. CCTV footage of the incident had also emerged, reportedly showing the vehicle pursuing the teenager before hitting him.
Tauqeer was subsequently arrested and remained in police custody on physical remand as investigators proceeded with the murder case.
However, authorities later reported that he had escaped from custody. The CCD later encountered Tauqeer near the Northern Bypass in Bahawalpur.
According to CCD District Officer Irfan Akbar, officers signaled two men travelling on a motorcycle to stop. Instead, the suspects allegedly attempted to escape and opened fire on the CCD team.
Police said officers returned fire during the exchange. Tauqeer was subsequently found critically wounded.
According to the CCD’s account, Tauqeer was hit by bullets fired by his own accomplice during the shootout. His companion managed to escape from the scene.
Tauqeer later succumbed to his injuries.
Authorities have launched efforts to trace and arrest the second suspect who allegedly escaped following the encounter.
The development comes after the killing of Waseem Abbas sparked widespread attention. The 15-year-old was an orphan and had reportedly been working when the incident occurred.
Police had earlier arrested Tauqeer after identifying him as the principal suspect in the case.

items.content: New Delhi: How long will a peda stay fresh? For India's mithai makers, the question is becoming a business concern ahead of Diwali as tighter food safety rules in several states require the display of manufacturing and use-by dates even on loose sweets.Watchdog agencies in states such as Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand are among those that have made this mandatory. The directive aims to help consumers assess freshness as inspections have revealed that buyers were not always given clear information about when sweets were made or how long they remained suitable for consumption, the agencies said.Also Read: FSSAI issues notice to Zepto over alleged delivery of expired besanHowever, small and medium-sized manufacturers and sellers said that the frequent inspections and notices have made it difficult for them to operate during the festive season, when sales are at their highest. "Determining shelf life for different varieties could mean hiring external agencies, adding to costs and workload during the industry's busiest season," said Firoz H Naqvi, president of the Federation of Sweets and Namkeen Manufacturers.135076403Eye on AdulterationProducts on shelves are replenished many times a day during the busy season, said Naqvi.The Uttar Pradesh Mithai Namkeen Bakery Association recently urged the state food safety department to adopt a what it described as a supportive approach during the festive season, allowing small and medium-sized traditional businesses adequate time, training and technical guidance to formalise such practices.Also Read: Nepal bans import, sales of Indian biscuit Priyagold over food safety violations"For minor documentation, display, record-keeping or other correctable deficiencies, businesses may kindly be guided and given a reasonable opportunity to rectify them, instead of facing immediate disruption of production or disproportionate action," the grouping wrote to the Uttar Pradesh Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) on October 11.Other states such as Maharashtra, Karnataka and Haryana have also stepped up vigilance against adulteration during festivals and other large gatherings, when demand for sweets, edible oils, dairy products and other food items typically rises.Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has been on a food safety, hygiene and anti-adulteration crusade that has led to widespread action with inspections of restaurants, hotels, cloud kitchens, dairies, quick-commerce dark stores and manufacturing units.The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has asked states to increase surveillance to prevent the sale of adulterated and counterfeit food items during the festive season. It has also intensified scrutiny of packaged food products, issuing notices to major companies over alleged misleading health and nutritional claims, labelling discrepancies and non-compliance with food regulations.This comes as prices of key ingredients - milk and other dairy products, dry fruits, sugar, gram flour (besan) - have risen to records this year.Impact on marginsThe rising prices of inputs including fuel has had a cascading effect on the end product and will squeeze manufacturers' margins, said Suresh Goel, chief executive officer, Bikanervala Foods."Inspections happen during all festival seasons and so good and hygienic practices have become a part of our processing and packaging systems," he said. Since the Covid pandemic, the industry has aligned itself with health trends with even unorganised players making efforts to adopt best practices, he said.

items.title: Can Tinubu campaign without campaigning?
items.summary:
By LANRE OGUNDIPE
There is something intriguing about President Bola Tinubu’s approach to the 2027 presidential campaign. He appears determined not to conduct the election as though the business of governing Nigeria can be suspended for the sake of campaigning. Rather than carry his campaign physically from one rally to another, he is placing considerable responsibility on governors, party officials, ministers, legislators and political allies to take the message into the country. At first glance, this could look like a candidate stepping back from the electorate. I see something more calculated. Tinubu may be testing whether the political organisation he has spent decades building is now strong enough to campaign on his behalf. That is the real question.

By LANRE OGUNDIPE
There is something intriguing about President Bola Tinubu’s approach to the 2027 presidential campaign. Rather than carry his campaign physically from one rally to another, he is placing considerable responsibility on governors, party officials, ministers, legislators and political allies to take the message into the country. Tinubu may be testing whether the political organisation he has spent decades building is now strong enough to campaign on his behalf. That is the real question.
The 2027 election may be the first major test of whether Tinubu can turn a presidential campaign from a candidate-centred operation into a system-wide political enterprise. If he can, it would say something important about the sophistication of his political organisation. But it would also expose the limit of political engineering: an organisation can carry a message into every state, but it cannot determine whether citizens believe the message.
Tinubu is not an accidental politician. He has spent decades learning the mechanics of power, from the difficult years of opposition politics to the construction of the Lagos political machine, the coalition that eventually became the APC, the struggle against an incumbent federal government and, finally, the presidency. He understands something many politicians learn too late: a serious political organisation cannot depend entirely on the physical presence of one man. The APC’s latest campaign structure suggests that this is precisely the calculation. The revised presidential campaign council places all 32 APC governors in charge of the presidential campaign in their respective states. It also reaches beyond the APC itself, assigning campaign responsibilities to Nyesom Wike in Rivers and the Federal Capital Territory, Chukwuma Soludo in Anambra and Ademola Adeleke in Osun. Tinubu remains at the centre of the structure, with Vice President Kashim Shettima and APC national chairman Nentawe Yilwatda as his principal deputies.
This is more than a distribution of campaign duties. It is an attempt to make the campaign a network rather than a procession behind one candidate. The President governs from Abuja. Governors take the political argument into the states. Ministers defend the administration. Legislators mobilise their constituencies. Party officials coordinate the structure. Political allies outside the APC widen the coalition. Tinubu is effectively asking whether the political system he has assembled can do much of the campaigning traditionally expected of the presidential candidate himself.
There is historical precedent for such an approach, but the lesson from history is more nuanced than the simple proposition that delegation works.
Richard Nixon’s 1972 re-election offers the closest parallel. His campaign allowed him to spend substantial time governing while surrogates carried the message across the country, and he went on to win 49 of 50 states. But the organisation worked because it was operating in a favourable political environment. Jimmy Carter’s defeat in 1980 showed the reverse. His limited campaigning during the Iran hostage crisis was only one element in an election already shaped by economic dissatisfaction, political fatigue and Ronald Reagan’s challenge. Four years later, Reagan benefited from an improving economy that allowed his record to become a powerful campaign argument in its own right.
Nigeria has its own cautionary history. Shehu Shagari’s 1983 re-election demonstrated the reach of incumbency and party organisation, but the controversy surrounding that election remains a reminder that political strength and democratic legitimacy are not interchangeable. The lesson is simple: political organisation can amplify a favourable political environment. It cannot manufacture one. That is where the Nigerian reality becomes decisive for Tinubu.
A governor can explain the administration’s reforms. A minister can defend its policy choices. Party officials can mobilise supporters and political allies can broaden the coalition. But Nigerians will not assess the 2027 election solely through political speeches. They will also assess it through the cost of feeding their families, moving to work, paying rent, keeping the lights on, sending children to school and dealing with insecurity. This is where public hardship deserves careful treatment. Hardship is politically powerful, but it is not politically deterministic. Nigerians can endure painful reforms if they believe the pain is temporary, necessary and producing visible results. They can also reject an administration that tells them the future will be better when their experience of the present offers little evidence of improvement. The real political question, therefore, is not whether Nigerians have suffered. They plainly have. It is whether enough Nigerians will believe that the suffering is producing a destination worth reaching. That is why the President’s own argument about reform matters. Tinubu has repeatedly maintained that Nigerians have endured necessary sacrifices and that the foundations for a stronger economy are being laid. He has also acknowledged the crucial next step: the benefits of reform must increasingly be felt in the daily lives of ordinary Nigerians.
By 2027, that will no longer be merely an economic argument. It will be an electoral proposition. Are Nigerians better off? The answer will not be determined by how convincingly the governors explain the reforms. Nor will it be determined simply by how angry critics are about them. It will be determined by whether citizens can see and feel enough improvement to conclude that the sacrifice was worth it. If food becomes more affordable, transport less punishing, electricity more reliable, security stronger, jobs more available and purchasing power better, the administration’s record may begin to campaign for itself. The governors and other surrogates would then have something much stronger than a talking point. They would have lived evidence. But if household hardship remains stubbornly dominant, the political calculation becomes much harder. 
A government can have respectable macroeconomic indicators and still struggle to persuade citizens who cannot reconcile those indicators with the arithmetic of their homes. That is not necessarily proof that the reforms have failed. It is proof that economic reform and political legitimacy do not always move at the same speed.
This is where Tinubu’s political sophistication will face its most serious test. Governors are not merely campaign operatives. They are politicians with their own futures, successors to produce, factions to manage, alliances to preserve and political debts to repay. Their interests may overlap with Tinubu’s, but they are not identical to his. The deployment of 32 governors therefore gives the ruling party extraordinary political reach while simultaneously creating a complex web of state-level calculations. Tinubu’s long political apprenticeship becomes significant here. His political strength has arguably never rested principally on speechmaking. It has rested on political engineering: building coalitions, identifying useful alliances, accommodating competing interests and keeping a broad political structure together long enough to achieve an objective.
The inclusion of politicians outside the APC can therefore be understood as an extension of that philosophy. The coalition is less about ideological purity than electoral arithmetic.
That is politics as Tinubu has practised it for decades. But political sophistication carries a danger of its own. Those who command a political structure can begin to confuse the strength of their organisation with the strength of their argument.
The 2027 electorate will not be a meeting of governors. It will be millions of individual decisions. A voter may cheer at a rally and vote differently. He may support the direction of the reforms but dislike their consequences. He may believe that the sacrifice is finally producing results. Or he may conclude that he has sacrificed enough. Those decisions cannot be read reliably from the size of a crowd, the number of governors behind a candidate or the prominence of the people assembled on a campaign platform. This is why Tinubu does not necessarily need to be everywhere. But he needs to be present where the political argument is most difficult. He needs to explain the choices his government has made, defend its record, answer its critics and, above all, demonstrate that he understands the distance between a reform that looks successful on a government balance sheet and one that feels successful in a Nigerian household.
That may ultimately determine whether his unconventional campaign strategy becomes a masterstroke or a miscalculation. If the political environment is improving, the governors can amplify it. If citizens are beginning to feel relief, the campaign can give that relief a political narrative. If hardship remains the dominant experience, however, political organisation will have a much harder task. It can explain hardship. It can ask for patience. It can present the promise of tomorrow. It cannot erase the experience of today. The machine can carry the message. It cannot determine whether Nigerians believe it. That is the real test of Tinubu’s 2027 strategy. And when the campaign finally gives way to the ballot, the most carefully constructed political architecture in the country will still have to confront the one variable it cannot organise away: the independent judgement of the Nigerian voter.
•Ogundipe, a public affairs analyst, wrote in from Abuja.
The post Can Tinubu campaign without campaigning? appeared first on Vanguard News.
