items.author: Shahbaz Khan
items.content:
Pakistan's power sector has been in crisis since 2004, when oil prices spiked by around 56% in a single year. The trend continued until 2008, when prices peaked at almost five times of their initial value in 2004. The country was then heavily dependent upon furnace oil for power generation. As a result, between 2004 and 2008, the annual energy import bill of Pakistan increased by around 2.5 times.
The government attempted to accommodate the impact on the power supply chain through subsidies. But the lack of required fiscal depth and the consequential delayed payments towards the independent power producers (IPPs) resulted in an acute crunch of working capital. This in turn gave birth to the venomous serpent we all know by the name of circular debt. The same pushed the country into the worst power crisis it has ever seen.
The new government in 2013, driven by highly ambitious growth targets and corresponding requirements of power on the grid, launched a new power policy and a massive plan for generation capacity augmentation. Consumption increased promisingly during the period but not as rapidly as capacity. The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra)'s State of the Industry report of 2017 aptly forewarned about the fast-emerging monster of capacity charge due to the increasing gap between generation capacity and consumption.
As per the report, the capacity payments made in FY2015-16 and FY2016-17 were, respectively, Rs280 billion and Rs350 billion. In the same paragraph, it also tells us that for the value to remain at that of FY2015-16 in FY2018-19, the power sold was required to be 57% higher than its preceding year, ie 2017-18. However, the actual gain was even less than 2%.
Unfortunately, since 2019 till 2026, GDP growth has generally remained sluggish. The same in turn has continued to further increase the ratio of the capacity charge in the payments to the sellers. As a result, we have already paid around $40 billion in this respect during the period. This could, of course, have been largely avoided by incorporating informed and stringent qualifiers, for situations triggering capacity payments, in the "take or pay" clauses of the power purchase agreements (PPAs).
A major catalyst was the introduction of the Net Metering Regulations in September 2015, associated with solar power. Due to the economic benefits it offered, it virtually caused an exodus of users from the grid. For example, industrial power consumption from the grid was 29,885 gigawatt hours (GWh) in FY2020-21 and 29,114 GWh by 2024-25, despite a 7.5% increment in users in this category on the DISCO grid during the period.
To me, the magnitude of the impact solar ingress has caused in our economy is that out of its aggregate installed solar capacity, hardly 13% is integrated with the grid. After applying the commonly used capacity utilisation factor in the range of 18% to 22%, the estimated maximum net capacity of the off-grid system alone comes out to be above 10,000MW. The utilisation factor is primarily a function of a solar panel's efficiency, its exposure to sunlight hours and associated irradiance in each such hour. The above deduced capacity is already 42% of the average power demand which prevails on our grid in summers. Solar batteries are also improving this off-grid capacity further by keeping the power available from the same source even after sunset.
While the above transformation continues along with the augmentation of installed grid capacity, the utility bills of those on the grid continue to balloon with the impact of the increasing capacity charge. Yet the tariff structure still largely operates in the mode of power scarcity by charging higher per unit for higher consumption. Otherwise, widespread use of electricity for domestic and commercial cooking and heating may help a lot in this regard. Additionally, even partial diversion of the pertaining gas to industry can also reduce imports of expensive liquefied natural gas (LNG).
A highly encouraging development, though initiated under International Monetary Fund (IMF) pressure, is the effort which is under way since early last year to eliminate captive power and divert the associated load to the grid. This would, of course, also result in sparing around 280 million standard cubic feet per day (mmscfd) of processed gas for more efficient applications. Available data for the past fiscal year also indicates the effort is on the right track. However, its long-term success is largely conditional on the dependability of power supply to industrial units as per their stringent operational requirements.
The above measures can definitely go a long way in increasing the consumption of the grid's load and minimising capacity charge. However, I apprehend that the recent introduction of net-billing may not prove to be of much use. The fact that purchase of solar batteries in FY2025-26 increased by around 2.5 times compared with the preceding year rather indicates that even those partially on the grid now may soon be 100% off-grid.
This trend of opting for alternative avenues is visible in energy uses other than electricity too. For example, as per the Energy Yearbook 2025, the aggregate conventionally documented consumption of energy by the industrial sector experienced marked reduction of around 46% since 2020 till 2025. Solar ingress is not the only factor accounting for the entire gap. Higher utility costs have compelled industry to adopt alternative fuels like coal and wood too. As per a recent study, coal contributes 20% of the textile sector's energy mix. No wonder use of solid fuel boilers has increased considerably in recent years.
Similarly, the Energy Yearbook reports decline of 58% by volume in the use of coal since 2021 till 2025 in the brick-kilns industry. Probably, to accommodate economic factors, it is being used together with crop residues and in some cases even fuels like used tyres, lube oil, plastic and textile waste.
What is to be done
Based on the above, it is evident that we should be very cautious while intervening in solarisation. It has proven to be the biggest saviour for our economy. In addition to its contribution in savings in energy imports, the GDP it is annually shouldering is many times more. Secondly, the perennially open drain on the economy called capacity charge continues to widen. Therefore, there is a clear and urgent requirement for renegotiating the evidently pro-sellers' power purchase agreements and bringing the required balance to them.
Thirdly, we need to keep an eye on the changes in our energy fabric in the context of our carbon footprint and commitments to the United Nations regarding reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
THE WRITER IS A PETROLEUM ENGINEER AND AN OIL AND GAS MANAGEMENT PROFESSIONAL

items.author: DR MANZOOR AHMAD
items.content:
Pakistan's National Tariff Policy 2025-30 is now in its second year of implementation. Yet questions persist about whether tariff reforms were necessary, whether the underlying data were reliable, and whether reducing import duties will benefit the economy. These are legitimate questions. But before judging the reforms, we must address a more fundamental issue: was Pakistan genuinely an open economy, or had decades of protectionism weakened its competitiveness and export potential?
Much of the confusion appears to stem from a misinterpretation of the tariff indicators published by the World Trade Organisation (WTO). These indicators are useful, but they must be understood in context. Headline figures on applied customs duties do not necessarily capture the full burden of protection created by Pakistan's regulatory duties (RDs), additional customs duties (ACDs) and other import taxes. Nor does a relatively low trade-weighted average tariff necessarily mean that an economy is open to international competition.
The distinction is important. A trade-weighted average reflects tariff rates weighted by the value of actual imports. Products imported in large quantities, such as petroleum, edible oil and machinery, have a greater influence on the average, while goods facing prohibitively high duties, such as cars and consumer goods, account for a relatively small share of imports precisely because those duties discourage their importation. A proper assessment must therefore examine not only average tariffs but also tariff peaks, additional duties and the overall tax burden on imports.
The evidence from government ministries, international financial institutions and independent researchers leaves little doubt that Pakistan needed to address its restrictive trade regime.
In 2019, the then government's National Tariff Policy for 2019-24 acknowledged the extent of Pakistan's tariff protection. It noted that Pakistan had the highest weighted average tariff among 70 countries with annual exports exceeding $20 billion. It also observed that, while all 20 of the fastest-growing export economies had reduced import tariffs during the preceding decade, Pakistan's tariffs had increased by 11%. While successful export economies were opening up to international competition, Pakistan was moving in the opposite direction.
The case for reform, therefore, did not originate with the current policy. For years, multilateral institutions, Pakistani think tanks and academic researchers had identified high import taxes as a major reason for the country's persistently weak export performance. The World Bank placed Pakistan among the world's most protected economies, ranking it seventh on the Overall Trade Restrictiveness Index. It highlighted how a complicated tariff structure, comprising customs duties alongside additional customs duties, regulatory duties and other measures, distorted investment decisions and favoured heavily protected industries over more competitive businesses. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) similarly identified persistently high tariffs and an increasingly complex tariff structure as important factors behind Pakistan's poor export performance.
The WTO's 2022 Trade Policy Review provides further evidence. More than 40% of Pakistan's tariff lines carried duties exceeding 15%, a threshold commonly used to identify tariff peaks. The corresponding proportions for peer countries were considerably lower. If the total burden of regulatory and additional duties were also included, this figure would have been much higher.
The Economic Advisory Group, comprising independent Pakistani economists, highlighted another striking distortion. In 2023, trade-related taxes accounted for more than 40% of Pakistan's total tax revenue, compared with a global average of approximately 5%. The need for tariff reform, therefore, was not based on questionable data or an arbitrary preference for liberalisation. It was recognised by successive governments and supported by a substantial body of national and international research.
When the current reforms were debated in 2024-25, dire predictions were made. Critics warned that reducing tariffs would devastate domestic manufacturing, severely damage government revenues and trigger a balance-of-payments crisis. Some estimates suggested that the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) could lose more than Rs2,000 billion annually in import-related revenue.
Fifteen months into the reform process, the evidence does not support the predicted doomsday scenario. Although it is still too early to assess the full impact of the five-year National Tariff Policy, Pakistan's manufacturing sector has recorded growth of more than 6.5% after years of weak performance. Pakistan now has its highest-ever foreign exchange reserves and its balance-of-payments situation is positive for the first time in over two decades. Exports typically take time to respond to changes in trade policy, but they recorded growth of 10% in the first quarter of the current financial year.
These developments should be interpreted cautiously. Manufacturing growth, export performance and the external account are influenced by many factors beyond import tariffs. Nevertheless, one conclusion is already warranted: the predicted collapse of manufacturing and the anticipated balance-of-payments crisis have not materialised.
Tariff liberalisation is not about opening the economy indiscriminately or abandoning domestic industry. It is about changing the incentives that shape investment and production. Businesses should be encouraged to compete through productivity, technology, quality and innovation rather than depend indefinitely on high import barriers.
No country can build a competitive export economy by insulating its industries indefinitely from international competition. Successful industrialisers have followed different paths and used different policy instruments, but integration with international markets has been central to their long-term success.
The National Tariff Policy should ultimately be judged by whether it helps Pakistan raise productivity, expand exports and create sustainable employment. These outcomes will take time, and the government must remain willing to correct implementation problems as evidence emerges.
But the starting point for this debate must be the facts. Pakistan's trade regime was not as open as some suggest, and the case for reform was established long before the current policy was introduced. The real choice is not between protecting Pakistani industry and opening the economy. It is between protecting industries from competition indefinitely and helping them become competitive enough to succeed in the world.
THE WRITER IS A SENIOR FELLOW WITH THE PAKISTAN INSTITUTE OF DEVELOPMENT ECONOMICS. PREVIOUSLY, HE SERVED AS PAKISTAN'S AMBASSADOR TO THE WORLD TRADE ORGANISATION

items.author: Faran Mahmood
items.content:
Heavy borrowing to build AI infrastructure, and an oil price that has surged since the Iran war began, have created a shock in the US bond markets that has raised US long-term borrowing costs to levels not seen in almost two decades. The Trump administration's attempts to cap them, including expanded buybacks of long-dated debt and coordinated yen support with Japan, have failed to turn yields lower.
Brent crude, around $70 a barrel in early July, has since climbed above $110. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan have all raised rates this summer. Because US yields anchor bond markets everywhere, the effects travel, though unevenly. Economies closely tied to America, or with fragile external finances, feel them most. Pakistan, an importer of both energy and capital, belongs to the second group.
However, this is not a sign of global recession fuelled by the Gulf crisis. The combined trade surplus of China, South Korea and Taiwan alone in September was a staggering $200 billion. What has changed is that this money is not flowing into the US bond market. The US needs the massive East Asian surplus to fund its deficit, but the surplus is landing in US equities instead. This phenomenon is known as de-reservification, where sovereign countries move dollars from traditional reserves to pension funds, banks and other investment funds.
Apparently, the dollar's role globally, and particularly in Asia, is increasingly driven by returns rather than safety. For Pakistan, higher yields matter less than what is driving them. The country sources roughly 90% of its energy from abroad, so every move in crude passes quickly into petrol, diesel, power tariffs, transport and food.
This year has already shown how fast it works. Domestic fuel prices were raised about 20% in early March as the conflict escalated. Headline inflation then rose from 7.3% in March to 10.9% in April and 11.1% in August, driven by energy, transport costs and food. Hence, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) raised its policy rate by 100 basis points to 11.5% in April and has held it there since, including at its September meeting. Officials have told the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that even with oil near $95, average inflation this fiscal year could stay below 9%, keeping real rates comfortably positive, but only if oil holds near $100. With Brent now above that level, the projection is being tested. A heavier fuel bill also eats into an import budget of roughly $69 billion to $70 billion, leaving less room for the machinery and raw materials that exporters need.
This removes the option of easing in the near future. That matters for the government, whose interest bill already absorbs a large share of the budget, and for businesses that need affordable credit to expand. It also complicates the official goal of 4% growth, after 3.7% in the last fiscal year. Despite that, Pakistan must keep borrowing abroad. It recently raised $3 billion through a Eurobond, a sign that market access has returned. But as US yields rise, investors demand wider spreads on frontier credits, so the next issuance, rollover or commercial loan will cost more. Capital also tends to drift towards the safety of dollar assets in such episodes, putting pressure on the rupee.
That pressure arrives at a delicate moment. Islamabad and the IMF remain divided over exchange-rate policy. The Fund wants a more market-determined rupee, while the government argues that stability contains imported inflation. Moreover, Pakistan is not entering this shock empty-handed. Reserves have been rebuilt, the current account has stayed relatively contained, and successive IMF reviews have unlocked official inflows. Dollar remittances stretch further when the rupee weakens, and domestic bond yields respond mostly to local inflation and SBP policy, so the pass-through from Washington is partial rather than automatic escalation.
What policymakers should do
Three priorities stand out. Firstly, continue to pass through fuel prices honestly and shield the poorest with targeted support rather than blanket subsidies, which would jeopardise fiscal targets the IMF is watching. Secondly, allow the rupee reasonable flexibility instead of burning reserves to hold a line the market doubts. Thirdly, use calm windows to lock in longer-dated financing and accelerate energy substitution, from solar to domestic gas and efficiency, because every dollar of avoided oil imports is also a dollar of avoided exposure to global rates.
Pakistan's recovery is intact but newly fragile. The sell-off in US Treasuries, which has pushed 30-year yields to a 19-year high of 5.36%, will make dollars costlier, narrow SBP's room to manoeuvre and raise the price of fuel that Pakistan cannot produce itself. Oil is the largest risk. The bond market is the amplifier. Islamabad's best defence is to protect reserves, avoid spending them on an unsustainable rupee, and use the breathing room it has to cut its dependence on imported energy. If oil falls and yields stabilise, Pakistan's recovery stays on track. If both keep climbing into 2027, just as large external repayments fall due, the margin for error will shrink quickly.
THE WRITER IS A CAMBRIDGE GRADUATE AND WORKS AS A STRATEGY CONSULTANT

items.author: Dr Ali Salman
items.content:
The National Tariff Policy 2025-30 has remained in the news for the right reasons recently, and it is time to offer a provisional assessment in the light of recent data. The good news first: the policy is working.
One of the underlying objectives of the policy was to stop treating customs tariff as a source of revenue and start treating it as a tool of industrial policy – to provide signals to industry and consumers. One year of experience indicates that the policy is succeeding, as the contribution of import-based revenue has come down from above 50% of overall tax revenue to less than 40%. This has happened despite an increase in import volume and customs revenue, while overall tariffs have gone down – exactly as the research had predicted.
Now the more difficult question is the impact of the tariff policy on industrial output, competitiveness and the overall trade balance. It is too early to comment on a policy that is designed for five years. However, some trends can be observed without necessarily establishing causal relationships. During the first quarter of fiscal year 2026-27 (1QFY27), Pakistan's provisional total goods exports reached $8.42 billion. This marks a 10.84% year-on-year growth compared with $7.59 billion during the first quarter of fiscal year 2025-26 (1QFY26). Agriculture and food rose by 23%, manufacturing, mining and energy by 17%, and textiles and apparel by 6%. This is broadly aligned with the goal of 14% growth due to tariff reforms by 2030.
However, there are strong headwinds against the National Tariff Policy. Pakistan's tariff debate is often framed as a choice between protecting domestic industry and exposing it to foreign competition. The real choice is different. It is whether the state should continue allocating resources through taxes, layers of customs duties, regulatory duties (RD) and additional customs duties (ACD), or establish a predictable, low and broadly uniform regime across industries and value chains.
If the state maintains different rates of taxes and tariffs, including ACD and RD, for different sectors of the economy, we are effectively selecting certain markets over others and obstructing competition. The durable principle is straightforward. Move towards low and uniform taxes and tariffs across industries and within value chains. Customs duties, regulatory duties and additional customs duties should cease to be instruments for selecting sectors, directing resources or shaping investment decisions. Firms should compete on productivity, quality and export capability rather than on their access to protection. A gradual transition may be necessary, but its destination must remain clear, and no sector should be treated as a favourite.
The discussion on whether we should include ACD or RD in our estimates of customs duty is peripheral at best. We should be discussing effective rates of tariffs in all cases. The argument from industry against tariff reduction can be summed up as follows. The local industry is at a cost disadvantage of around 20% to 30% against its foreign competitors on account of energy cost, bad infrastructure, expensive capital, deteriorating rule of law and other frictions like poor regulation. Therefore, to provide a level playing field, the state must provide a tariff protection wall to local firms by the same degree. Hence, some sectors get 10% protection, some get 20%. This is the underlying philosophy of all protectionists. The National Tariff Policy essentially puts a stop to this philosophy and provides a framework towards free and competitive markets.
For the sake of argument, let us consider this point of view sympathetically and extend the argument to include other problems of governance. The problem of corruption, for example, is very "taxing" and "tarrifying". We can add a few percentage points of tariff protection on its account. This is an unending debate. Also, no firm in the same market faces the same cost structure.
However, I want to acknowledge one point made recently at a seminar. The industry says customs duty is now less of a problem, and that they face a greater problem due to the high rate of General Sales Tax (GST), which is 18%, as it provides a huge advantage to the informal sector that does not pay any GST. The solution is not to seek protection from customs duty. The solution is to bring GST down to 5% across the board. This will wipe out the informal market as it will lose the incentive to stay undocumented.
The push for continuation of protective tariffs is not universal. Some sectors, like the steel industry, are adjusting well to the changing dynamics, where all other factors remain the same. A significant reduction in the cost of capital and the emergence of alternative sources of electricity are two major developments of the last two years. This can compensate for higher costs in other factors of production.
Another moot point is the cascading structure. Continuation of the existing cascading structure in tariffs is likely to preserve the existing inefficient structure of the economy. The new tariff policy is gradually reducing overall tariff rates, but it is broadly preserving the cascading. It retains tariff escalation by continuing to apply higher protection at later stages of processing. An overall reduction in tariff rates will reduce the impact of cascading but will not dismantle it.
The industrial policy idea that we should import components, assemble them locally and provide advantage to assemblers by erecting tariff walls on finished goods is deeply flawed. As the failure of the mobile phone device manufacturing policy has shown, a country cannot achieve competitive advantage through assembly and protection only. It must first establish an ecosystem around certain products where it has comparative advantage, and then establish value-chain linkages with leading global producers. This needs removal of tariff walls and investment in research and development (R&D), not support for the emergence of new classes of auto-assemblers.
THE WRITER IS CEO OF PRIME INSTITUTE, AN INDEPENDENT ECONOMIC POLICY THINK TANK

items.title: Policeman Injured From Accidental Gunshot During Tri-Nation Series Duty
items.summary:
A Dolphin Force officer deployed for security of the tri-nation ODI cricket series in Rawalpindi was injured after his own rifle accidentally went off during duty.
The officer was on the security route for the series between Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and England. He was immediately shifted to a hospital after the incident.
Rifle Fell During Patrol Duty
According to officials, the officer was deployed on patrolling duty along the route from Double Road to Faizabad. During the patrol, his rifle fell to the ground.
Following standard operating procedures (SOPs), he picked up the rifle and removed its magazine.
Bullet Hit His Foot
Officials said the rifle had become loaded when it hit the ground, and a round had moved into the chamber.
To check whether the chamber was empty, the officer pointed the rifle toward the ground and pulled the trigger. The rifle fired, and the bullet hit him in the foot.

The department described the service as another step towards improving public facilitation and making traffic-related services easier to access.

Why Early Treatment Matters
Doctors stress that rabies is almost always fatal once clinical symptoms appear, but it is preventable if wounds are cleaned and vaccines are given soon after a bite. Anyone bitten or scratched by a dog should wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical care.
Earlier this month, Sindh recorded another rabies death linked to a dog bite in Tharparkar, underscoring gaps in timely post-exposure treatment across the province.

Losses in Procurement and Bank Dealings
The report said five procurement cases caused a loss of more than Rs. 3.26 billion to the national exchequer. Unauthorized administrative dealings with a commercial bank caused a further loss of Rs. 20.85 billion.
Auditors also found that Pakistan Post opened more bank accounts than it was allowed to. Transactions worth Rs. 20 billion were made through these accounts.
In another case, the government suffered a loss of Rs. 492.5 million. The audit also identified recoveries of more than Rs. 3.74 billion in 11 different cases.
The largest share came from 15 other cases, which involved irregularities of more than Rs. 194.54 billion. The audit findings come weeks after Pakistan Post announced higher charges for postal services.

The governor met executives from JP Morgan, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, Barclays, Bank of America, and others at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from October 12 to 17, according to an SBP statement.

He said inflation has fallen sharply from FY23 highs to almost within the target range in FY26, despite a major oil price shock. Real GDP growth reached 3.7 percent in FY26 and is projected at 3.5-4.5 percent in FY27.

He added that the current account deficit is expected to stay within 0-1 percent of GDP in FY27, while the primary fiscal balance posted a third straight annual surplus in FY26.
The governor also mentioned the staff-level agreement with the IMF on the EFF and RSF reviews, saying reforms have boosted investor confidence and led to sovereign credit rating upgrades.

The Nvidia-backed AI group, which competes against CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe and Lambda, has grown rapidly ⁠since ​its launch, scaling from $100 million to ​more than $103 billion in total contracted value in just two-and-a-half years.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has been a key driver of global growth, but also poses economic risks should investment in the technology falter, experts and policymakers said this week at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
Propelled by spending on data centres and microchips, AI has helped cushion the economic shock of rising global energy prices caused by war in the Middle East, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a report on Tuesday.
The fund's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted this week that global trade rose 8.3 per cent between 2023 and 2025 -- a figure she said would be closer to 4.6 per cent without AI-related products.
"It is everywhere in the global economy," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said of AI on Friday.
"You see it in GDP. You see it in the stock market. You see it in the bond market... So it is here, and it's just the beginning."
But some top officials gathered in Bangkok this week cautioned against relying too heavily on AI investment.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh called AI the "most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime, and said it had "a huge benefit". Still, he warned the road ahead would be "bumpy".
"The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don't know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies," he said.
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva similarly noted the AI boom's boost to global growth, but she told AFP that any slowdown in the industry "would be felt across the world".
"If there is loss of confidence and money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks," Georgieva said.
An IMF report released this week projected that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 per cent by 2028.
"Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction," the report said.
While AI investment and trade have softened the global economic impact of the Middle East war, economists at Moody's Analytics have warned that if the conflict drags on, it could "puncture" the boom.
They said higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions could push up operating costs and interest rates, adding to doubts over "the long-term profitability and viability of AI business models".
"A drawn-out conflict would put serious strain on the economics behind AI investment," the group said.
The uncertainty around regulation has also clouded the technology's outlook.
Leaders like US President Donald Trump have urged more limited government regulation, even as some in the industry have called for legislation to mitigate risks.
Georgieva, the IMF chief, appeared on Friday to link such regulation to future investment.
"If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities," she said in Bangkok.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will ​bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models ‌forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act.
Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares ​to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery.
He said the forecast ​assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that ⁠new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion".
Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an initial ​public offering expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion.
Humans in control, for now
Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about ​the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control.
"We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially ​great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials.
AI was a major topic at the IMF and World ​Bank meetings, as both a source of growth offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer ‌and stock ⁠valuations crash.
Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind.
But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants.
More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the ​data center computing capacity needed to ​power AI, he said.
Strictest controls ⁠on biological research
Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology.
"Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the ​misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have ​many choices to make," ⁠he said.
Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety."
Despite some recent high-profile incidents where rogue AI systems have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to ⁠impose safeguards ​was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years."
Read: Artificial Intelligence: Dawn of a new global order
Clark ​also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he ​said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) has renewed its call for new administrative units in Sindh, arguing that the devolution of powers and authority is essential to address longstanding civic problems in Karachi, Hyderabad and other urban areas.
“Establishing new and empowered administrative units is the biggest challenge and the solution to ensuring that people receive their rights at their doorstep,” MQM-P Chairman Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui said during a meeting with legal experts at the party’s Bahadurabad headquarters.
The meeting brought together members of the Muttahida Lawyers Forum, the party’s Legal Aid Committee and prominent legal experts to discuss urban Sindh’s civic challenges, constitutional and legal reforms, judicial performance and strategies for securing the release of party activists in detention.
Read: 'The country's system is about to be reset': Naqvi says move will bring improvement in affairs
Senior MQM-P leader Wasim Akhtar and other party leaders attended the meeting, while former judge Qazi Khalid was also present.
Addressing the gathering, Siddiqui said the lack of basic facilities and the failure to devolve powers had fuelled public discontent in Karachi, Hyderabad and other urban districts. He called for a new administrative arrangement to restore balance in governance and ensure that citizens could access their rights and essential services more effectively.
Legal experts briefed the party leadership on what they described as shortcomings in existing laws and regulations that could be exploited to deprive citizens of their rights. They presented legal proposals and draft amendments aimed at addressing procedural and constitutional gaps.
The participants also discussed the need for far-reaching judicial reforms to ensure timely, affordable and transparent justice, particularly for disadvantaged and marginalised communities.
Members of the Legal Aid Committee pledged to expand and strengthen legal assistance for citizens facing difficulties in accessing justice. The meeting also considered legal strategies concerning detained party workers and efforts to secure their release.
At the conclusion of the meeting, MQM-P leaders and legal experts reiterated their commitment to pursuing the party’s demands through political, constitutional and legal means, including advocating new administrative units and reforms to existing laws.
The current debate over new provinces began on July 30, when Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi called for additional administrative units or provinces as part of a broader overhaul of the country’s governance system. Naqvi argued that meaningful structural reforms were needed to improve governance, deliver justice and create opportunities for young people.
Also Read: Governance system has collapsed: Naqvi
A day later, his proposal appeared to receive support from Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, who said an administrative reset, if required, should be undertaken to ensure good governance
The proposal quickly became politically sensitive in Sindh, where the PPP strongly opposed any move to divide the province. Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah rejected Naqvi’s assessment that the governance system had collapsed and called the proposal outdated, warning that no bloodshed would be allowed over the creation of new provinces.
The debate widened in August when Muttahida Qaumi Movement–Pakistan (MQM-P) backed the creation of new provinces and called for a national dialogue with political parties. The party argued that Pakistan’s growing population, poor governance and concentration of political power made greater administrative devolution necessary. The move put the party, which is part of the federal coalition but sits in opposition in Sindh, at odds with the PPP’s position on the province.
The PPP, meanwhile, maintained that administrative reform and the division of Sindh were separate questions. Sindh minister Nasir Hussain Shah said the provincial government was willing to discuss measures to improve governance and devolve power, but rejected linking those reforms to the creation of a new province.
The dispute reached the Sindh Assembly at the beginning of September. On September 3, the house unanimously passed a resolution rejecting any proposal to divide Sindh or alter its territorial limits. The resolution described Sindh as a “historic, civilisational and constitutional entity” and declared that “Sindh is one and shall remain one”.
Read More: PTI's Barrister Gohar warns against dividing provinces without broad public consensus
Naqvi, however, showed no sign of backing away. On September 5, he said he would continue to support new provinces regardless of whether he remained in office, arguing that the ultimate decision should belong to the people rather than politicians or governments. He said the public should first be told the “pros and cons” of creating new administrative units before being allowed to decide.
That position has since raised another question over how public opinion could be formally established. A constitutional debate emerged over whether a referendum could be used to gauge support for new provinces. Article 48(6) allows a matter of national importance to be put to a referendum following approval by a joint sitting of Parliament, although a referendum itself would not create a new province; any change to provincial boundaries would still have to follow the constitutional process.
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan warned on September 7 that dividing Sindh or any other province without the consent of its people and representatives would weaken the federation. He called for a commission and extensive deliberations before the issue was taken to parliament.
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, while accepting that Sindh had the right to take its own position, also said a final decision would have to emerge through consensus. Asif separately suggested that Islamabad could be used as a starting point for any future administrative restructuring, while Prime Minister’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah said the question of new provinces should be taken up at the relevant forums and resolved through consensus among political parties.

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
Nearly four months after a K2 Airways aircraft plunged into the sea off Ormara, the search for its black box, wreckage and cockpit crew is entering a new phase, with Pakistan stepping up efforts to enlist international expertise for a deep-sea recovery operation.
With the aircraft believed to lie around 3,000 metres below the surface, the search is expected to rely on advanced sonar systems, autonomous underwater vehicles and remotely operated vehicles equipped with high-definition cameras and specialised recovery tools.
The government has intensified contacts with foreign experts and several international companies to determine the best way to locate and recover the aircraft’s remains from the seabed, according to sources. The black box and wreckage are considered crucial to establishing what happened in the aircraft’s final moments.
Read: K2: families demand deep-sea search
The aircraft, operated by the privately owned domestic cargo carrier, crashed into the sea on July 7 this year after encountering adverse conditions near Ormara. Sources said the transmitter beacon fitted to the black box stopped emitting signals about a month after the accident, making the search more difficult.
The Pakistan Navy had earlier used specialised equipment and side-scan sonar to identify a possible location of the black box on the seabed. Acoustic signals were used to scan the area at a depth of around 3,000 metres, but further progress now depends on more sophisticated underwater technology and specialised deep-sea salvage expertise.
As part of the proposed operation, a detailed three-dimensional map of the seabed will be prepared using a multibeam echo sounder. The technology can map underwater terrain, measure depths and identify potential obstructions, helping search teams narrow down the area where the aircraft’s wreckage may be located.
Autonomous underwater vehicles may also be deployed to survey the seabed using sonar, cameras and other sensors. Data and images collected by these unmanned systems could help identify suspicious objects and pinpoint areas requiring closer inspection.
Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), controlled from a support vessel, could play an equally important role. Equipped with high-definition cameras, powerful lights and robotic arms, the machines can examine wreckage at close range and, where feasible, retrieve smaller objects or position specialised equipment around the debris.
Search teams may also use a towed pinger locator to detect acoustic signals from the black box beacon. However, with the transmitter reportedly no longer functioning, its usefulness could be limited, increasing reliance on other methods.
A magnetometer could provide another means of locating the wreckage by detecting variations in the magnetic field associated with large metallic objects. Combining sonar readings, magnetic measurements and underwater imagery could help investigators verify the suspected location of the aircraft.
Specialised deep-sea salvage vessels may be required to support the operation. Such ships can carry heavy-duty winches, cranes, remotely operated systems and other equipment needed to access and recover wreckage from extreme depths. Operating at around 3,000 metres requires specialised machinery, technical expertise and careful planning.
Also Read: Deep-sea hunt for K2 crash wreckage to begin next month
The recovery of the black box and wreckage is considered essential to the investigation, as flight data and cockpit voice recordings could help investigators reconstruct the aircraft’s final moments, examine cockpit activity and determine the possible causes of the crash.
Sources said the company that owns the cargo aircraft would bear 50 per cent of the search costs. Raja Tariq, who owns up to 60pc of the cargo aircraft company’s shares, has been informed of the decision, they added.
The next phase of the search is expected to depend on assessments by international specialists, the availability of suitable equipment and the identification of the most promising locations on the seabed.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistani freelancers earned a record $197 million in export receipts in September 2026, marking the highest monthly earnings in the country’s history. The strong performance pushed their total earnings during the first quarter of fiscal year 2026-27 to approximately $550 million.
According to figures shared by Adviser to the Finance Minister Khurram Schehzad, freelance earnings increased by 11% compared with August and rose 49% from September 2025. Total earnings for the July-September quarter also increased by 46% compared with the same period last year.
Schehzad said Pakistan’s growing freelance economy was turning the skills of young digital professionals into export revenue and foreign exchange earnings without adding to the country’s debt.
Pakistani Freelancers Set New Monthly Export Earnings Record in September 2026
The latest figures reflect a strong start to the current fiscal year. Pakistani freelancers earned $175.44 million in July 2026, while their combined earnings for July and August reached approximately $352 million.
The record $197 million earned in September further strengthened this performance, taking first-quarter receipts to around $550 million.
Pakistan’s freelance sector has also recorded significant growth over the past fiscal year. Freelancers earned a total of $1.76 billion in FY2025-26, highlighting the increasing role of online work in the country’s digital economy.
The growth also comes as Pakistan’s broader information technology sector continues to expand. IT exports reached $435 million in September 2026, marking their second-highest monthly level on record.
Limited Jobs Drive More Professionals Toward Freelancing
Pakistan Freelancers Association (PAFLA) Chairman Ibrahim Amin said the continued increase in earnings showed that more Pakistani digital professionals were participating in the international freelance market.
He noted that many IT graduates and experienced professionals were turning to freelancing because of limited job opportunities in the domestic market.
Online platforms allow these professionals to offer services to international clients and earn income in foreign currencies. This income helps them support their families while contributing to Pakistan’s foreign exchange earnings.
Freelancing also provides an alternative source of employment for the country’s growing workforce, particularly for people with skills in software development, graphic design, digital marketing, and other technology-related fields.

Industry representatives believe Pakistan can further expand its freelance economy by investing in professional training, skills development, and support services for digital workers.
Better access to training and international markets could help more Pakistanis secure projects from overseas clients and increase the value of their services.
The latest record highlights the growing contribution of freelancers to Pakistan’s export earnings. Continued investment in digital skills and improved support for independent professionals could help the country strengthen its position in the global freelance market and generate additional foreign exchange in the coming years.

items.author: Life And Style Desk
items.content:
Former Pakistan cricket captain Wasim Akram has shared a humorous message for people aged over 50, offering advice on how to use mobile phones, WhatsApp and social media without overwhelming others with messages and calls.
Sharing the video on Instagram, Akram wrote, “Viewer discretion: THIS VIDEO IS AVAILABLE FOR PEOPLE OVER 50 ON HOW AND WHEN TO USE A MOBILE PHONE/ WHATSAPP. AND YOU ARE WELCOME...”
In the video, Akram said he could understand Gen Z and Gen Alpha because they were always on their phones. However, he suggested that older generations should learn to use their devices more thoughtfully, particularly when communicating with younger people.
“This is special for 50+ that they should use WhatsApp, social media and their phones the correct way,” he said, before advising viewers to stop sending random content to people every day.
“Firstly, most importantly, stop sending random stuff to people every day,” Akram said, explaining that such messages could become annoying, even when the sender had good intentions. He added that people should not feel obliged to send good morning messages to everyone daily.
Akram also highlighted the importance of considering people's attention spans before forwarding videos. He suggested that lengthy videos were less likely to be watched in full, with shorter clips of around two minutes being more suitable for many viewers.
“I get you mean well, but it annoys people. Also, you don't have to send good morning to everyone every day. The third thing is when you send videos, please know that attention spans are short these days. Nobody will watch a 30-minute-long video, only 2 minutes”, he added.
His next piece of advice concerned constant phone use. Akram urged people not to remain available on WhatsApp around the clock, pointing out that there was nothing wrong with replying to a message five minutes later. Constantly checking notifications and responding immediately, he suggested, could create unnecessary stress.
Reflecting on his own experiences, Akram said he had friends who never seemed to put their phones down, even when spending time together. He encouraged people to take things easy, enjoy life and manage their messages rather than feeling pressured to respond to everything immediately.
Akram explained that he still checked and forwarded messages but preferred to keep things under control instead of allowing his phone to dominate his time.
The video sparked a discussion among social media users, with some agreeing with Akram's advice while others felt his message needed a more compassionate approach.
One user wrote, “At some part, I agree with you but never make someone feel like a burden because they are trying to stay connected.”
Another commenter expressed complete agreement, particularly with his point about daily good morning messages and people forwarding disaster videos.
The differing reactions highlighted a familiar dilemma in the digital age: while excessive messages and unsolicited videos can overwhelm recipients, such gestures may also be a way for some people to maintain relationships and feel connected to family and friends.
Akram's light-hearted advice highlights the importance of digital etiquette in an age when smartphones and social media have become central to everyday communication. His message is not necessarily about discouraging older people from using technology, but about encouraging them to be mindful of other people's time, attention and boundaries.
At the same time, staying connected should not make anyone feel like a nuisance or a burden. Whether it is forwarding videos, sending daily greetings or making frequent calls, a little consideration can go a long way. Ultimately, the goal is to use technology to strengthen relationships, not strain them, while remembering that meaningful connections matter far more than the number of messages exchanged.

items.content:
The Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry on Sunday urged traders and people affected by the closure of the Pakistan-Iran border not to believe any “negative propaganda”, expressing hope that the situation would improve soon.
The appeal came as cross-border commercial activities between Pakistan and Iran were suddenly halted at the Taftan border crossing on Saturday following the unexpected closure of the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) immigration gate and withdrawal of an important import waiver, leaving traders concerned over potential multi-million-rupee financial losses.
According to a statement issued by the president of the Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the president, while in contact with senior officials regarding the closure of the borders adjoining Iran, informed the Ministry of Commerce about the difficulties being faced by traders, importers and other businesses.
Read: Trade at Taftan comes to a grinding halt
The statement said the Ministry of Commerce assured the chamber that the border closure was on technical and temporary grounds, with the sole purpose of addressing incidents involving vehicles on the Pakistan-Iran highway in recent days and issues faced at customs.
The chamber urged all traders and people affected by the border closures to remain hopeful that the situation would improve soon and not to believe any “baseless negative propaganda” in this regard.
Sources said the immigration gate at Taftan — a vital commercial artery connecting the two neighbouring countries — was closed on the instructions of senior officials in Islamabad.
However, the exact reasons behind the decision remain undisclosed, and authorities have yet to issue an official notification explaining the suspension or providing a timeline for reopening.
The border closure coincided with regulatory developments from the Ministry of Commerce.
On Friday, the ministry issued an office memorandum, No. 9(3)/2017-IRAN, withdrawing its earlier order dated Oct 3, which had extended the Electronic Import Form (EIF) waiver for imports from Iran.
Also Read: FM Dar, Iranian FM discuss regional situation, OIC meeting in Baghdad
Responding to the evolving situation, the Chamber of Commerce and Industry Quetta, Balochistan, issued an urgent advisory to its members and the broader business community, recommending a temporary suspension of all new purchases, product bookings and trade commitments from Iran.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei, commenting on reports about the closure of the land border with Pakistan, said: “Due to certain technical issues and the need to take precautionary measures, border crossings and exchanges have been temporarily suspended. However, the relevant authorities of the two countries are in close contact and are holding consultations to resolve the issue as soon as possible and restore normal operations at the border crossings.”

He further alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency (PR) arrangements had fled after collecting substantial sums of money from several influential bureaucrats.
Asif said several troubling accounts were circulating in connection with the matter, although he did not provide details or identify the individuals allegedly involved.
Questioning the commitment of senior officials who had occupied high offices and enjoyed the privileges and respect associated with public service, Asif asked whether their loyalty to Pakistan remained beyond suspicion throughout their careers.
He also questioned the conduct of officials who, he said, had enjoyed opportunities to accumulate wealth through both legitimate and illegitimate means while remaining favoured by politicians.
“Does it rise above all doubt and suspicion, or are they merely in transit?” Asif asked, questioning whether such officials viewed Pakistan as their permanent home or merely a temporary stop before settling abroad.

His remarks have brought renewed attention to questions surrounding the overseas settlement plans of serving and retired civil servants, particularly those holding influential positions in the government.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Pope Leo pledged on Sunday ​to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he ‌greeted crowds in St Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.
Smiling from ​a window of the Vatican's Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear ​voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and ⁠said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule.
Read: Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
"Having overcome this delicate phase... I will now gradually resume ​my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers," Leo said.
The pope, who was discharged from Rome's Gemelli ​hospital on Saturday, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual.
He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God "without compromise".
Nun cries as Leo makes appearance
Leo has been diagnosed with lung ​adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only ​in May 2025, caused shock.
Read More: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer
His doctors discharged him on Saturday after blood tests and chest imaging that day showed him well enough ‌to return ⁠home. They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently.
Crowds in St Peter's Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared at the window on Sunday. One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face.
A few steps away, a group of other nuns held aloft a sign ​reading, "Best wishes, Holy Father. We ​love you, and we are ⁠praying for you".
Pope's calendar in flux
Leo usually keeps a busy schedule, but the Vatican has cancelled his other public events until at least Wednesday, when he is due to hold ​a weekly general audience in St Peter's Square. It has not said whether he ​will hold that ⁠audience.
The pope is also planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader in decades.
Dr Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said on Saturday that Leo could be ⁠fully recovered ​in time for that trip.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, ​has however expressed scepticism. He told journalists on Friday the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition ​of his health".

For Adeel Nasir, 24, who has albinism and lives in Kot Radha Kishan, a town in Kasur district, Punjab Province of Pakistan, school meant constant adjustment to challenges that many people around him did not understand.
Because of low vision, he struggled to read what was written on classroom whiteboards. Some teachers seated him closer to the board, improved the lighting, and gave him written notes. But one classroom incident remained painful.
Adeel once asked a teacher what qualifications a fighter pilot needs. He expected encouragement about his ambition. Instead, he received a response focused on his eyesight.
“First of all, you should be able to see clearly with your eyes,” Adeel recalled the teacher saying.
His classmates laughed. Years later, he says people still notice his condition before they recognise his abilities.
“My abilities, my degrees, and my skills were ignored because of my weak eyesight and physical appearance,” he said during an in-person interview with Global Voices.
Adeel’s experience reflects a concern that Malooka-Anne Miti-Drummond, the UN Independent Expert on the enjoyment of human rights by persons with albinism, raised during her June 2026 visit to Pakistan. She said policies, programmes, and data systems overlook people with albinism.
Albinism is a rare, non-contagious, genetically inherited condition caused by reduced or absent production of melanin, the pigment responsible for colour in the skin, hair, and eyes. Reduced melanin can result in visual impairment and increased vulnerability to ultraviolet (UV) radiation because melanin provides natural protection against sun damage. People with albinism are born with the condition; it is not contagious and does not affect their intellectual ability.
Pakistan has no separate national estimate of how many people with albinism live in the country. The UN notes that country-level data on albinism is scarce worldwide, and many countries collect no official statistics on it. Available estimates put prevalence at roughly one in 17,000 to 20,000 people in many European and North American populations, and higher in some African communities. The UN has called for better data collection to understand the challenges people with albinism face.
The absence of a national estimate does not mean that people with albinism are absent in Pakistan. Researchers have documented albinism among Pakistani families despite the missing estimate. A study of 94 previously unreported Pakistani families with non-syndromic oculocutaneous albinism found disease-causing variants mainly in the TYR and OCA2 genes, two of the major genetic causes of albinism worldwide. Genetic studies of affected families cannot establish how many people with albinism live in the country.
For Adeel, the lack of recognition shapes how institutions treat his needs. After a long effort, he obtained a disability certificate, but as he explained, “The disability certificate we received is also issued on the basis of our weak eyesight, not because of albinism itself.”
“There is no place in any office or government institution where a separate form or category under the name of ‘albino’ exists where we can register ourselves,” Adeel added.
When a community is missing from data
The difficulty of documenting albinism ties to a broader gap in disability data. Many national systems measure disability through functional difficulties and do not record each medical condition separately. Pakistan’s 2023 Population and Housing Census asked about difficulty seeing, hearing, walking, communicating, remembering, and caring for oneself rather than individual conditions.
A Pakistan Bureau of Statistics representative, who spoke to Global Voices on condition of anonymity, said the bureau keeps no separate official data on people with albinism. The person said collecting information on rare conditions requires well-designed questionnaires, and Pakistan would have to choose the best method before adding albinism to future data collection.
Asim Zafar, a disability rights advocate, emphasised that data is essential during an interview with Global Voices via WhatsApp:
“Data is very important for any country because planning is done on the basis of data, and budget allocation is done on the basis of planning.”
Miti-Drummond identified that missing data limits access to healthcare, education, and social protection: “When communities are not visible, their needs are not visible.”
Education, healthcare and everyday barriers
Sundus Arif, 39, was born and raised in Lahore, Pakistan. She has albinism and low vision, and she said in an online interview with Global Voices that her biggest challenge has often been getting others to understand her needs.
Her schools had no structured accommodations, so she had to explain her condition and advocate for adjustments herself. As a student, she needed simple measures: a seat in the shade during outdoor assemblies, larger-print material, and extra time to copy notes from the board. She said:
“There are neither clear guidelines nor effective arrangements in educational institutions of Pakistan to accommodate students with albinism.”
Adeel said small adjustments helped him stay in school, but he received no extra time in examinations despite his visual difficulties.
Miti-Drummond said bullying and a lack of support erode the confidence of children with albinism and hurt their education: “If a child is bullied, they are more likely to drop out of school.”
People with albinism also face specific healthcare needs for their skin and vision. Because melanin protects against UV radiation, they are more vulnerable to sun damage and need sun protection and regular medical care. Access to dermatological and eye care is a concern for people with albinism worldwide.
Sundus, also a parent of a child with albinism, said children need sunscreen and sunglasses to protect their skin and eyes from sunlight.
Miti-Drummond explained family income decides whether households can afford that protection:
“If you have to choose between sunscreen and buying food, and you are already struggling to buy food, this is something that becomes inaccessible.”
The World Health Organization (WHO) says early eye care, sun protection, and access to health information can reduce many of the complications linked to albinism. It recognises sunscreen as an important preventive measure because reduced melanin raises vulnerability to UV damage.
Qualified but excluded
Education does not remove social barriers for many people with albinism. Adeel said finding work was one of his biggest challenges after he finished his studies. He believes employers focused on his eyesight and appearance instead of his qualifications.
Miti-Drummond also pointed to employment discrimination worldwide: “You may be very well qualified, but actually getting employment, there was still stigma and discrimination.”
During the interview, Sundus said women with albinism face discrimination beyond disability-related barriers. Social expectations about appearance, marriage, and femininity add pressure. In her experience, people judged her appearance before they noticed her education, professional abilities, or personality. Women with albinism often have to challenge misconceptions about both their condition and their role in society.
Climate change adds another risk
Rising temperatures and frequent heatwaves in Pakistan add to the risk of sun exposure for people with albinism. Pakistan is among the countries most affected by climate change, and national climate assessments document rising temperatures, extreme heat events, and growing climate-related risks.
A study in the BMJ Global Health journal reported that climate change may increase vulnerability among people with albinism by intensifying exposure-related risks and creating barriers to preventive healthcare in low-resource settings.
For Adeel, heat and sunlight shape daily life. Sensitivity to sunlight makes it hard for him to move around outdoors, and he described problems with his skin and eyesight.
Lesson for Pakistan
Several countries have built specific frameworks for people with albinism. Miti-Drummond told Global Voices that efforts in Malawi, Cameroon, Tanzania, Mozambique, Uganda, Angola, and Panama improved awareness, healthcare access, education and protection from discrimination. For Pakistan, the first step is better information and inclusive planning.
Zafar said laws and policies fall short without implementation:
“Policies are available, laws have been made, but there is a lack of implementation.”
For Adeel, recognition means people with albinism should not have to fight individually for basic support.
Albinism is present across Pakistan, and existing systems do not recognise the needs of the people who live with it. Better data would make them visible. Inclusion also takes accessible healthcare, inclusive education, climate-sensitive planning and a voice for people with albinism in decisions that affect their lives. Miti-Drummond put the principle in four words: “Nothing for us without us.”
For Pakistan’s people with albinism, being counted is the first step, but being heard and included is the ultimate goal.
Umair Khan Abad contributed to the post.
Written by Mahpara Zulqadar

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Samsung is reportedly preparing a major overhaul of its One UI software with the upcoming One UI 10 update. According to a new leak, the company plans to change not only the interface but also how users interact with apps, access information, and connect their Galaxy devices.
The report suggests that Samsung wants to move beyond the small visual updates and gradual AI improvements introduced in recent versions. Instead, One UI 10 could bring a new software approach focused on simplifying everyday tasks and creating a more connected user experience.
Samsung Reportedly Planning Major Overhaul of One UI 10
The claims come from a source close to Nokia Power User and have received partial support from well-known Samsung tipster Ice Universe. However, Samsung has not officially confirmed these plans.
One UI 10 Could Change How Users Access Apps
One of the biggest reported changes involves moving away from the traditional app-based system. Samsung is said to be prioritizing what the report describes as “Contextual Flow,” which would bring relevant information from different apps together in a single view.
Currently, users often need to switch between multiple apps to check calendar events, find location details, and review conversations. Under the proposed approach, One UI 10 could combine this information to help users complete tasks without constantly moving between applications.
The concept appears to build on Samsung’s existing Now Nudge feature, potentially making it more useful by connecting information from different sources according to the user’s needs.
If implemented successfully, this approach could make Galaxy phones more convenient to use and reduce the time required to complete everyday activities.
Samsung Aims to Make One UI Simpler
Another reported priority is reducing the effort required to navigate the interface. Samsung reportedly wants to remove unnecessary taps, complicated menus, and extra steps that make certain tasks difficult to complete.
The goal is to make the software feel more direct and responsive, allowing users to find features and complete actions without navigating through multiple layers.
This could lead to changes in how settings, apps, and system features work together. However, the leak does not provide specific examples of the interface changes Samsung may introduce.
Better Connectivity Across Galaxy Devices
Samsung is also reportedly planning to improve the connections between its smartphones, tablets, and wearable devices.
The company already offers several ecosystem features, but One UI 10 could make switching between devices more seamless. For example, users could benefit from smoother handoffs when moving between a Galaxy phone, tablet, and compatible wearable.
Such improvements would help Samsung create a more unified experience for people who use multiple Galaxy products.
Advanced AI Features Could Require a Subscription
Artificial intelligence is expected to remain an important part of Samsung’s software strategy. However, the report suggests that the company may consider introducing a two-tier model for certain AI features.
Under this possible approach, basic everyday functions would remain free, while advanced processing tools and selected third-party AI integrations could require a paid subscription.
Running advanced AI features can require significant computing resources, which may encourage Samsung to explore additional revenue sources. However, the company has not confirmed any subscription plans for One UI 10, so this possibility should be treated as speculation.
One UI 10 Release Timeline
Samsung could face challenges in delivering such a major software overhaul in time for its next-generation foldable phones. According to the report, the company may instead target the Galaxy S29 series for the release.
The timing would also coincide with the tenth anniversary of One UI, making it a potential opportunity for Samsung to introduce a more significant change to its software.
The source also suggests that Samsung could release early developer previews well before the final version becomes available. These previews would give developers time to prepare their apps for the new software.
Despite the expected changes, users may not need to upgrade their phones to experience One UI 10. Recent Galaxy S-series and Galaxy Z foldable flagships are expected to remain compatible with future software updates under Samsung’s long-term support strategy.
For now, Samsung has not officially announced One UI 10 or confirmed its features and release date. More details are likely to emerge as development progresses.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Xiaomi has launched the Redmi G27Q 2026 Standard Edition gaming monitor in China. The new 27-inch monitor features a 2K display, a 240Hz refresh rate, and a 1ms response time, making it an option for gamers looking for smooth visuals and responsive gameplay.
Xiaomi Launches Redmi G27Q 2026 Gaming Monitor With 240Hz Refresh Rate
The new model shares most of its specifications with the standard Redmi G27Q 2026 but offers a lower refresh rate at a more affordable price. While the original version supports a 320Hz refresh rate, the Standard Edition comes with a 240Hz panel.
Redmi G27Q 2026 Standard Edition Specifications
The monitor features a 27-inch IPS panel with a resolution of 2560 x 1440 pixels. Its 240Hz refresh rate is designed to deliver smoother motion during fast-paced games, while the 1ms gray-to-gray (GTG) response time helps reduce motion blur.
The display offers a peak brightness of 500 nits and viewing angles of up to 178 degrees. It also covers 100% of the sRGB color space and 95% of DCI-P3, with support for 8-bit color depth.
Xiaomi has added AMD FreeSync Premium support to the new model. This technology helps synchronize the monitor’s refresh rate with a compatible graphics card to reduce screen tearing and stuttering during gameplay.
Gaming Features and Eye Protection
The Redmi G27Q 2026 Standard Edition includes several features designed to improve the gaming experience. These include a dynamic crosshair with five modes and adjustable colors, a night vision mode, and Darkfield Enhancement Pro, which brightens darker areas to help players spot details more easily.
For eye comfort, Xiaomi has included its Green Mountain Eye Protection technology alongside TÜV Rheinland blue light certification. These features aim to make the display more comfortable to use during extended gaming sessions.
Connectivity and Adjustable Design
The monitor offers two DisplayPort 1.4 ports, two HDMI 2.0 ports, and a headphone jack for connecting gaming PCs, consoles, and other devices.
It also supports height, pivot, swivel, and tilt adjustments, allowing users to position the screen according to their preferences. A VESA mount provides the option to install the monitor on a compatible wall mount or monitor arm.
Redmi G27Q 2026 Standard Edition Price and Availability
Xiaomi has priced the Redmi G27Q 2026 Standard Edition at CNY 999, which is approximately $149. The original Redmi G27Q 2026 costs CNY 1,299, or around $189.
The Standard Edition will be available to purchase in China through JD.com starting October 21, 2026. Xiaomi has not yet announced plans for a global launch.
With its 2K resolution, 240Hz refresh rate, and gaming-focused features, the Redmi G27Q 2026 Standard Edition offers a combination of high refresh rates and useful display features at a relatively affordable price. However, buyers outside China will have to wait for further details about its international availability.
