Read: President calls for stronger Pakistan-Malaysia cooperation in law enforcement, security
It added that the exercise reaffirmed the longstanding military cooperation between the two countries and their shared resolve to strengthen collaboration in the counter-terrorism domain.
Separately, the 16th meeting of the Pakistan-Malaysia Joint Committee on Defence Cooperation (JCDC) was held earlier today, with both sides reaffirming their commitment to strengthen bilateral defence and security cooperation further.
Both sides reviewed progress made since the previous meeting in 2025 and discussed matters of mutual interest, according to a statement.
The meeting was held at the Malaysian Ministry of Defence, where the Pakistani delegation was led by Secretary Defence Lieutenant General (retired) Muhammad Ali, while the Malaysian delegation was headed by Deputy Secretary General (policy) Mohd Yani bin Daud.
During the plenary session, the delegations reviewed progress since the 2025 JCDC meeting in Malaysia, appreciated recent achievements and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral defence and security ties.
Pakistan and Malaysia have longstanding ties dating back to 1957, when Malaysia gained independence on Aug 31. Pakistan was among the earliest countries to recognise Malaysia as a nation and also helped in drafting its constitution. The two countries have since maintained close ties.
Also Read: Pak-Malaysia joint military exercise concludes
Last year, during Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s visit to Malaysia, the two countries agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, trade and emerging technologies, while Kuala Lumpur also agreed to import $200 million worth of meat from Pakistan.
The two countries are also bound by the Malaysia-Pakistan Closer Economic Partnership Agreement, signed in 2007, which promotes trade in goods and services, regulates investment flows and supports cooperation in intellectual property, healthcare, telecommunications, tourism and construction.

POVA is back, and it didn’t come quietly. TECNO today launched the POVA Curve 2 5G in Pakistan, a phone built on one bold idea: Beauty and Beast. You shouldn’t have to choose between a phone that turns heads and a phone that never quits. The POVA Curve 2 5G is both, with 8GB RAM + 256GB ROM, priced at PKR 99,999.
The Beast Inside: Dimensity 7100 5G
At the heart of the POVA Curve 2 5G is the MediaTek Dimensity 7100 5G processor, built for the way Pakistan uses its phones: gaming, streaming, multitasking and always-on connectivity. For gamers, that means 90 minutes of smooth, stable Free Fire gameplay at 60fps, with Ice Cooling 3.0 helping keep things steady. And the phone is made to last: it is TÜV Rheinland certified to stay lag-free for six years. Signal gets the same treatment: 20 5G bands and TECNO’s own technology deliver up to 100% stronger signal in buildings and basements and 60% stronger Wi-Fi, TÜV certified. It is what TECNO calls the Pakistan Signal King.
8000mAh in 7.42mm: The Slimmest Phone with a Battery This Big
The POVA Curve 2 5G packs an 8000mAh battery into a body just 7.42mm thick and 195g in weight, making it the thinnest phone among those with an 8000mAh battery. It is the end of the old rule that a big battery means a brick.
What does 8000mAh mean in real life? You can charge every two days, with more than 15 days of standby, and a TÜV certification for extended battery life of more than three days. When you do plug in, 45W wired fast charging takes the phone from empty to full in 82 minutes. It also supports 10W reverse charging and bypass charging. The battery is built for 2,000 cycles, which TECNO says is six years of safe, durable use.
A Curved 144Hz AMOLED Display That Shines in the Sun
The screen is a curved 144Hz AMOLED display, with a high refresh rate for smooth scrolling and gameplay and comfortable viewing on the eyes. Peak brightness reaches up to 4,500 nits, so the screen stays clear even in direct sunlight.
For gamers, the touch experience is tuned as hard as the screen. It features 16x touch resolution and a 2160Hz instant sampling rate, with ultra-low response times for games like PUBG and MLBB. Multi-scenario anti-mistouch means wet or oily hands won’t cost you a move.
Beauty on the Outside, Beast Underneath
Inspired by interstellar spaceships, the POVA Curve 2 5G pairs bold, flowing lines and a minimalist, pure finish with a symmetrical layout that echoes the triangular deco. It is also made for real life, with IP64 dust and water resistance for sandstorms, splashes and harsh weather, a Corning Gorilla Glass 7i display and SGS-certified 1.5m drop resistance. It comes in three colours: Melting Silver, Mystic Purple and Storm Titanium.
Smart Camera, Smarter Every Day
The POVA Curve 2 5G pairs a 50MP primary camera and a 2MP macro camera with a 13MP front camera, and TECNO AI does the rest: AI Eraser 2.0 removes unwanted people, pets and clutter, AI Flare Remover fixes glare and haze, and Image-to-Live turns still photos into moving ones. AI Noise Cancellation keeps calls clear, and the Ella voice assistant handles two-way call translation (now supporting WhatsApp), WhatsApp summaries and one-tap Q&A.
Price and Availability
The TECNO POVA Curve 2 5G is available across Pakistan from October 15, in 8GB RAM + 256GB ROM, at PKR 99,999. TECNO has teamed up with PalmPay for launch day, so buyers who purchase the POVA Curve 2 5G through PalmPay’s instalment service get PKR 5,000 off. On Daraz, online shoppers can also get PKR 5,000 off the POVA Curve 2 5G with TECNO Fans discount vouchers.

items.summary:

items.author: Ankush Das
items.content:
India’s AI story is moving beyond the model. Until last year, the big question in Indian boardrooms was which large language model (LLM) enterprises should standardise on. Now, as AI agents move from answering questions to executing tasks, the focus is shifting to what these agents can do for businesses, which workflows they should handle, and how enterprises can measure their performance.
In September, Inc42 reported that Swiggy is opening food delivery, Instamart, Dineout, and Scenes to external AI agents. Through four Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and 66 tools, the company lets AI assistants outside its app build carts, place orders, and book tables. The same month, we explored how Flipkart is reworking product discovery for a future where customers may no longer begin their shopping journeys with keyword searches.
As AI agents take on more tasks, enterprises must look beyond the underlying models to the systems that make them useful and reliable. That means building workflows that allow agents to execute tasks effectively and evaluation systems that measure whether they deliver the intended results.
Meanwhile, investor interest in the sector remains strong. Indian AI startups raised $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q3 2026, up 265% YoY, according to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026.
Against this backdrop, Inc42 returns with the 13th edition of the AI Startups To Watch series. This edition features five emerging ventures tackling distinct opportunities: agentic commerce, screen-free learning, AI agent reliability, automated customer conversations and AI-powered recruitment.
Here are the five startups from the 13th edition of Inc42’s AI Startups To Watch.
Editor’s Note: This is not a ranking. The startups featured here are a curated selection by the Inc42 editorial team and are listed alphabetically.
Agnost AI | Keeping A Closer Eye On AI Agents
A chatbot that gives a wrong answer frustrates users. An AI agent that fails silently can cost a business its customers. Users may correct it, repeat their requests or abandon the interaction altogether, while dashboards continue to record the exchange as a success.
Agnost AI is building tools to detect these failures and help teams fix them. Founded in 2025 by Shubham Palriwala and Parth Ajmera, the platform monitors AI agents in production by analysing their conversations with users. It identifies recurring problems, flags instances where users correct the agent or abandon a task, and traces failures back through the agent’s tool calls to identify what went wrong.
It then suggests fixes and tests them against the conversations in which the agent failed before deployment. It adds cases where fixes work to a regression test suite to help prevent the same errors from recurring.
Agnost integrates with agent-building frameworks such as LangChain and CrewAI, and counts Exa and Comp AI among its users. It is backed by Y Combinator, Entrepreneurs First and Transpose Platform Management. The startup is targeting the agentic AI monitoring and observability tools market, estimated at $500 Mn in 2025 and projected to reach $2 Bn by 2030, growing at a 30.1% CAGR.
Dialflo | AI Voice Agents With ROI
Many Indian enterprises have spent the past two years experimenting with AI voice bots, only to find it difficult to measure their impact. The challenge isn’t just getting an AI agent to handle calls, but understanding how well it performs, what business outcomes it delivers, and when human intervention is needed.
Bengaluru-based Dialflo is building a platform to address this gap. Founded in 2024 by Abhishek Kumar, the startup combines AI voice agents and human agents in a single contact centre, helping businesses automate customer interactions while tracking their outcomes.
Its voice agents handle high-volume tasks such as qualifying leads, verifying cash-on-delivery orders to reduce returns, recovering abandoned carts and providing multilingual customer support around the clock. What sets Dialflo apart is its focus on attribution: it scores each conversation and links it to a business outcome, helping customer experience teams measure the revenue generated by calls alongside the costs saved.
This focus comes as the global call centre AI market expands, with its value projected to rise from $1.9 Bn in 2024 to $7.1 Bn by 2030, at a CAGR of 23.8%, according to Grand View Research.
Dialflo works with more than 10 enterprise customers, including Tata Digital, Intugine and Careernet.
HireBound | AI Agents For End-To-End Hiring
Recruiters often spend a lot of time chasing candidates, screening resumes and conducting repetitive initial interviews rather than evaluating the people best suited for a role. As hiring volumes grow, these tasks become harder to manage without adding to recruitment teams.
Bengaluru-based HireBound is using AI agents to automate much of this work. Founded in 2024 by Sharad Vij and Kumar Vikramaditya, the startup aims to help recruiters move candidates through the hiring process faster.
Its platform uses separate agents for sourcing, screening and evaluation. These agents engage candidates through voice calls, WhatsApp, text messages and email, gathering information to assess their suitability for a role. Looking to capitalise on the growth of India’s HR tech market, projected to reach $2.3 Bn by 2034, the platform integrates with companies’ existing applicant tracking systems and human resource management systems. Its customers include staffing firms and enterprise talent acquisition teams in India and the US.
HireBound has conducted more than 3 Mn candidate conversations and trained its systems on over 2 Mn resumes and 30,000 job openings. It raised $2 Mn (₹18.2 Cr) in a seed round led by Kalaari Capital, with participation from Antler, Infinyte Club and CareerNet. The startup is targeting a fivefold increase in annual recurring revenue over the next year.
MyWonder | Screen-Free AI Learning Companion
For children aged three to ten, finding ways to make learning engaging without relying on screens remains a challenge.
MyWonder is building a screen-free alternative. Founded in 2024 by Chandramouli K, formerly of Amazon and RedBus, and Venkat Potluri, formerly of Flipkart and ZestMoney, the startup wants to make learning interactive through voice-led play.
Its WonderPod combines a voice-first device with figurines and cards that unlock stories, quizzes and games. A conversational AI layer adapts to each child’s speech and learning level, while a companion app lets parents track activities and manage content access. The startup also sources content through publisher partnerships.
MyWonder operates in India’s tech toys market, expected to reach about $3.6 Bn by 2030, expanding at a CAGR of 14.7%.
Tru Commerce | Commerce Infra For AI Agents
Shopping is moving into chat windows, where consumers can ask AI assistants to recommend products and receive a shortlist. But even when brands appear in these recommendations, shoppers cannot always buy from them directly. Many brands lack product catalogues that AI agents can read and checkout systems that work within these conversations.
Tru Commerce is building the infrastructure to bridge that gap. Founded in 2024 as Asva AI by Viren Inaniyan and Umang Chhaparia, the startup rebranded this year to focus on helping brands sell through AI agents.
Its platform has three core functions. It converts product pages into structured data that AI agents can understand, connects brands’ existing stores to agent-led checkouts through protocols such as MCP, ACP and UCP, and tracks brand mentions, product recommendations and orders attributed to AI agents. Brands remain the merchant of record and retain their customer relationships.
Tru Commerce works with Amazon, ITC MasterChef, MyMuse, Provogue and House of Zelena. The startup is targeting the global agentic commerce market, estimated at $1.9 Bn in 2025 and projected to reach $54.2 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 39.81%.
With inputs from Venu Rathore & Akshit Pushkarna
Edited by Shishir Parasher
Creatives by Abhyam Gusai

items.author: Albert Cuesta
items.content:
Ericsson ha aumentado sus ingresos en el tercer trimestre de 2026 gracias a las mayores ventas de su división de Redes y a las medidas de eficiencia, aunque su nuevo CEO, Per Narvinger (en la foto), ha advertido de posibles dificultades en 2027.
Tras presentar sus primeros resultados desde que relevó a Börje Ekholm al frente de la empresa hace unas semanas, el hasta ahora responsable de Redes ha explicado que ha dedicado el trimestre a reunirse con clientes y que ha surgido un tema recurrente: “la necesidad de redes más inteligentes y autónomas para mejorar el rendimiento, la eficiencia, la robustez y la resiliencia”.
De cara al futuro, ha añadido: “El mercado de redes de acceso radio (RAN) está estancado, la incertidumbre geopolítica sigue siendo elevada y los costes de los componentes suponen un obstáculo para el margen bruto en 2027”.
Narvinger confía en que, con una actuación disciplinada y apostando por el liderazgo tecnológico, la empresa esté bien situada “para afrontar estos desafíos y lograr un crecimiento rentable a largo plazo”.
Los ingresos del trimestre han subido un 6% interanual, hasta 59.500 millones de coronas suecas (unos 5.200 millones de euros), con un incremento del 9% en las ventas de la división de Redes, que se sitúan en 38.700 millones de coronas (unos 3.400 millones de euros).
El software y los servicios en la nube han crecido un 3%, hasta 15.800 millones de coronas (unos 1.400 millones de euros), mientras que las ventas del segmento empresarial han caído un 10%, hasta 4.600 millones de coronas (unos 400 millones de euros), como consecuencia de la desinversión de iconectiv.
Por mercados geográficos, las ventas han crecido en la mayoría, entre ellos Asia y Europa, aunque las dificultades en América Latina han compensado en parte ese avance.
Los ingresos por licencias de propiedad intelectual han alcanzado los 3.900 millones de coronas (unos 340 millones de euros), frente a los 3.100 millones (unos 270 millones de euros) anteriores, impulsados en parte por ingresos retroactivos de productos que antes no contaban con licencia.
El beneficio neto ha disminuido un 49%, hasta 5.800 millones de coronas (unos 510 millones de euros).
Reestructuración del grupo
Junto con los resultados, el proveedor sueco ha presentado una nueva estructura de grupo con la que busca aprovechar mejor sus capacidades de I+D y ganar eficiencia en costes.
La reorganización contempla la creación de una nueva Área de Mercado de Asia-Pacífico a partir de principios de 2027, que combinará las áreas del Noreste de Asia, el Sudeste Asiático, Oceanía e India. Según la empresa, esto le permitirá operar de forma más eficaz en toda la región.
La nueva división estará dirigida por Patrick Johansson, actual responsable del área de mercado de Europa, Oriente Medio y África (EMEA), cuyo relevo ya se está buscando.
Ericsson también reorganiza el área de negocio de Soluciones Inalámbricas Empresariales para centrarla más en las soluciones para interiores, y traslada la cartera actual de la unidad a otras partes del grupo, entre ellas la división de Redes.
Con información de Kavit Majithia.
The post Las ventas de redes móviles impulsan los resultados de Ericsson en el tercer trimestre appeared first on Mobile World Live.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
US-based AI healthtech startup Confido Health has raised $12.5 Mn (about ₹119 Cr) in a Series A extension led by Z47, taking its total Series A funding to $22.5 Mn.
Existing investors Together Fund and Blume Ventures also participated in the round. Healthcare private equity investor Justin Saks has joined the startup as an investor and board adviser.
The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its CareOS platform across healthcare organisations with multiple sites and develop AI agents for additional workflows and medical specialities.
Founded in 2022 by Chetan Reddy and Vichar Shroff, Confido Health develops AI agents to automate administrative tasks for healthcare providers, including patient calls, appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills, and payment collection.
Its CareOS platform integrates with more than 50 healthcare systems, including electronic health records, practice management software, and billing platforms. This allows providers to automate tasks across their existing systems without replacing their technology infrastructure.
Confido Health initially focused on voice AI for patient calls before expanding into broader healthcare administration. Its platform connects related tasks, allowing a patient interaction to trigger follow-up work such as scheduling an appointment, processing a prescription refill, or collecting a payment.
The startup primarily targets healthcare groups operating across multiple sites, particularly those backed by private equity firms. Its distribution strategy involves working with private equity investors to secure introductions to their portfolio companies.
Confido Health said it serves 3,200 providers across more than 1,500 sites in 27 US states, with its AI agents enabling one in 50 Americans to access healthcare. It claimed 15-fold growth since its previous funding round but did not specify the metric.
The startup reported AI handling rates above 95% across key end-to-end administrative workflows. It said deployments added operational capacity equivalent to three to five full-time employees on average within three months, while patient satisfaction averaged 4.55 out of five across approximately one million tasks.
The fundraise comes amid investor bets on AI applications across healthcare, from administrative automation to patient guidance and early disease detection.
Earlier, Inc42 reported that AI health companion startup August AI was in talks to raise about $4 Mn from Peak XV Partners. The startup helps users understand symptoms, prescriptions, medications, and medical reports.
Earlier this year, Practo cofounder Shashank ND’s new venture Cent raised about $5 Mn from his family office OneFlow Holdings and South Park Commons. Cent uses AI and health data to detect critical diseases early.
Indian healthtech startups raised $93 Mn across 13 deals in Q3 2026 till September 24.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
ByteDance, the Chinese company behind TikTok, is nearing an agreement to buy custom artificial intelligence (AI) chips from Taiwanese semiconductor maker MediaTek. The deal would help ByteDance secure computing hardware for its data centers while allowing MediaTek to expand beyond its traditional smartphone processor business.
According to a Bloomberg report, the discussions involve application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), which manufacturers design to perform specific computing tasks. These chips could support ByteDance’s growing AI infrastructure requirements.
ByteDance to Buy Custom AI Chips From MediaTek for Data Centers
If the agreement goes ahead, ByteDance would become MediaTek’s second major customer for custom ASICs after Alphabet, Google’s parent company.
MediaTek Targets the AI Data Center Market
MediaTek has traditionally focused on processors for smartphones and other consumer electronics. However, rising demand for AI computing has encouraged the company to expand into the data center market.
A major contract with ByteDance could strengthen MediaTek’s position against established competitors, including Qualcomm and Broadcom, which are also competing for opportunities in the AI semiconductor industry.
According to the report, MediaTek expects its AI chip sales to reach around $2 billion in 2026. The company is also targeting a 15% share of the estimated $80 billion market next year.
These ambitions highlight MediaTek’s growing interest in custom chips as technology companies invest heavily in AI computing infrastructure.
ByteDance Plans Massive AI Investment
ByteDance is also preparing to spend heavily on data centers and AI infrastructure. The company is considering investments of up to $70 billion in 2026, with spending potentially reaching $100 billion in 2027.
The company reportedly secured a $30 billion loan in September to help finance its expansion plans.
This investment reflects the growing importance of computing infrastructure as technology companies develop and deploy more advanced AI systems. Custom chips could help ByteDance meet its processing needs and support its expanding range of AI services.

items.content:

Planning to buy the iPhone 18 Pro on installments in Pakistan? MCB, Bank Alfalah, and Faysal Bank have promoted different financing options, but their monthly payments, tenures, and charges are not directly comparable. A longer plan can bring the monthly bill down while increasing the total amount you ultimately pay.
Here’s what the publicly advertised offers actually say, and how to work out which one is cheaper before making a purchase.
iPhone 18 Pro Installment Plans: MCB vs Alfalah vs Faysal Bank
Bank
Advertised offer
What buyers should verify
MCB
0% markup up to 36 months; no processing fee on eligible plans up to 30 months
Phone price, qualifying tenure, any 36-month fees, and credit-card eligibility
Bank Alfalah / AlfaMall
Eligible credit-card installments generally range from 3 to 36 months, with charges varying by listing and tenure
Exact iPhone listing, selling price, processing fee, markup, and checkout total
Faysal Bank / Digimall
Advertised iPhone 18 Pro for Rs. 20,717 monthly over 60 months
Full repayment schedule, upfront contribution, charges, and eligible model
Important: These are advertised terms, not final bank quotations for the identical handset. Offers and availability can change.
1. MCB: 0% Markup for Up to 36 Months
MCB’s iPhone 18 Pro series promotion, offered with GNext, advertises 0% markup installments for eligible credit card customers for up to 36 months. The promotion also states that no processing fee applies to qualifying installment plans of up to 30 months; that fee waiver should not automatically be assumed for the 36-month plan. The advertised offer runs until October 31, 2026, subject to terms and availability.
Buyers may also receive Shield+ protection benefits, including specified extended warranty and repair coverage. Read the exact coverage conditions before treating these extras as equivalent to cash savings.
At a purely illustrative retail price of Rs. 563,999, dividing the purchase price into 30 equal installments with zero additional charges would give approximately Rs. 18,800 per month. This is a calculation, not an MCB quotation; the actual transaction price and applicable charges determine the real payment.
Source: PhoneWorld’s MCB offer report.
2. Bank Alfalah: Compare the AlfaMall Checkout Cost
AlfaMall offers eligible credit-card customers installment options that may span 3, 6, 9, 12, 24 or 36 months. However, its charges depend on the particular product and selected plan. A 0% markup label does not necessarily mean the plan has no processing costs.
Under AlfaMall’s published terms, the card’s available limit is blocked by an amount equal to the product price, even though the customer pays monthly installments. Its terms also mention processing fees and applicable FED. As of July 1, 2026, the platform discloses a minimum processing fee of 2.5% or Rs. 1,500, whichever is higher, plus FED, subject to the relevant plan and bank terms.
Importantly, AlfaMall’s PTA approval service for the iPhone 18 Pro is separate from buying the handset itself. Readers should not compare a PTA-tax-only installment with the full-price phone offers from the other banks.
For an accurate comparison, open the actual AlfaMall iPhone 18 Pro listing and record the identical storage variant, selling price, installments, one-time charges and total payable. See AlfaMall’s terms and conditions.
3. Faysal Bank: Rs. 20,717 Monthly for 60 Months
Faysal Digimall has advertised the iPhone 18 Pro at Rs. 20,717 per month for 60 months. That is a five-year commitment, considerably longer than the other offers discussed here. A published offer also describes a two-year warranty and Mercantile protection benefits, subject to terms.
The arithmetic is worth checking: Rs. 20,717 × 60 = Rs. 1,243,020 in scheduled monthly payments. This is not necessarily the all-in payable amount: any upfront payment, processing charge or other amount must be added, and the advertised arrangement’s financing terms should be confirmed with the bank. The difference from a current cash price cannot automatically be labelled ‘interest’ because the public promotion does not explain every component.
See PhoneWorld’s Faysal Bank report and Faysal Digimall.
Which iPhone 18 Pro Installment Plan Is Actually Cheaper?
Based on the advertised conditions, MCB’s qualifying zero-markup and zero-processing-fee plans appear to have the clearest potential for a lower total financing cost. But an exact winner between MCB, AlfaMall, and Faysal Bank cannot honestly be declared without current, itemized quotes for the same iPhone 18 Pro storage variant and condition.
Faysal Bank’s longer tenure can make payments more manageable for some buyers, but its 60 scheduled payments add up to a significant commitment. Bank Alfalah’s flexibility may suit existing eligible cardholders, though its actual costs depend on the chosen AlfaMall listing.
How to Compare the Three Plans Before Buying
Choose one identical model and storage capacity, for example, the PTA-approved iPhone 18 Pro 256GB.
Ask each provider for its current cash or financed selling price.
Record any down payment, processing fee, FED, markup, taxes, and other mandatory charges.
Multiply each monthly installment by the number of months, then add all upfront and one-time charges.
Check credit card limit requirements, cancellation rules, warranty and protection exclusions.
Total payable = upfront payment + (monthly installment × number of months) + one-time mandatory charges. If a charge is already included in the monthly installment, do not add it twice.
Final Thoughts
For Pakistanis considering the iPhone 18 Pro on installments, the most attractive-looking monthly payment is not automatically the cheapest deal. MCB’s promotional fee waiver may offer meaningful savings on eligible tenures; AlfaMall gives cardholders multiple repayment choices; and Faysal Digimall’s five-year option spreads payments over a longer period.
Before paying, request written confirmation of the total amount payable for the exact PTA-approved device you want. That is the fairest way to decide which bank is cheaper.
Which installment plan would you choose for the iPhone 18 Pro? Let us know in the comments.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
WhatsApp has introduced a new guest calling feature that allows users to invite anyone to join a voice or video call, even if they do not have a WhatsApp account. The feature makes it easier to connect with colleagues, classmates, tutors, and friends without requiring everyone to install the app.
WhatsApp Introduces Guest Calling Without an Account or Time Limits
The company says guest calls are free and end-to-end encrypted. They also have no time limits, allowing participants to continue their conversations without worrying about calls ending unexpectedly.
How WhatsApp Guest Calling Works
To start a guest call, users need to open WhatsApp and go to the Calls tab. They can then tap the “+” icon, create a call link, and share it with the people they want to invite.
Recipients can open the link in their computer browser, enter their name, and wait for the host to let them into the call. They do not need a WhatsApp account to join. However, only existing WhatsApp users can create and share call links.
The feature supports both one-to-one and group calls with up to 32 participants. This makes it useful for online meetings, study sessions, and other conversations involving multiple people.
See Also: WhatsApp Introduces New Security Alert for Android and iPhone Users
Privacy and Security Features
WhatsApp has included several restrictions to protect users’ privacy during guest calls. Every guest must receive approval from the host before entering a call. Guests remain in a waiting room until the host admits them.
Hosts can also remove guests from a call whenever necessary. Meanwhile, guest participants cannot see other participants’ phone numbers, send messages, or directly invite additional people to the call.
These restrictions give hosts greater control over who joins their conversations while helping protect participants’ personal information.
Screen Sharing and Other Call Features
Guest participants can access several essential calling features. They can share their computer screens to review documents, discuss presentations, or collaborate on other tasks.
Participants can also react with emojis, including thumbs-up and heart reactions, or raise their hands to indicate that they want to speak. These tools can make group discussions more convenient, particularly for remote work and online learning.
WhatsApp Plans Calendar Integration
WhatsApp also plans to introduce calendar integrations later this year. The upcoming feature will allow users to create WhatsApp call links directly from Google Calendar or Microsoft Outlook.
Users will be able to install the WhatsApp plugin, connect their accounts, and add call links to calendar invitations. Invitees will then be able to join calls whether or not they have a WhatsApp account.
The integration could simplify the process of arranging online meetings by allowing users to schedule calls and invite participants through their existing calendar applications.
A Step Towards More Accessible Calling
The guest calling feature is part of WhatsApp’s broader effort to improve its calling services. By allowing people without accounts to join calls, the company is making it easier for users to communicate across different platforms.
The combination of free calls, end-to-end encryption, browser-based access, and a 32-participant limit could make the feature useful for both personal and professional conversations. With calendar integration also on the way, WhatsApp aims to make joining a call more convenient for everyone.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) has introduced a digital attestation system in Pakistan that will allow citizens to get their documents verified online without visiting its offices in routine cases.

The digital system aims to simplify the document attestation process and reduce the need for applicants to visit government offices in person. Citizens will be able to complete routine attestation procedures online, saving time and travel expenses.
However, applicants may still need to appear in person in certain cases, depending on the nature of their applications and the requirements of the attestation process.
The ministry said the initiative aims to make document attestation more convenient, transparent, and efficient. It will also help citizens avoid unnecessary travel and repeated visits to government offices.
Citizens seeking digital attestation services can visit the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ official portal at https://portal-attestation.mofa.gov.pk to submit their applications and follow the prescribed procedure.
The introduction of the digital system is also part of the government’s efforts to improve public services through digital solutions. By moving routine attestation procedures online, the ministry aims to make the process more accessible for citizens across Pakistan.

items.title: How Nigeria’s Proc360 is making China-Africa trade safe for wholesalers, cutting out the middleman
items.summary:
Nigerian startup Proc360 is helping African wholesalers buy stock directly from China without the risk of fraud – verifying suppliers, holding payments in escrow, inspecting goods before they ship, and handling freight, customs and delivery.
Launched in February 2025 after more than six years of research into the trade corridor, Proc360 is targeting a market where traders have long paid a premium simply to feel safe.
“African wholesalers buy most of their stock from China, and there has never been a safe way to do it. So traders buy safety instead. They hand the trade to a middleman and pay a heavy markup for it,” Fara Popoola, co-founder and CEO of Proc360, told Disrupt Africa.
“That markup is the price of trust, and it is the single biggest thing holding these businesses back. Proc360 removes the need to buy safety at all. Trust is built into the trade itself, so our customers stop paying a premium for it.”
The startup’s customers save 38 per cent
items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian startup Proc360 is helping African wholesalers buy stock directly from China without the risk of fraud – verifying suppliers, holding payments in escrow, inspecting goods before they ship, and handling freight, customs and delivery.
Launched in February 2025 after more than six years of research into the trade corridor, Proc360 is targeting a market where traders have long paid a premium simply to feel safe.
“African wholesalers buy most of their stock from China, and there has never been a safe way to do it. So traders buy safety instead. They hand the trade to a middleman and pay a heavy markup for it,” Fara Popoola, co-founder and CEO of Proc360, told Disrupt Africa.
“That markup is the price of trust, and it is the single biggest thing holding these businesses back. Proc360 removes the need to buy safety at all. Trust is built into the trade itself, so our customers stop paying a premium for it.”
The startup’s customers save 38 per cent on average, Popoola said, money they put back into stock. The experience begins on WhatsApp through Ruby, Proc360’s artificial intelligence (AI) procurement assistant.
“Ruby speaks their language, and guides them to use a simple platform where they take their control back,” Popoola said.
The founders identified the gap after surveying 500 African traders. Of these, 67 per cent had lost money to procurement fraud or knew someone who had, while 92 per cent complained of broken logistics.
“And 71 per cent said they would rather pay a middleman a high markup than pay a supplier directly, which is a market pricing its own fear,” Popoola said.
Proc360’s biggest natural competitors are the offline agents traders currently rely on, while logistics and procurement players such as Heroshe, Aquantuo, GIG, Centi and Getitfy also operate in the space.
“They still keep an agent somewhere in the chain. We remove the need for one, backed by a supplier verification database seven years in the making,” said Popoola.
The angel-funded startup has so far enabled US$750,000 in trade across 4,900 transactions in Nigeria and Ghana. It has 2,700 businesses transacting on the platform, growing at 12 per cent month-on-month, with 81 per cent retention.
“That retention number is the one that matters. This is a market where people have been burned, so they test us with one small order, it arrives as promised, and the next one is bigger,” Popoola said.
The startup has also launched Ruby on WhatsApp and set up a partnership-powered inspection operation in China.
“The landmark we are proudest of is US$250,000 in losses prevented, money that would have gone to fraud and process errors, now sitting in our customers’ businesses instead,” said Popoola.
Proc360 makes money through four usage-based revenue streams: a fee on completed trades, transaction fees, partner commissions and foreign exchange (FX) margins. It generates around US$150 in revenue per user, per year, and has generated almost US$100,000 in revenue to date.
“We are not profitable yet, as every dollar goes back into growth,” Popoola said.
Nigeria was a deliberate starting point, with half of all finished goods sold in the country imported from China, and the China-Nigeria corridor alone accounting for 12 per cent of Africa-China trade. The next focus is depth, with Proc360 set to onboard offline traders in eight Lagos markets, including Balogun, Idumota, Alaba, Trade Fair and Computer Village.
“We will do that in person, through agents who speak their language. Then the broader West African corridor from 2028,” said Popoola.
The road has not been without challenges, chief among them trust.
“We were asking people burned before to pay a platform they had never met, and we solved that by taking small orders and never missing one,” Popoola said.
Currency volatility has been another hurdle, with naira swings capable of wiping out a margin between quote and payment.
“The wallet had to be built to hold a price,” said Popoola. “And then there is the unglamorous middle: customs, port delays, suppliers who ship the wrong thing. We chose to own those problems rather than hand them to the customer. It is expensive. It is also the entire business.”

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Enterprise AI startup Shamrock AI has raised $5 Mn (about ₹47.4 Cr) in a seed funding round led by Endiya Partners, with participation from Capria Ventures.
The Shillong-headquartered startup said it will use its first institutional funding round to accelerate product development, expand its team across India and the US, scale go-to-market efforts, and expand its presence in the Middle East.
Founded in 2026 by Sarat Addanki, Anuraag Nallapati, and Michael Gallagher, Shamrock AI is building an agentic assurance platform that helps large enterprises deploy AI agents across critical business processes, ensuring they operate reliably in complex environments.
Its platform uses an Enterprise Business Knowledge Graph to connect business processes, systems, data, and configurations, giving AI agents context about how an enterprise operates.
The startup is initially focusing on using AI agents to automate testing across large enterprise resource planning (ERP) transformations, including SAP S/4HANA migrations.
Shamrock AI said continuously testing and validating business processes helps its platform build an increasingly accurate representation of an enterprise’s operations. It plans to use this foundation to extend into data observability and autonomous business process automation.
The startup said it already serves multiple Fortune 500 customers, including a Fortune 100 AI hardware manufacturer and a Fortune 100 healthcare company.
Shamrock AI expects 70%-80% of its workforce to be based in India and plans to build a client-facing team in the US. Besides its Shillong headquarters, it has offices in Hyderabad and San Francisco.
The fundraise comes amid a rise in funding for India’s AI startups. In Q3 2026, Indian AI startups raised $438 Mn across 35 deals, up 265% YoY.
Investors are bullish on startups helping enterprises put AI to work across business functions. Yesterday, Parallel Loop raised $6.6 Mn in a seed round led by 3one4 Capital to help enterprises integrate AI into existing systems and workflows.
A day earlier, Clueso raised $10 Mn in a Series A round led by Dharana Capital to automate enterprise video creation and updates using AI agents.

items.author: Daria Dergacheva
items.content:
The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest
Originally published on Global Voices
Moscow subway cameras are connected to a facial recognition system. Screenshot taken from the YouTube video “Facial recognition cameras help detain dissidents in the Moscow metro” by the DW YouTube channel; fair use.
This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Sonya, from Stavropol Krai, Russia, is 15 years old. In June 2026, she was sentenced to 70 hours of compulsory labor, connected to a February 2026 incident in which she had written the surname “Navalny” on a bus stop. That stop happened to be in a district that was being monitored by officers from the Center for Combating Extremism, commonly called Center E. Similarly, Yuri, a pensioner from Astrakhan who was also identified from surveillance footage, was given three years of restricted freedom for writing “No to War” in red marker on buildings.
Authoritarian regimes are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) as a technology of political survival. Cameras with facial recognition, video analytics, biometric databases, digital IDs, social media monitoring, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) systems, and public service platforms are gradually merging into a single infrastructure of control.
Such a system makes it possible not only to observe citizens in real time, but also to reconstruct their past movements, connections, habits, communications, and political activity. The main risk is that AI and related technologies make repression faster and less visible: the state no longer needs to constantly demonstrate force if citizens know they can be identified retroactively.
Modern digital authoritarianism is not developing in isolation, but through the international exchange of technologies, standards, and practices. China, Russia, Iran, Belarus, Venezuela, countries in Africa, Western and Central Asia, and companies connected to them, sell and exchange AI infrastructure tools that are being used for the purpose of repression. Western technologies are also being bought and exchanged within authoritarian regimes.
Large language models
In early June 2026, Sberbank Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin told Reuters that the company was offering countries in the Global South access to Russian AI models that would take “local values” into account. Vedyakhin was referring to specific large language models (LLMs) — GigaChat and YandexGPT — which Russia had been trying to develop since 2019.
However, as IT expert Alexander Isavnin told journalists at the podcast Zhivoy Gvozd, Russian generative AI models lag behind American and Chinese models and cannot even generate text in Cyrillic. Yet, new national and sovereign AI models are supposed to reflect traditional values, including patriotism, service to the Fatherland and responsibility for its fate, a strong family, historical memory and continuity between generations, and unity of the peoples of Russia. These models are expected to be trained on domestic, authentically Russian material.
It is reasonable to assume that in countries like those in Western Asia, Russian AI models will reflect adherence to Islamic traditions, while in Argentina, perhaps, they will reflect respect for football from an early age. Developers, meanwhile, do not understand how people with no idea about how any of this works can write AI laws: “In places, the document reads as if it was written by people who had only ever seen LLMs in local news.” From the perspective of global democracy, however, this illiteracy among Russian lawmakers suggests that Russia is unlikely to supply LLMs to autocracies around the world.
China, by contrast — unlike American developers — makes its language models open in principle, meaning that anyone can take the code and modify it for their own needs. In China, all LLMs are controlled and tightly regulated by the state, so party censorship is written into the code from the start — for example, you cannot get an answer about the Tiananmen Square protests. However, the models are distributed as open source, which is why more than 50 percent of Chinese model users come from developers, including those in the Global South.
At the same time, the U.S.-based ChatGPT can easily replicate AI-generated Iranian propaganda videos, in which the main characters are Lego figures. Only once, a France 24 investigation showed, did the chatbot alert the journalist that he might be inadvertently reproducing propaganda, but desisted when he said it was only satire.
Mass surveillance systems
AI also includes other tech developments, like the so-called “smart city” systems which, in the Chinese version, imply comprehensive surveillance of a state’s own citizens. This can include video surveillance, wiretapping, internet censorship, facial recognition systems, ethnic profiling, and so on. In supplying such systems to the Global South, China has overtaken Russia.
Yet, Russia is not lagging behind in the use of AI to surveil its own citizens. State media write that Moscow has long moved beyond the threshold implied by the concept of a “smart city.” Today, it includes a complex digital urban ecosystem made up of video surveillance, AI, big data, and the “internet of things.”
According to estimates by Comparitech, two of the ten cities outside China with the highest number of cameras per person are Russian: Moscow and St. Petersburg. The list also includes four Indian cities, Seoul in South Korea, Baghdad in Iraq, Kabul in Afghanistan, and Singapore. In China itself, the number of cameras has practically reached a ratio of one camera for every two people: the largest mass-surveillance system in the world.
Russia has sold, and in some cases, continues to supply its surveillance software products to other authoritarian states, while remaining technologically dependent on China. In 2024, up to 80 percent of all cameras used in Russia were made in China and sold under Russian brands.
China has built one of the most sophisticated domestic systems of digital control; it has also turned the export of digital infrastructure into part of its foreign policy via the Digital Silk Road, launched back in 2017. Through the initiative, China promotes digital infrastructure, technological cooperation, standards, and solutions for countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Formally, these projects are described as support for the digital transformation of developing states, but they deepen partners’ dependence on Chinese technologies and create channels for the spread of AI systems, especially mass-surveillance technologies.
Experts from the Carnegie Endowment, the European Parliament, and Freedom House agree that the main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest before it has even properly materialized. AI systems can help authorities detect early signals: unusual online activity, preparations, movement patterns, and links between activists.
All of this has, among other things, already been done in the digital Gulag that Moscow has built. As journalist Andrei Zakharov writes in his new book “Russian Cyberpunk,” Moscow authorities have been collecting comprehensive data on Muscovites since as early as 2014, and have been using AI to bring information from different agencies into a single database. After the 2021 protests, activists were arrested using facial recognition systems. According to Zakharov, in Moscow in 2023, there were already more than 220,000 video devices connected to a unified data storage and processing center.
Now, against the backdrop of sentences of ten-plus years for publishing an article in a foreign journal, for example, the sentences handed down in 2021 to people prosecuted after the so-called “Palace Case” seem small — but this was the first instance in which people in Russia were arrested as a result of video surveillance analysis. Police came to Yevgeny Yesenov’s apartment and arrested him the day after the rally; he became the first prisoner in the case and was sentenced to four years in a penal colony, though he was released on parole after a year and a half. While things like this happened in pre-war Russia, now, as a result of organized surveillance by the “smart city” system, anyone’s address can be found using their face.
After the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, people were arrested in the same way for anti-war graffiti or for setting fire to military enlistment offices — any forms of protest that had been captured and analyzed by the country’s AI surveillance system.
As T-Invariant writes, Russia is also developing AI for drones and cryptography at Moscow State University under the leadership of Putin’s daughter, using Chinese and American gray-market chips and open Western AI technologies. It is also sharing such technologies with China and North Korea.
China and Western Asia
Chinese participation in “smart city” projects in Western Asia is unfolding in a region where, according to the EIU Democracy Index for 2023, 16 out of 20 territories are classified as authoritarian regimes. These projects are most highly concentrated in the Gulf states: the UAE has 11 projects, while Saudi Arabia has seven. Outside this bloc, Turkey plays the most visible role with five projects, while the remaining projects are distributed among Algeria, Egypt, Iraq, Iran, Morocco, and Tunisia.
The latest Chinese concept of the “smart city,” from 2022, involves real-time information monitoring across virtually all aspects of urban life. This technology makes it possible to establish continuous real-time digital monitoring of a city, giving the government the ability to multiply its control over citizens.
China and Russia’s links with Iran
In February 2026, research by the civil society organization Article 19 found that the architecture of internet control in Iran relies heavily on Chinese technologies. The report said that China supplied Iran with facial recognition technologies, internet filtering equipment, and surveillance tools from companies such as Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision, Tiandy, as well as smaller Chinese suppliers.
At the same time, an investigation by Le Monde and Forbidden Stories showed that Iran acquired the Russian facial recognition system FindFace, developed by NtechLab, through Iranian intermediary companies. The software was resold to entities linked to the Iranian state, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Ministry of Intelligence.
As early as 2019, when Iranian women began receiving fines by mail for not wearing the hijab while in a car, citizens have been talking about their government’s use of digital surveillance. In December 2025, Iran and Russia signed a cooperation agreement in the fields of AI, cybersecurity, the digital economy, blockchain, fintech, and partnerships with the private sector.
Surveillance of people in authoritarian regimes is organized by both cameras and control of internet traffic. The Russian company Protei, headquartered in Jordan but rooted in St. Petersburg, has reportedly supported Iran’s efforts to introduce systems for interception, monitoring, and traffic management, as well as to integrate DPI into network architecture. Its clients include MTN Irancell, Iran’s largest telecom provider, as well as operators and government entities in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Kenya, Namibia, Qatar, and other countries.
Taraneh M., an artist living in Iran who was detained during the “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, said that in 2022 she had prepared for the possibility of arrest by securing her devices, deleting confidential information, and setting self-destruct timers for personal chats. Nevertheless, investigators presented her with a thick dossier of her social media posts, some of which dated back five years. Although she has been released, Taraneh is now afraid to speak on the phone lest she is being monitored.
The China-Russia relationship
Although AI development in China has surpassed Russia’s, cooperation exists in the supply of Chinese technologies, as well as scientific development.
In January 2025, on the heels of Russia’s attempts to create a network of AI alliances with BRICS and other non-Western partners, Vladimir Putin instructed the Russian government and Sberbank to deepen cooperation with China, especially with regard to AI “technological research and development.”
The immediate stimulus was sanctions, Russia’s access to advanced chips and AI equipment was restricted after its invasion of Ukraine, but its dependence on China has persisted in recent years. Supplies for new servers, for example, which Russia does not manufacture, came from China through intermediary firms.
As T-Invariant discovered, however, joint developments are being conducted in two areas: training AI for drones and mass surveillance of people. In November 2025, the creation of two joint laboratories was announced: one for nano-structured optoelectronic materials and devices, and another for AI algorithms and their applications.
North Korea gets involved
Russia and North Korea are cooperating in testing AI in military operations: North Korea supplies weapons that are tested in Russia’s war on Ukraine, and data that may improve North Korean systems, including AI-guided systems, is passed back to North Korea. In May 2026, North Korea tested high-precision cruise missiles and artillery systems with AI guidance.
According to analysts, “AI” likely refers to automatic target recognition and terminal-stage guidance, although the level of technological sophistication remains unclear.
Since late 2023, North Korea has supplied Russia with ballistic missiles and artillery rockets, and their use on the battlefield in Ukraine is believed to have given Pyongyang, and likely Russia, valuable operational data.
The China-Venezuela-Belarus triangle
In Venezuela, authoritarian digital control is being built through international supply chains. Regimes do not necessarily create such systems themselves. Instead, they buy cameras, servers, video analytics platforms, DPI systems, algorithms, and software, often from countries also experiencing digital authoritarianism.
China’s Dahua, despite being added to the U.S. Entity List in 2019 because of its involvement in repression in Xinjiang, retained access to the Venezuelan market and discussed the integration of AI into surveillance systems with the authorities. Possible participation by Huawei, ZTE, and China CAMC in projects is also mentioned, although their role remains unspecified.
Between 2021 and 2023, the Venezuelan interior ministry also held talks with the Belarusian company Synesis, which is under U.S. sanctions for technologies that Belarusian authorities used to identify and arrest protesters. The Kipod software offered to Venezuela included facial recognition; searches for specific people and routes; license plate recognition; detection of weapons, abandoned objects, smoke, and crowds; perimeter control; and monitoring of traffic violations.
Countries on the African continent
A 2026 Institute of Development Studies (IDS) report on surveillance in “smart cities” in Africa showed the spread of Chinese AI-surveillance systems in 11 countries, including Algeria, Egypt, Kenya, Rwanda, Senegal, and Zimbabwe.
Carnegie’s study on the global use of AI in human surveillance predicted that the adoption of such technologies in Africa is likely to grow. Chinese exports of surveillance systems are being used in authoritarian contexts — including in Uganda and Myanmar, often through companies such as Huawei, Hikvision, and Dahua.
As in Western Asia, China-Africa cooperation in AI may look like assistance in developing “smart cities,” but its repressive use is connected with control over citizens.
Central Asia included
Governments in Central Asia have actively purchased Chinese digital public-security systems. A report by the Caspian Policy Center says that in 2013, Tajikistan cooperated with Huawei to create a safe city surveillance system in Dushanbe worth about 22 million USD, largely financed by a Chinese loan.
Other publications note that Chinese companies occupy leading positions in “safe” and “smart city” projects across Eurasia, especially because the region offers relatively open markets for Chinese technologies.
Chinese censorship systems and related tools have also appeared in Kazakhstan, Pakistan, and Ethiopia, but cooperation between China and Central Asia mainly represents the export of AI surveillance technologies under the rhetoric of crime prevention.
What can be done?
Even supposedly democratic states have employed surveillance technologies to spy on their citizens. One of the most functional proposals to hinder the development of such authoritarian digital tools is to make Western technologies open source, and move digital strategies away from sovereignty and towards inclusion of the majority world : not as territories of extraction for the energy and water to run powerful data centers that serving Western AI models, but as actual participants in digital strategies and AI governance.
Such an approach would include sustainable development and practical concerns like agriculture, healthcare, education, transport, urban planning, adaptation to climate change, and many more human-centered priorities.
Written by Daria Dergacheva

items.content:
Jio All Set For Its Mega IPO
Reliance’s digital crown is heading down the Dalal Street. In what could be India’s biggest IPO yet, Jio Platforms has filed its RHP with SEBI for a ₹30,213 Cr listing. So, what does Jio Platforms’ IPO stack look like?
India’s Biggest IPO: Jio Platforms’ public issue, which consists entirely of a fresh issue of 27 Cr equity shares, will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23. The digital giant has set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 per share for its issue, which will value the company at a nifty ₹10.3 Lakh Cr.
Who Owns Jio? Reliance Industries holds 66.43% of the company, while big tech giants Meta and Google own 9.98% and 7.73%, respectively. Beyond the captable, Jio Platforms will use ₹27,500 Cr of the IPO proceeds to repay borrowings. The remaining ₹2,713 Cr will support corporate purposes, growth, capex, working capital and marketing.
The Number Game: Jio Platforms is stepping into D-Street with a profitable stack and robust top line growth.
Here is a quick look at Jio Platforms’ Q1 FY27 numbers:
Operating revenue rose 11.8% YoY to ₹39,173 Cr
Net profit jumped 9.2% YoY to ₹7,764 Cr
EBITDA improved 15.1% YoY to ₹20,865 Cr
Jio Mighty Scale: What works for the digital giant’s IPO is its massive subscriber base, nationwide 5G network and strong financial growth. On top of this, Jio’s expansion into AI, data centres and SaaS could unlock new revenue streams for the company, while the debt repayment will lower interest costs and strengthen the balance sheet. The issue’s record size and RIL’s backing could further support demand.
The Valuation Friction: Despite the tailwinds, Jio’s sky-high valuation could face pushback from public investors. With wireless subscriber growth plateauing, future earnings rely heavily on ARPU hikes that could lead to user churn. Additionally, high capex for satcom rollout and infrastructure upgrades could further squeeze margins and cash flows.
With the ball now in investors’ court, here is all about Jio Platforms gearing up for India’s biggest IPO till date…
From The Editor’s Desk
Zetwerk’s Anchor Haul
Ahead of the commencement of the bidding for its IPO today, the B2B manufacturing startup raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors. Zetwerk allotted 14.91 Cr shares to anchor investors at ₹151 apiece, the upper end of its IPO price band.
Zetwerk’s ₹5,012 Cr public issue comprises a fresh issue worth ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS component of up to 14.45 Cr shares. At the upper end of its ₹143-₹151 IPO price band, the public offering values the company at around ₹25,583 Cr.
Separately, defence tech startup Tonbo Imaging has also raised ₹255 Cr from 43 anchor investors ahead of the opening of its IPO. It has set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per share for its ₹852 Cr IPO, which consists entirely of an OFS of up to 1.22 Cr shares.
Groww’s Q2 Profit Run
The investment tech company’s consolidated net profit zoomed 54% YoY to ₹724.7 Cr in Q2 FY27. This came on the back of operating revenue rising 47% YoY to ₹1,501.5 Cr as well as healthy growth in margin trading and commodity derivatives verticals.
Consolidated EBITDA improved 60% YoY to ₹969 Cr in the quarter ended September 2026. However, expenses continued to bite and rose 28.5% YoY to ₹555.9 Cr in the quarter under review.
Going forward, the company expects businesses with lower penetration, such as MTF and commodity derivatives, to grow faster and contribute a larger share of its income in the coming quarters.
Scimplify Nets $25 Mn
The speciality chemical manufacturing startup has raised ₹238 Cr in a strategic funding round led by Hitachi Ventures to expand its R&D and manufacturing capabilities, enter new emerging categories and scale its agentic AI offering.
Founded in 2023, Scimplify offers end-to-end sourcing and manufacturing of speciality chemicals. It operates a network of more than 500 manufacturing partners and caters to more than 1,000 clients across 40 countries. It has raised $80 Mn to date.
Scimplify operates in the broader Indian deeptech sector, which continues to draw investor attention on the back of regulatory push, subsidies, a thriving talent pool and growing demand. The sector raised $290 Mn in Q3 2026, up 176% YoY.
Infotech Acquires Zluri
The IT advisory firm has acquired the Bengaluru-based SaaS startup for an undisclosed amount. Once the deal materialises, Zluri will operate as a standalone division within Infotech and will retain its product development and core engineering teams.
Founded in 2020, Zluri helps businesses track and manage all the digital tools their employees use. The startup claims to cater to over 250 enterprise clients globally and has raised more than $32 Mn in funding to date.
The deal is in line with an emerging trend of global companies acquiring Indian SaaS startups to expand their capabilities. Homegrown SaaS major Freshworks acquired Torii earlier this week, while Adobe acquired Peak XV-backed Rilo last month.
Traya Eyes ₹300 Cr
The haircare startup is in talks with Belgian VC giant Verlinvest to raise around $31 Mn. With the talks still in early stages, the proposed round could value the startup at up to ₹3,000 Cr and will include both primary and secondary components.
The funding talks come amid a sharp uptick in Traya’s top line. The startup is said to be currently clocking an annualised revenue rate of ₹900 Cr to ₹1,000 Cr. It has also been expanding its offline presence and operates more than 20 centres across India.
Founded in 2019, Traya combines hair assessment, recommendation algorithm and doctor approval to offer personalised hair treatment plans for customers. It reported a net loss of ₹22.5 Cr in FY25 against a revenue of ₹338.4 Cr.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
How EV91 Is Electrifying India’s Last-Mile Deliveries
India’s delivery economy is growing fast. But gig workers still face fragmented access to EVs, financing, charging, maintenance and fleet support. To solve this, EV91 is building an integrated electric mobility platform that connects riders, EVs and delivery businesses under one roof.
An Electric Ecosystem: Founded in 2023, EV91 initially used to supply electric two-wheelers to delivery workers. It has since expanded into EV subscriptions, fleet management, charging, battery swapping and rider support. With this, it is positioning itself as a full-stack platform for last-mile delivery.
Electrifying Last Mile: The startup’s rider app allows delivery partners to rent EVs, find delivery jobs and access charging and battery-swapping services. For aggregator platforms, the startup offers fleet management solutions and a steady supply of gig workers. EV91 currently operates in Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi-NCR and Mumbai.
Growing Steadily: The startup claims to have completed 10 Lakh orders in FY25, with more than 600 EVs and 1,000+ riders. EV91 is targeting the homegrown last-mile delivery market, which is projected to become a $5.5 Bn economy by 2030.
As delivery platforms seek cleaner and more reliable logistics, can EV91 build the backbone for India’s last-mile deliveries?

items.content: San Francisco: The Federal Reserve will probably need to increase short-term interest rates further to rein in too-high inflation, San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said on Wednesday, but she also signaled there's no need to do so at the US central bank's October 27-28 meeting."We are more likely than not to need additional adjustments, but the timing of those adjustments to me is something we're still deliberating," Daly told Reuters in an interview. "I don't feel urgent that we have to decide with a limited set of information. I think we have the time that we need."Also Read: US inflation worsened last month to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections nearSeveral of Daly's colleagues have also signaled in recent weeks that the Fed is unlikely to raise rates this month. The Fed's policy rate is in the 3.75%-4.00% range, and longer-term borrowing costs are even higher, with some -- like 7.5% mortgage rates -- putting an increasingly obvious damper on demand in some parts of the economy.Daly said she feels financial markets understand the Fed's "reaction function," pointing to how traders responded to data earlier on Wednesday that showed consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.7% in the 12 months through September, a bit faster than economists had anticipated. The Fed targets 2% inflation by a different, but related, measure.Though the initial reaction was "robust," she said -- rate futures traders quickly piled into bets on an October Fed rate hike -- investors "calmed" after parsing through the data. Higher gasoline prices drove the overall increase, and underlying inflation, while still sticky, did not take a sharp turn upward."Definitely this data point suggests that the risk to inflation remains elevated," Daly said. "The risk to inflation has gone up more, but risks are not realities, and reacting on risk when you have time to make a good decision, to me, feels imprudent."Also Read: More expensive gas, semiconductors likely pushed up inflation in US last monthDaly said that the labor market's continued stability gives the Fed room to focus on price stability.But, she said, "why force urgency when you don't need to have urgency? Why not take the time to be thoughtful and deliberate? And we have more meetings ahead of us."Financial market pricing now puts about a 40% chance of a second straight Fed rate hike at the central bank's next meeting, up from before the data but no longer seeing an increase as the most likely outcome.

items.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri
As the number of death row inmates in the country continues to swell, stakeholders in the justice sector and concerned foreign missions have nonetheless commended Nigeria for going ten consecutive years without a state execution.
The Nigerian Correctional Service (NCoS) recently disclosed that 4,329 persons are currently awaiting execution in various custodial facilities across the federation.
Of this number, more than 82 are women.
In its presentation at an event commemorating the 2026 World Day Against the Death Penalty, the NCoS acknowledged the need for national action on capital punishment, a process it said would ultimately require a constitutional amendment.
“Everybody in our custody has a story, and the way we treat those stories says a lot about our society,” the Comptroller-General of the NCoS, Mr. Sylvester Nwakuche, stated.
The World Day Against the Death Penalty is observed every year on October 10.
This year’s event was jointly organised by the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) and Avocats Sans Frontières France (also known as Lawyers Without Borders), with support from the Australian High Commission in Nigeria, the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany, and the Embassy of Spain.
A key outcome of the programme was participants’ unanimous call for a moratorium on executions and for the commutation of existing death sentences to life imprisonment.
The last execution in Nigeria took place on December 23, 2016, when three death row inmates were put to death in Benin, Edo State.
Unsurprisingly, the executions drew varied reactions, with Amnesty International condemning them in strong terms.
It noted that they were carried out even though one of the inmates, Apostle Igene, was sentenced to death in 1997 by a military tribunal and was never afforded the opportunity to appeal the verdict.
The Executive Secretary of the NHRC, Dr. Tony Ojukwu, SAN, observed that, under Nigerian law, capital punishment presents a constitutional duality.
He stated that whereas Section 33(1) of the 1999 Constitution (as amended) protects the right to life, it also contains an explicit exception for court-ordered executions.
On the other hand, Section 34(1)(a) guarantees the right to human dignity and protection against inhuman or degrading treatment.
According to Ojukwu, the Supreme Court affirmed the constitutional validity of capital punishment in Onuoha Kalu v. The State (1998) 13 NWLR (Pt. 583) 531, reaffirmed in Joseph Amoshima v. The State (2011) 14 NWLR (Pt. 1268) 547.
“However, the constitutionality of the penalty does not dilute the non-negotiable requirement of fair trial guarantees under Section 36.
Systemic issues, such as inadequate pro bono defence, forced confessions, and pre-trial delays, undermine procedural justice,” he added.
Ojukwu, SAN, argued that Nigeria, having achieved 10 consecutive years without a state execution, has satisfied the international standard for a de facto moratorium.
“Yet, mandatory death sentencing continues, leaving over 3,000 individuals on prolonged death row detention.
“To resolve this limbo, statutory and executive mechanisms exist. Section 12(2)(c) of the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, 2019 authorises the commutation of death sentences for inmates who have exhausted appeals and remain unexecuted after a specified period.
“Furthermore, State Governors possess explicit constitutional powers of prerogative of mercy under Section 212 (and the President under Section 175) of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.
“Pursuant to Section 5 of the NHRC (Amendment) Act 2010, the Commission calls for three immediate policy steps:
Transition Nigeria’s 10-year pause into an official executive moratorium on executions.
“Urge State Governors to systematically invoke Section 212 of the Constitution and Section 12(2)(c) of the NCoS Act to commute death sentences to life imprisonment.
“Re-evaluate mandatory death penalty statutes to allow judges to weigh mitigating circumstances and systemic vulnerabilities during sentencing,” he added.
Prior to 1990, only one country in Africa, Cape Verde, had abolished the death penalty.
However, of the 55 African Union member-states, 28 have now abolished it in law, with Zimbabwe the latest to join the list.
While 20 countries apply a long-term moratorium on executions, seven nations, including Nigeria, still retain and use capital punishment.
German Ambassador to Nigeria, H.E. Stefan Rössel, said that although the death penalty remains part of Nigerian law, the 10-year mark since the last execution is an important milestone that deserves to be celebrated.
Drawing on his country’s experience, the Ambassador said: “Germany opposes the death penalty unconditionally. Working towards its permanent abolition is a pillar of our human rights policy.
“We believe that the right to life is universal, as laid out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and must not be denied by law.
“The last execution on German soil took place in 1981. Today, Article 102 of the German constitution states simply: ‘Capital punishment is abolished.'”
He said the death penalty raises important questions about justice, human dignity and the protection of human life.
“We recognise the deep suffering caused by serious crimes. The grief of victims and their families must be acknowledged, and their need for justice, truth and support deserves our continued attention.
“At the same time, every justice system must protect human rights and guard against the possibility of error. A death sentence is irreversible. If a conviction is later found to be wrong, the consequences cannot be undone.
“We must also not forget that those sentenced to death often spend years, sometimes decades, behind bars before being executed. At the same time, our understanding of crimes and justice continuously evolves.
“For instance, we have gained a much more nuanced understanding of mental illness in recent decades, and how that might affect the way we judge the circumstances of a crime committed many years ago.
“Ultimately, we need to ask ourselves: do we want to live in a society in which the state is tasked to take a human life?” he queried.
The German Ambassador concluded by recognising that the issue of the death penalty is complex, involving legal questions, public concerns and the needs of victims and their families.
“We hope that Nigeria’s approaching 10-year milestone can be a source of pride. We believe: not using this ultimate form of punishment is a sign of strength, not weakness,” he added.
Likewise, the Australian High Commissioner to Nigeria, H.E. Ms. Leilani Bin-Juda, PSM, described the 10-year non-execution achieved by Nigeria as “a significant milestone that calls for a reflection of how far Nigeria has come and the next step to be taken.”
She urged the country to build on the achievement and chart a way forward, insisting that capital punishment is a cruel, inhumane and degrading punishment that has no place in any modern justice system.
For his part, the Ambassador of Spain to Nigeria, H.E. Félix Costales Artieda, categorically opposed the use of the death penalty “under any circumstance and for any crime.”
He insisted that life is an inalienable fundamental right that no state has the right to take, stressing that there is no evidence that capital punishment has helped to reduce crime anywhere in the world.
The Ambassador noted that in the United States alone, 130 persons sentenced to death have been found innocent and released from death row since 1973.
He urged Nigeria to take appropriate measures to commute the sentences of those already facing the death penalty.
The Country Head of ASF France, Angela Uwandu Uzoma-Iwuchukwu, said the organisation, on the basis of its conviction that the right to life is sacrosanct, had embarked on a series of projects aimed at highlighting the need for Nigeria to do away with capital punishment.
She said it has since represented over 1,000 persons through its Right To Life project.
Referencing the case of Arthur Angel, who spent 16 years in prison, 10 of them on death row at Enugu Prison, before his release in 2000, she argued that lapses in a justice system run by humans cannot be overlooked.
“Arthur Angel spent 16 years in jail for a crime he did not commit,” she noted, insisting the death penalty is “discriminatory as it targets the weakest in the society.
“There are people who cannot afford the services of good lawyers. We all know that the quality of defence provided for a defendant matters so much.
“A lot of those on death row in Nigeria were represented by inexperienced lawyers, some of whom were National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members.
“A mistake made at the trial stage may not be corrected at the appeal stage,” the ASF Country Head added.
She also referenced a recent case involving a poor farmer, Sunday Jackson, who was sentenced to death for self-defence but later pardoned by the Adamawa State Government.
For now, Nigeria’s position is a contradiction: a death penalty on the books, thousands waiting under sentence, and no one carrying it out.
Hopes are high that the 10-year milestone will become a step towards the abolition of capital punishment in the country.
